scenarios.name: Customer Support Resolution Agent
scenarios.desc: An Agent SDK agent resolves support tickets end to end. It looks up customers and orders through MCP tools, issues refunds within policy, escalates to human agents, and keeps state across long multi-turn conversations.

scenarios.name: Code Generation with Claude Code
scenarios.desc: A product team uses Claude Code to build and change features in a large production codebase, relying on CLAUDE.md, plan mode, custom skills and commands, and tests as the feedback loop.

scenarios.name: Multi-Agent Research System
scenarios.desc: A coordinator agent breaks research questions into parts, delegates them to search, analysis and synthesis subagents, and assembles a cited report.

scenarios.name: Developer Productivity with Claude
scenarios.desc: A platform team gives engineers Claude-powered tooling: shared team configuration, MCP servers for internal systems, custom tools, and help exploring large, unfamiliar codebases.

scenarios.name: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenarios.desc: Claude Code runs non-interactively in the CI/CD pipeline to review pull requests, generate tests and propose fixes, under tight permission, reliability and cost constraints.

scenarios.name: Structured Data Extraction
scenarios.desc: A pipeline extracts structured fields from invoices, contracts and forms using JSON schemas, validation and retry loops, batch processing, and human review of uncertain results.

lessons.title: Translate business problems into Claude solutions
lessons.summary: The exam gives you a vague business ask and checks that you turn it into a measurable problem before choosing technology: who has the pain, what success looks like in numbers, which part is genuinely language work for Claude, and which parts belong to deterministic code or people.
keyPoints: Start from the **business outcome and baseline**, not the model: what is slow, costly or error-prone today, how it is measured now (handle time, backlog, error rate, cost per case), and what change would count as success.

Good success criteria are **specific, measurable, achievable and relevant** (Anthropic's "Define success criteria" guide). Most use cases need several dimensions at once: task fidelity, consistency, tone, privacy handling, context use, latency and price.

Find the **Claude-shaped part** of the problem: reading, classifying, extracting, summarising, drafting or reasoning over unstructured language. Exact arithmetic, lookups, policy rules and transactions stay in deterministic systems that Claude calls or feeds.
Decide **who decides**. Where errors are costly, irreversible or regulated, Claude drafts or recommends and a person approves; autonomy is earned with measured accuracy, not granted up front.

Choose the **simplest shape that meets the criteria**: one well-prompted call, then a workflow, and only then an agent ("Building effective agents"). Agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance, so the value of the task must pay for it.

Check the **inputs exist**: the documents, records and tools Claude will need, their quality, access rights and residency constraints. A great prompt can't compensate for missing or wrong source data.
**Prove feasibility cheaply**: a small eval set from real historical cases (with known outcomes) and a prototype measured against it, before committing to a platform or a large build.

Pick the surface from the users and the integration need: a team with no developers may need only claude.ai Projects; output that must flow into a system of record needs an API integration with structured output and validation.
traps: Jumping to an architecture ("build a multi-agent platform") before the problem, baseline and success metric are agreed.
Using Claude for a step that has a correct deterministic answer (tax rules, totals, eligibility thresholds) instead of calling code.
Accepting "fully autonomous" as a requirement when the action is irreversible and there is no way to catch errors.
Success defined as adoption or number of AI calls rather than a business outcome against a baseline.
Assuming the data needed is available and clean without checking.

code.src:
Problem framing card
  Pain today:   claims adjusters spend ~35 min/claim reading attachments
  Baseline:     35 min, 4.1% rework rate, 2-day backlog
  Claude part:  read attachments, extract facts, draft summary with citations
  Code part:    policy lookup, coverage rules, payout calculation
  Human part:   coverage decision, payout approval
  Success:      <=15 min/claim, rework <=4.1%, 0 uncited facts in 200-case eval
  Constraint:   PII stays in-region; decisions auditable

lessons.drill: Take one vague request you've heard ("use AI for onboarding"). In 15 minutes fill the framing card above: pain, baseline numbers, which steps are language work, which are code, who approves, and three measurable success criteria. Then list the data sources you'd need and who owns them.

lessons.title: Design end-to-end architectures
lessons.summary: Questions follow a request from input to output and back: how data enters and is validated, where state lives, how long jobs are handled, how outputs are checked before they reach users or systems, and how real-world feedback flows back into evals and prompts.
keyPoints: **Input**: validate and normalise before the model sees it (file type, size, required fields, PII handling); attach the identifiers you'll need to trace the request end to end.
**State**: the Messages API is stateless; the application owns conversation history and job state. With several stateless servers, keep history in a shared store and rebuild `messages` per request.

**Processing**: match the call style to the latency need: interactive requests stream; long jobs run asynchronously (`202 Accepted` + job ID + polling or callback); bulk, non-urgent work goes to the Batch API.

**Reliability**: at-least-once delivery and client retries mean duplicates; use idempotency keys, dedupe tables and upserts. Persist results as they finish so one failure doesn't discard completed work.
**Output**: validate in code before anything is written or sent: schema validation, business-rule checks (totals add up, IDs exist), and a routing rule to human review on failure.
**Handoffs between stages** use typed contracts (fields, units, nulls, source references), not prose summaries.

**Feedback loop**: capture user ratings, reviewer corrections and downstream outcomes with the inputs and versions that produced them; turn them into new eval cases and use them to drive prompt, retrieval or model changes, re-run evals before releasing.
Version prompts, models and retrieval indexes together and log them per request, so a quality change can be traced to a specific release.
traps: Treating reviewer corrections as a one-off fix instead of a data source for the eval set.
Holding long model calls inside a synchronous HTTP request behind a load balancer timeout.
Retrying non-idempotent side effects (emails, payments) without a deduplication key.
Relying on sticky sessions or server memory for conversation state.
Writing model output straight to a system of record with no validation step.

code.src:
input -> validate/normalise -> enqueue(job_id, idempotency_key)
      -> worker: retrieve context -> Claude (structured output)
      -> code checks (schema, business rules) -- fail --> human review queue
      -> write (upsert) -> notify user
feedback: user rating + reviewer edits + outcome
      -> stored with prompt/model/index versions -> new eval cases
      -> change prompt/retrieval -> re-run evals -> staged release

lessons.drill: Draw the pipeline for one feature you run (or would build) as boxes: input, validation, state store, model call, output checks, write, feedback capture. For each box write its failure mode and the control that handles it. Mark where a reviewer correction becomes an eval case.

lessons.title: Select architectural patterns
lessons.summary: The exam names the patterns from "Building effective agents" (augmented LLM, prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer, agents) and asks which fits a scenario. The default right answer is the simplest pattern that meets the requirement; autonomy must be justified.
keyPoints: **Workflow vs agent**: workflows run LLMs and tools through predefined code paths; agents let the LLM direct its own process and tool use. Workflows give predictability and auditability; agents give flexibility when the path can't be known in advance.
**Augmented LLM**: the building block, a model with retrieval, tools and memory. Many business problems need nothing more than one augmented call.
**Prompt chaining**: fixed sequence of steps with programmatic gates between them; trades latency for accuracy by making each step easier. Retry the failing step, not the whole chain.
**Routing**: classify, then dispatch to a specialised prompt, tool set or model (including cheaper models for simple cases). Known categories mean routing, not a coordinator agent.
**Parallelization**: *sectioning* runs independent subtasks at once (e.g. a guardrail check alongside the response); *voting* runs the same task several times for confidence or recall.

**Orchestrator-workers**: a central model decides subtasks at runtime (unknown number of files or sources), delegates and synthesises. **Evaluator-optimizer**: a generator plus an evaluator with explicit criteria and an iteration cap, used when feedback measurably improves output.

**Agents** fit open-ended tasks with ground truth from the environment (tests, tool results), clear success criteria and a way to catch errors (tests, review, rollback). Regulated fixed processes with audit needs stay workflows.
Frameworks can help, but keep the actual prompts and tool calls visible; start with direct API use and add abstraction only when it earns its place.
traps: An agent or multi-agent design for a fixed, well-specified, high-volume process.
Calling parallel voting "orchestrator-workers" (or vice versa): the orchestrator decides subtasks dynamically.
Evaluator-optimizer with a vague rubric or no cap.
Picking a framework whose abstractions hide the prompts you need to debug.

code.src:
Can the steps be fixed in advance?  yes -> workflow
   one step enough?                yes -> single augmented call
   ordered steps w/ checks?        -> prompt chaining + gates
   known input categories?         -> routing
   independent parts / need votes? -> parallelization
   subtasks known only at runtime? -> orchestrator-workers
   clear rubric, feedback helps?   -> evaluator-optimizer (capped)
Open-ended, verifiable, errors recoverable -> agent (with caps)

docs.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

lessons.drill: List five Claude features you know of (yours or public examples). For each, name the pattern, say what would break if you used the next more autonomous pattern, and what would break with the next simpler one.

lessons.title: Design multi-agent systems and orchestration
lessons.summary: Expect coordinator/subagent scenarios: when multiple agents pay off, what the coordinator owns, how to brief workers, how results and failures flow back, and how to keep cost and runtime bounded.
keyPoints: Multi-agent systems help most on **breadth-first, parallelizable** work that exceeds one context window. Anthropic reports agents use about 4x the tokens of chat and multi-agent systems about 15x, so the task's value must justify the spend.
Poor fits: tasks needing **shared context** or with many dependencies between agents; most coding tasks have fewer truly parallel parts than research.

The **coordinator** owns decomposition, dependency ordering, routing, and synthesis (including resolving contradictions). Workers do narrow execution. Information between workers flows through the coordinator.
A non-fork subagent starts with a **fresh context**: the brief must carry the objective, scope boundaries, sources/tools to use, exclusions and the output format. Only its final message returns.
Ask workers for **condensed, structured returns** (findings with sources, gaps, errors with category and partial results), not transcripts.
Run independent subtasks in **parallel**; run dependent ones in sequence and pass outputs in the next brief.
**Scale effort to the query** in the coordinator's prompt and enforce turn and spend caps in the harness. Use cheaper models for reading-heavy workers and capable ones for planning and synthesis.

**Resilience**: transient errors retried locally in the worker's tool layer; persistent failures reported with context; checkpoint the plan and completed results so a crash resumes instead of restarting.
traps: Spawning many subagents for a small, coupled change; one agent is faster and cheaper.
Letting workers message each other to share intermediate results.
Briefs that reference "what we discussed": the subagent never saw it.
Treating any worker failure as fatal instead of synthesising with a coverage note.
Restricting a worker's tools by instruction rather than by its tool list.

code.src:
Brief to worker 3 of 5
  Objective: EU lithium-refining capacity announced since 2024
  Scope: commercial plants only; exclude pilots; EU-27
  Sources: company filings, government statistics; no vendor blogs
  Return JSON: {claims:[{text, source_url, pub_date}], gaps:[], errors:[{category, retryable}]}
  Budget: <= 15 tool calls

docs.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

lessons.drill: Write the coordinator plan and one worker brief for "Compare the five largest cloud providers' EU data-residency options". Mark which stages run in parallel, what each worker returns, the caps, and what the coordinator does if one worker fails.

lessons.title: Apply decomposition techniques
lessons.summary: Questions ask how to split a hard problem so each piece is reliable and the pieces still add up: fixed chains versus dynamic plans, per-item then cross-item passes, moving deterministic parts to code, choosing granularity, and making each unit verifiable.
keyPoints: **Fixed decomposition** (prompt chain) when the steps are known; **dynamic decomposition** (orchestrator plans per input) when they depend on the input. Example decompositions for each question type teach the planner better than "be complete".
Map the problem's **dimensions first**, then check subtasks against the map: non-overlapping scope and full coverage.
**Per-item then cross-item**: extract or review each document/file separately, then run a cross-item pass for contradictions, precedence (later amendments win) and interfaces between modules.
**Split by kind of work**: let Claude extract and interpret; let code do arithmetic, lookups, joins and rule checks; feed computed results back for explanation.

**Granularity**: too coarse misses detail; too fine breaks coherence (fields that must agree, like line items and totals, belong in one call) and multiplies cost. Group things that are checked together.
**Map the territory before deep dives**: on large codebases or corpora, survey structure first (search, indexes), then explore subsystems in isolated contexts and synthesise.
**Make each unit verifiable**: small units with their own acceptance check (test, schema, reconciliation) and a progress record, so failures are retried locally and long jobs can resume.
Sequence dependencies: settle the shared contract (schema, interface) first, then fan out the independent work.
traps: One call over everything because "the context window is big enough".
One call per field, which loses cross-field consistency.
Independent per-document passes with no reconciliation step.
Asking the model to compute totals that code can compute exactly.
A long single agent run with no checkpoints or per-unit checks.

code.src:
Financial ratio review, 200 line items
 1. Claude: extract line items -> JSON (schema-validated)
 2. Code:   compute ratios, flag thresholds (exact)
 3. Claude: explain flagged ratios with citations to source pages
 4. Code:   check every cited figure exists in step-1 output

docs.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

lessons.drill: Take a task that currently fails in one big prompt. Split it into units, label each unit Claude / code / human, write the acceptance check for each unit, and identify the one cross-unit pass you need.

lessons.title: Align solutions to business value pillars
lessons.summary: The exam checks that you can tie an architecture to the value it is supposed to deliver (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs), measure that value against a baseline, and choose cost and latency levers that keep quality above the agreed bar.
keyPoints: **Efficiency** does the existing process faster or cheaper; **productivity** raises output per person (time saved, cases per hour); **transformation** changes what the business can offer or how it works (a new service, a process that wasn't feasible before). Name which pillar a proposal targets and measure that.
**Baseline first**: capture today's handle time, error rate, backlog and cost per case before the pilot, otherwise no value can be shown.
Measure **cost per business outcome** (per resolved ticket, per processed claim) including retries, escalations and human review, not just cost per token or per call.

**Cost levers** that keep the model's answers the same: prompt caching for a repeated static prefix (cache reads are billed at a fraction of base input, 0.1x on most models), the Batch API for non-urgent bulk work (50% off input and output), shorter prompts and outputs.

**Cost levers that need evals**: routing easy cases to a smaller tier, lowering effort, an orchestrator with cheaper workers. Tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models. Adopt only if the change beats the single model across the cost-quality curve on your evals.
**Multi-agent cost**: about 15x the tokens of chat in Anthropic's research system, so reserve it for high-value tasks where it measurably helps.

**Performance SLAs** come from measured evals and load tests: percentile latency (p95/p99, and time to first token for streamed chat), a quality threshold on a fixed eval set, availability and the behaviour on overload or failure (fallback, queueing, human handoff). Never promise 100% accuracy.
Engineer for correctness first, then reduce latency (Anthropic's latency guide): model choice, shorter prompts/outputs, streaming. Streaming improves perceived latency, not total generation time.
traps: Promising an SLA (latency or accuracy) before measuring it on representative traffic.
Using average latency in an SLA; tails matter to users.
Choosing the cheapest model by price per token without checking cost per resolved outcome.
Reporting adoption or call volume as business value.
Using the Batch API for an interactive feature, or a frontier model for every trivial request.

code.src:
Value scorecard: invoice exceptions (productivity pillar)
  Baseline:  12 min/exception, 3.0% error, $6.10/exception (labour)
  Pilot:     5 min/exception, 2.6% error, $2.40 labour + $0.35 model
  SLA:       p95 draft <= 20 s; eval accuracy >= 97% on 400 cases;
             on API overload -> queue, notify, no silent drop
  Review:    monthly, eval re-run on each prompt/model change

lessons.drill: For one Claude feature, write a value scorecard: pillar, baseline metrics, target metrics, cost per outcome (model + human review), and a draft SLA. Then list which two cost levers you'd try first and which eval would prove they don't hurt quality.

lessons.title: Select Claude models on trade-offs
lessons.summary: The exam tests whether you choose a model tier (and effort level) from measured quality, latency and cost per completed task on your own eval, rather than from price lists, benchmarks or 'biggest to be safe'. It also tests lifecycle decisions: pinning, deprecation notices and multi-model designs that only pay off in specific workload shapes.
keyPoints: **Tier heuristics**: Haiku-class for high-volume, latency-sensitive, checkable work (classification, routing, extraction, simple subagents); Sonnet-class for a balanced everyday default; Opus-class for complex reasoning and long-horizon agentic coding; the top frontier tier only when evals at high effort still fall short.

**Two starting strategies** (Anthropic's model-selection guide): *efficiency-first* (start small, test, upgrade only for proven capability gaps; suits prototypes, tight latency, high-volume simple tasks) or *capability-first* (start with the strongest model, optimise prompts, then lower effort or step down tiers as the workflow matures; suits complex reasoning where accuracy outweighs cost).

**Effort is often a better lever than switching models**: sweep `output_config.effort` on the current model first. A larger model at lower effort can beat a smaller model at higher effort on cost per solved task. Defaults differ by model, so set effort explicitly and re-sweep after a migration.

**Decide on cost per completed task**, not per token: (cost per attempt / success rate) + downstream cost of failures (rework, escalations, refunds). The bill is usually decided by the tasks the cheaper model fails.

**Multi-model designs must beat the single model's whole score-vs-spend curve.** Orchestrator + cheaper workers pays off when work fans out across genuinely independent items, especially more than one context window of it; for one dependent chain that fits in one context, the orchestrator's model alone at lower effort did better in Anthropic's measurements. An executor-escalates-to-advisor design helps only when the executor actually consults the advisor.
**Choose the model per route or per conversation, not per turn**: caches are model-scoped, so switching models mid-conversation re-reads the whole history uncached.

**Lifecycle**: models move Active → Legacy → Deprecated → Retired; requests to retired models fail. Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice before retiring publicly released models, and the Console usage export breaks usage down by API key and model so you can find every caller. Partner platforms (Bedrock, Google-managed Vertex) set their own retirement schedules.

**Pin production to a specific model ID**, upgrade deliberately: run your eval suite on the replacement, fix breaking request changes, re-baseline token counts, re-tune effort, then roll out gradually (shadow or canary).

**Check feature and data-handling fit per model and platform before committing**: capabilities, context/output limits and feature availability (and eligibility for arrangements such as zero data retention) vary by model, feature and platform. Read the models overview and feature pages; query the Models API for live capability data.
traps: Choosing the most capable tier 'to be safe' for simple high-volume routing, or the cheapest tier for deep synthesis without an eval.
Building a small-model/large-model cascade before measuring the single model at lower effort.
Per-message model routing inside one conversation: every switch forfeits the prompt cache.
Ranking models by per-token price or public benchmarks instead of your own eval's cost per solved task.
Ignoring a deprecation notice until the retirement date, or switching all traffic to the replacement without running evals.
lessons.drill: Take one production route and 30 labelled real requests. Run them on two tiers at two effort levels each (four configurations). Record pass rate, p50/p95 latency and total cost from `usage`. Compute cost per completed task including an assumed cost per failure, and write a one-paragraph decision record naming the configuration you would ship and the trigger that would make you revisit it.

lessons.title: Design system prompts, templates and guardrails
lessons.summary: Expect questions on what belongs in a system prompt versus the user turn or code, how to build reusable templates that separate fixed instructions from variable input, and where prompt-level guardrails stop and deterministic controls must take over. The best answer usually pairs a clear, explained prompt with a code-level control for anything that must never happen.
keyPoints: **System prompt = role, standing rules, context and output contract.** Even one role sentence focuses tone and expertise. Be clear and direct: if a colleague with minimal context would be confused, Claude will be too.

**Give the why**: a rule with its reason ('the output is read aloud by a TTS engine, so never use ellipses') generalises to cases the rule didn't list. Define observable criteria instead of vague qualifiers ('be careful', 'only important issues').

**Templates**: keep a fixed, versioned instruction block and inject variable data through clearly named slots (for example `{{customer_record}}`), wrapped in XML tags such as `<instructions>`, `<context>`, `<document>`, `<input>` so instructions and data never blur. Put the stable part first so it can be cached.

**Untrusted content is data, not instructions**: deliver retrieved or user-supplied text in `tool_result` blocks or tagged user content, never interpolated into `system` (that gives attacker text operator authority). State in the system prompt that such content is data.

**Prompt wording is not an enforcement boundary.** Refund ceilings, data-access rules and mandatory steps belong in code: tool gating, schema validation, permission checks, hooks, human approval. Prompts improve judgment; code guarantees.

**Format guarantees** come from structured outputs (`output_config.format`) or strict tool schemas, not from begging for JSON. Prefilling the final assistant turn is rejected on current models; use structured outputs or a direct instruction instead.

**Calibrate tone**: current models follow instructions closely, so old 'CRITICAL: you MUST ALWAYS' emphasis causes over-triggering. Use normal phrasing and say *when* a behaviour applies. Tell Claude what to do rather than what not to do.
**Layered guardrails** for risky inputs: a lightweight pre-screen (a small, fast model classifying input), clear system-prompt policy, output validation, and monitoring with escalation to humans.
**Operator instructions mid-conversation**: on supporting models, append a `role: "system"` message to `messages` rather than editing the top-level `system`, which keeps the cached prefix intact.
**Version and test prompts like code**: store templates in source control, change one thing at a time, and gate releases on an eval set.
traps: Fixing a policy breach by adding 'NEVER do X' in capitals instead of a code-level control.
Concatenating retrieved web or email text into the system prompt 'so it gets more attention'.
Carrying a JSON prefill into a current model and getting a 400.
Writing a long list of prohibitions with no reasons or examples, then seeing inconsistent edge-case behaviour.
Editing the top-level system prompt per turn (for example a timestamp), silently breaking caching for every request.

code.src:
SYSTEM = [{
  "type": "text",
  "text": open("prompts/claims_v7.md").read(),  # fixed, versioned
  "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
}]
user = f"<claim>\n{claim_json}\n</claim>\nAssess this claim."
resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=2000,
    system=SYSTEM, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user}],
    output_config={"format": CLAIM_SCHEMA})

lessons.drill: Take an existing production prompt and split it into: (1) a fixed system block with role, rules and their reasons; (2) tagged variable slots; (3) a list of rules that must never be violated. For each item in (3), name the code control (validation, tool gating, approval step) that will enforce it, then delete any shouting from the prompt and rerun your eval.

lessons.title: Apply zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought
lessons.summary: The exam asks which technique fixes a given failure: unclear instructions (zero-shot clarity), inconsistent format or borderline judgments (few-shot), or multi-step reasoning errors (thinking and effort, or explicit reasoning when thinking is off). It also tests when to split work into a prompt chain.
keyPoints: **Zero-shot** is instructions only. Start here with clear goals, audience, constraints and success criteria; most failures of zero-shot prompts are missing context, not missing technique.

**Few-shot (multishot)** is one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure. Anthropic suggests **3–5** relevant, **diverse** examples wrapped in `<example>` tags inside `<examples>`, covering edge cases (missing field, 'other' class, no findings).

Claude copies examples closely: near-identical examples get their length and phrasing copied onto very different inputs. Vary surface form and pair **contrastive** examples near the decision boundary to cut false positives.

**Reasoning on current models**: adaptive thinking plus the `effort` setting is the main control. Prefer general instructions ('think thoroughly about the trade-offs') over a hand-written step-by-step plan; Claude's reasoning often exceeds what you would prescribe.
**Worked examples shape thinking**: present each as problem, method, answer, and Claude applies the method in its own thinking.

**Manual chain-of-thought is the fallback when thinking is off**: ask Claude to reason before answering and put the final answer in `<answer>` tags you can extract. Reasoning must come *before* the verdict, because tokens already emitted condition what follows.
**Self-check**: appending 'before you finish, verify your answer against [criteria]' catches errors, especially in code and math.

**Prompt chaining** (separate calls) is still useful when you need to inspect, log or branch on intermediate outputs, or enforce a fixed pipeline; the common pattern is draft → review against criteria → refine.
**Long inputs**: documents at the top, query and instructions at the end; ask Claude to extract relevant quotes first, then answer from them.
Prove a technique change with an eval set, multiple trials per case, not by eyeballing one run.
traps: Adding paragraphs of rules for an ambiguity that two contrasting examples would settle.
Five examples from the same template: the model copies their structure onto every input.
Asking for the verdict first and the justification after, then trusting the justification.
Writing an elaborate prescriptive reasoning script when adaptive thinking at a higher effort would do better.
Examples whose output format contradicts the stated schema: the model follows the examples.
lessons.drill: Pick a classification prompt with a known error cluster. Run it zero-shot on 40 labelled cases. Add three diverse examples including two contrastive boundary cases and rerun. Then try a higher effort level instead of examples. Compare accuracy and cost for all three and note which lever fixed which errors.

lessons.title: Optimise context windows and token usage
lessons.summary: Questions present an agent or long conversation that degrades, overruns the window or costs too much, and ask for the root-cause fix: fewer, higher-signal tokens through just-in-time retrieval, trimmed tool output, context editing, compaction, persistent memory or subagent isolation, rather than a bigger window or a bigger model.
keyPoints: **Context is a finite attention budget.** Recall of any one detail degrades as total tokens grow (context rot), well before the hard limit. Aim for the smallest set of high-signal tokens; a larger window is not a fix.

**Everything shares the window**: tool definitions + system + messages + generated output (including thinking). Measure with `messages.count_tokens` for the target model, and read `usage` (input, cache creation, cache read, output) rather than guessing from characters. Tokenizers can differ between model generations.

**Trim at the source**: tools should return only the fields the agent needs, support filtering and pagination, and truncate with a hint on how to get more. A raw 40k-token payload is paid for on every later turn.

**Just-in-time retrieval**: hold lightweight references (paths, IDs, queries) and load content through tools when needed; hybrid designs load a small always-on brief (for example CLAUDE.md) and search for the rest.

**Context editing** clears stale tool results (and optionally thinking) server-side with a placeholder; **compaction** summarises earlier history into a compaction block when input approaches a trigger. Append the full `response.content` so the compaction block is kept. **Memory** (a memory tool or notes file) persists state across sessions.
Each clear or compaction changes the prefix and invalidates the cache from that point, so clear in larger chunks rather than small frequent ones.
**Summaries are lossy**: exact amounts, IDs, dates and commitments disappear first. Keep a structured case-facts block, updated by code from tool results, outside the summarised history.
**Subagents isolate noisy work**: each explores in its own window and returns a condensed result, keeping the lead agent's context small.
**Tool definitions cost tokens too**: with large tool catalogues, defer loading and let Claude discover tools via tool search; in Claude Code, `/context` shows what fills the window.
**Output side**: `max_tokens` caps output only; lowering it to save money truncates answers. Control spend with effort, concise-output instructions and structured outputs.
traps: 'The window is huge, so load everything' — context rot makes stuffing worse even when it fits.
Confusing context editing (drops old tool results) with compaction (writes a summary) or with cross-session memory.
Appending only the response text after compaction, losing the compaction block.
Asking the model to 'ignore irrelevant fields' in a huge tool result instead of filtering in the tool.
Raising `max_tokens` to fit a bigger document — it limits output, not input.

docs.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

lessons.drill: Log `usage` for every turn of one long agent run and plot input tokens per turn. Identify the top three contributors (a tool payload, repeated documents, tool definitions). Fix the largest at the source (field filtering or pagination), rerun, and compare total tokens, cache hit rate and task success.

lessons.title: Reuse prompts: caching, modular prompts and Skills
lessons.summary: The exam tests prompt caching mechanics (prefix order, breakpoints, TTL choice, silent invalidators), modular prompt design that keeps stable content first, and Agent Skills as on-demand, reusable expertise. Answers favour stable prefixes and progressive disclosure over pasting the same long guidance into every request.
keyPoints: **Caching is a byte-exact prefix match** in the order `tools` → `system` → `messages`. Any change at position N invalidates everything after it. Put frozen content first and volatile content (timestamps, IDs, the user question) after the last breakpoint.

**Up to 4 `cache_control` breakpoints**; place them at stability boundaries (end of tools/system, then the conversation tail). Top-level automatic caching marks the last cacheable block, which only helps if that block repeats.

**TTL and price**: default 5-minute TTL (refreshed free on each hit) with writes at 1.25x base input; 1-hour TTL with writes at 2x; reads cost a small fraction of base input (0.1x on most models). Choose TTL by the gap between requests; a 5-minute TTL on traffic with longer gaps pays the write every time.

**Silent failures**: prefixes below the model's minimum cacheable length don't cache and return no error; verify with `usage.cache_read_input_tokens`. Invalidators include timestamps in the system prompt, unsorted JSON, per-request tool sets, image changes, and changes to thinking or effort settings.

**Scope**: caches are model-scoped and never shared across organisations; on the Claude API they are isolated per workspace. A cache entry becomes readable once the first response starts, so warm it before fan-out.
**Modular prompts**: compose versioned building blocks (role, policy, examples, schema) in a fixed order so shared modules form a cacheable prefix; keep per-tenant or per-request modules at the end.

**Agent Skills** package instructions, scripts and resources as a folder with `SKILL.md`. Progressive disclosure: only `name` + `description` sit in context (roughly 100 tokens each); the body loads when triggered; bundled files load only when read; scripts run and only their output enters context.

**The description drives triggering**: say what the skill does and when to use it. On the API, skills run in the code execution container (listed in `container`), with no network access and no runtime package installs; custom API skills are shared workspace-wide.
**Skills don't sync across surfaces**: claude.ai, the API and Claude Code (filesystem `.claude/skills/` or `~/.claude/skills/`, or plugins) are managed separately.

**Governance**: treat a skill like installing software — use only trusted sources and audit scripts and external fetches. Check data-handling eligibility (Agent Skills are not covered by zero data retention).
traps: Putting `datetime.now()` or a request ID at the top of a cached system prompt.
Expecting 40 simultaneous requests to share a cache entry that doesn't exist yet.
Pasting a long style guide into every prompt instead of packaging it as a skill or a cached prefix.
Writing a vague skill description ('helpers') and wondering why it never triggers.
Assuming a skill uploaded in claude.ai is available to the API or Claude Code.

code.src:
resp = client.messages.create(
  model=MODEL, max_tokens=4000,
  tools=TOOLS,                       # deterministic order
  system=[{"type": "text", "text": POLICY,
           "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}}],
  messages=history + [{"role": "user", "content": question}],
)
print(resp.usage.cache_read_input_tokens,
      resp.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens)

lessons.drill: Send the same request three times with a cached system prompt and log the cache usage fields. Then add a timestamp to the system prompt and repeat to watch the hit rate collapse. Move the timestamp after the breakpoint and confirm hits return. Finally, turn one long instruction block you paste often into a skill with a precise description.

lessons.title: Evaluate tool and agent configuration for capability bloat
lessons.summary: The exam gives you an agent or subagent with too many, too broad or overlapping tools and asks for the root-cause fix. Expect to remove or scope capabilities at the configuration layer, replace generic power tools with narrow task-shaped ones, and promote risky actions to dedicated tools the harness can gate, rather than adding prompt rules or a bigger model.
keyPoints: **More tools hurt selection.** Anthropic's tool search docs say Claude's ability to pick the right tool degrades once more than about **30–50 tools** are available, and a multi-server setup can spend ~55k tokens on definitions before any work starts.

**Least privilege per role.** Each agent or subagent gets only the tools its job needs. In Claude Code / the Agent SDK, a subagent with no `tools` field **inherits every tool**; `allowedTools` only pre-approves and does not restrict.

**Capability is blast radius.** An agent that reads untrusted content (email, web pages, tickets, documents) and also holds send, delete, pay or forward tools turns a prompt injection into an action. Remove the capability, or gate it with a human approval step in the harness.

**Bash vs dedicated tools.** A shell tool gives breadth but hands the harness an opaque command string. Promote an action to a dedicated, typed tool when you need to gate, audit, render or parallelise it (for example refunds, outbound messages, deletes).

**Fewer, higher-level tools.** Anthropic's tool-writing guidance favours tools shaped like the workflow (`schedule_event`, `search_contacts`) over one-to-one API mirrors (`list_users`, `list_events`, `create_event`). Consolidate overlapping tools and namespace names by service (`crm_`, `billing_`).
**Narrow beats generic.** `get_order_status(order_id)` backed by a fixed read-only query, with ownership checked from the authenticated session, beats `run_sql(query)` plus a prompt rule.

**Restrict in configuration, not prose.** MCP connector: `mcp_toolset` with `default_config: {enabled: false}` plus an allowlist in `configs` keeps vendor-added tools off. Claude Code: `tools` / `disallowedTools`.

**Audit with traces and evals.** Look for tools never called, tools called interchangeably, and tools called wrongly; prune, then re-run the eval suite to confirm nothing depended on what you removed.
traps: A system-prompt rule ("never use `send_email`") instead of removing the tool: prompts are not a security boundary.
Moving to a bigger model so it can cope with 100+ tools, instead of shrinking the tool set.
Adding more granular tools "for flexibility", which adds overlap and selection errors.
Treating `allowedTools` as a restriction: unlisted tools are still available.
Over-correcting by exposing every CLI subcommand as its own tool, which recreates bloat in a different form.
lessons.drill: Take one agent you run (or a sample config). List every tool, map each to the tasks in its job description, and mark it keep, merge, remove, or gate behind approval. Note which tools touch untrusted input and which can act outside the system, then write the new `tools` / `mcp_toolset` config and the eval you would re-run.

lessons.title: Analyse authentication and authorisation for security gaps
lessons.summary: The exam asks you to spot where identity, credentials and permissions are enforced in the wrong place, usually in the prompt or the model's arguments. The correct answers move enforcement into deterministic code and infrastructure: host-side credentials, authorisation checks from the authenticated session, scoped keys and roles, and the MCP authorisation rules.
keyPoints: **Authorise in the tool handler.** Take the tenant or user from the authenticated session, not from a model-supplied parameter or a prompt rule; reject objects the caller does not own.
**Credentials stay host-side.** Never put API keys or OAuth tokens in prompts or messages; assume prompt contents can be extracted. The tool attaches the credential when it executes.
**Secrets management.** Store keys in a secret manager and inject them at runtime for the service identity; not in images, code or committed config. Use a distinct key per service and environment.
**Isolate environments** with a workspace per environment, workspace-scoped keys and workspace-level limits, so a staging load test cannot throttle production and spend is separable.
**Rotation and exposure.** Rotate by creating the new key, deploying it, then revoking the old one. On exposure, **revoke first**, then investigate usage.
**CI without static keys:** Workload Identity Federation exchanges the CI system's OIDC token for short-lived Claude API credentials.

**MCP authorisation:** remote (HTTP) servers use OAuth; servers must validate that tokens were issued for them (audience) and must not pass the client's token through to upstream APIs. Local Streamable HTTP servers should validate `Origin` and bind to localhost. Committed `.mcp.json` should reference `${ENV_VARS}`, not secrets.

**Cloud IAM and multi-tenant agents:** a dedicated role scoped to the models and resources the workload needs; per-tenant working directories, settings and memory scopes so nothing leaks across tenants.
traps: Adding `tenant_id` to the tool schema: the model can still pass the wrong one; the check must come from the session.
Prompt instructions such as "never reveal the key" instead of removing the key.
Rewriting git history or making the repo private before revoking a leaked key.
One organisation-wide key "to simplify rotation".
Forwarding the MCP client's bearer token to an upstream API.
lessons.drill: Draw the request path for one agent action (user, app, model, tool, downstream API). At each hop write where identity comes from, which credential is used and who can see it. Mark every place where the model could choose an identity or see a secret, and redesign those hops.

lessons.title: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration
lessons.summary: Questions give you accuracy and latency numbers, a requirement, and several levers, and ask for the configuration you can justify. The exam rewards measuring candidates on the same eval, choosing the cheapest configuration that clears both bars, and using levers that cut the actual term dominating the wait, not reflexively downgrading the model.
keyPoints: **Decompose the wait:** task time ≈ calls × time to first token + output tokens ÷ output speed + time outside the model (tools, network, retries). Fix the term that dominates.
**Know the measures:** time to first token, time to first *visible* output (later if the model thinks first), time to finish, and output tokens per second. Judge per completed task, not per request.
**Perceived vs actual:** streaming makes a reply feel faster but barely changes total generation time; it also keeps long requests from idling out.

**Free-ish levers first:** a tighter output shape (fewer output tokens), prompt caching (cuts time to first token on long prefixes; little effect on short prompts), executing parallel tool calls concurrently and returning them together, prefetching predictable lookups.

**Trading levers:** lower effort (fewer tokens and calls, some capability), a smaller tier (faster but may need more turns), fast mode (same model, higher output speed, premium price), thinking off where the model allows it (steepest quality risk).

**No win without evidence:** a change counts only when the eval shows quality held and a measurement in the same run shows latency fell; service speed drifts, so don't compare against last week's number.
**Justify per route:** pick the cheapest configuration that meets the accuracy bar and the latency SLA for each traffic type; batch work nobody waits on.
**Errors as latency:** 429 = your rate limit (cap concurrency, back off); 529 = service overload (back off with jitter, queue non-urgent work or fall back to another tier).
traps: Smallest model everywhere "because latency" without checking the accuracy bar.
Raising `max_tokens` to make responses faster; it is a ceiling, not a speed control.
Assuming prompt caching cuts latency for short, varying prompts.
Disabling parallel tool use or returning parallel results in separate messages, which serialises the loop.
Turning off streaming to "save overhead".
lessons.drill: Pick one workload and build a 3×3 grid (three tiers × three effort levels). For each cell record eval accuracy, p50/p90 time to finish and cost per completed task, all from one interleaved run. Circle the cheapest cell that meets your accuracy and latency targets and write a two-sentence justification.

lessons.title: Observability challenges and monitoring strategies at scale
lessons.summary: The exam tests whether you can make an LLM system debuggable and measurable at production volume without leaking sensitive data. Expect questions on correlation IDs and request IDs, what to log per call, tracing multi-step agents, content capture versus privacy, sampling, quality monitoring beyond HTTP status, and using the right source of truth for cost.
keyPoints: **Correlate everything:** generate a trace ID per user request, propagate it through retrieval, tool and model calls, and log each response's API request ID (the `request-id` header; `_request_id` in the Python SDK). W3C `traceparent` links your spans to the provider's.
**Per-call record:** model, `usage` (input, output, `cache_creation_input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`), `stop_reason`, time to first token and total latency, tool names and error flags.

**Signals that catch silent failures:** cache reads dropping to zero (a prefix invalidator such as a timestamp), `max_tokens` stop reasons rising (truncation), refusal rates, tool error rates, turns per task.
**HTTP 200 is not quality.** Sample production traffic and score it with an LLM-as-judge rubric calibrated against human review; alert on score drift by version.
**Agents need step-level traces.** Anthropic's multi-agent research post credits full production tracing with diagnosing why agents failed, and notes agents are stateful so errors compound.

**Privacy:** OpenTelemetry export for the Claude API defaults to **metadata only**; full prompt/response content is opt-in, and the backend then holds it under its own access and retention rules. Anthropic monitored agent decision patterns and interaction structure without reading conversation contents.

**Scale:** keep cheap metrics for 100% of traffic and full traces for errors, flagged or low-scored items plus a random sample. Traces are sampled or best-effort, so use the usage and cost reports, not traces, for billing and per-key spend.
**Claude Code fleets:** set `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY` and `OTEL_*` in managed settings; prompt text is redacted unless `OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1`.
traps: Dumping full prompts and responses into a shared log index "for debugging".
Logging only the question and final answer for a multi-step agent.
Building finance reports from sampled traces.
Monitoring only error rates and latency when the failure is answer quality.
Putting personal data into IDs or labels that are exported in every telemetry mode.

docs.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

lessons.drill: Write the telemetry schema for one Claude-backed endpoint: the fields recorded for every call, the extra fields kept only for sampled or failed calls, who can read each tier, and how long each is retained. Then list three alerts (for example cache-read ratio, `max_tokens` stop rate, judge score) with thresholds.

lessons.title: Design a RAG pipeline: chunking and indexing
lessons.summary: This objective covers the ingestion side of retrieval: whether you need RAG at all, how to chunk, how to give chunks context, which embedding model and index to use, what metadata to store, and how to keep the index correct over time. Anthropic's contextual retrieval post supplies most of the testable numbers.
keyPoints: **Maybe skip RAG.** If the knowledge base is under about **200,000 tokens (~500 pages)**, Anthropic suggests putting all of it in the prompt and using prompt caching.

**Pipeline:** parse → chunk (typically no more than a few hundred tokens) → add context → embed **and** build a BM25 index → store with metadata. Chunk boundaries, size and overlap all affect retrieval; chunk along document structure and tune on an eval.

**Contextual retrieval:** Claude writes 50–100 tokens of chunk-specific context from the whole document and prepends it before embedding and BM25 indexing. Top-20 retrieval failures fell **35%** (contextual embeddings), **49%** (plus contextual BM25) and **67%** (plus reranking).

**Make it affordable:** load each document once into a cached prefix and generate every chunk's context against it; Anthropic estimated a one-time ~$1.02 per million document tokens. Generic per-document summaries gave very limited gains.

**Embeddings:** Anthropic does not offer its own embedding model; its docs describe Voyage AI and advise assessing several vendors. Choose on domain fit, latency and customisation, measured on your own labelled queries. Use query vs document input types where the model supports them.
**One model per index:** vectors from different embedding models are not comparable. Changing models means re-embedding the corpus into a new index, validating it, then switching.

**Metadata at index time:** source, section, version/effective date, jurisdiction, tenant and access groups. These support filters, permission-aware retrieval, freshness and citations. On update, replace or retire the document's old chunks.

**Citations:** pass chunks as `document` blocks with `citations.enabled`. Plain text and PDF are chunked into sentences; custom content documents are not chunked further. `cited_text` doesn't count toward output tokens, and citations can't be combined with structured outputs (400).
traps: Building a vector database for a 90k-token handbook.
Raising top-K to compensate for context-free chunks.
Prepending the same document summary to every chunk and calling it contextual retrieval.
Mixing vectors from two embedding models in one index.
Enforcing document permissions with a prompt instruction instead of a retrieval filter.

code.src:
# Contextualise each chunk against a cached copy of its document
for chunk in chunks:
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-5-5", max_tokens=200,
        system=[{"type": "text", "text": f"<document>{doc}</document>",
                 "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}],
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
            f"<chunk>{chunk}</chunk>\nGive a short context situating this chunk "
            "within the document to improve search retrieval. Answer only with the context."}])
    ctx = resp.content[0].text
    index(embed(ctx + "\n" + chunk), bm25_text=ctx + "\n" + chunk, meta=chunk.meta)

lessons.drill: Take 20 pages of a real document set. Chunk it two ways (fixed 300 tokens vs structure-aware with overlap), add contextual prefixes to one variant, and write 15 questions with known answer passages. Measure recall@20 for each variant and note which change moved it most.

lessons.title: Match retrieval strategy to data shape and query pattern
lessons.summary: Here the exam describes the data (prose, codes, tables, one long contract, many sources) and the questions people ask, and asks which retrieval approach fits. Correct answers combine lexical and semantic search for mixed queries, rerank, scope with metadata filters, use query tools for structured data, use long context or agentic search when single-shot top-K can't work, and diagnose retrieval separately from generation.
keyPoints: **Exact identifiers** (error codes, part numbers, clause IDs) are where embeddings miss and **BM25** shines; Anthropic's example is an error code. Run both and merge with **rank fusion**, deduplicating results.
**Rerank:** retrieve wide, then rerank. Anthropic's setup retrieved the top 150 and passed the reranked top 20; reranking adds some latency and cost, so tune the candidate count against your budget.
**Top-K:** passing 20 chunks beat 5 or 10 in Anthropic's tests, but always confirm with your own evals.
**Structured data** (aggregates, rankings, joins) needs a query tool (read-only SQL/API) or code execution over an extract, not similarity search over rows.
**One long document** that fits the window and needs cross-clause reasoning: put it in context (document first, question last) and cache it for follow-ups.
**Multi-hop, multi-source questions:** give an agent search tools so it can query iteratively (just-in-time retrieval) instead of one top-K over the whole question.
**Scope with metadata filters** (country, tenant, product, effective date) known from the user or query, before ranking. Rewrite conversational follow-ups into standalone queries before retrieval.

**Long-context layout:** documents at the top and the query at the end can improve quality by up to 30%; wrap each document in tags with source metadata; ask for relevant quotes first. **Diagnose:** measure retrieval recall on labelled questions, then review answers where the right passage *was* retrieved.
traps: A bigger embedding model to fix exact-code lookups.
Stuffing 150 unranked chunks into the prompt.
Embedding warehouse rows and expecting correct totals.
Prompting the model to discard out-of-scope chunks instead of filtering.
Changing the generator when retrieval recall is the real problem, or the reverse.

docs.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

lessons.drill: List ten real questions your users ask. Tag each by query pattern (exact ID, semantic, aggregate, single long doc, multi-hop, conversational follow-up) and write the retrieval path you'd use for each tag. Check whether one pipeline really serves them all.

lessons.title: Select the integration mechanism: MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent
lessons.summary: The exam asks which mechanism should connect Claude to a capability: a custom tool, an MCP server, a CLI, a server tool, or another agent. Choose by who needs the capability, where it runs, how it authenticates and how much you want to build and maintain.
keyPoints: **Custom tool in `tools`** when one application needs an in-process function; run it in your loop or the SDK Tool Runner. No server needed.

**MCP server** when the same capability must serve several clients (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, claude.ai connectors, Agent SDK, Messages API MCP connector). Prefer a maintained existing server over writing your own.

**Transports:** stdio for a local process the client launches; Streamable HTTP over HTTPS with OAuth for a central, multi-user server. The older HTTP+SSE transport is superseded. claude.ai and the API MCP connector reach **remote** servers only.
**Primitives:** tools are model-controlled, resources are application-controlled context, prompts are user-invoked templates.

**CLI first in Claude Code:** if a system has a CLI that is installed and signed in, that is usually the easiest way in (Claude Code can read `--help`). Use MCP for systems without a CLI. Connected MCP servers add their tool names and instructions to context even when unused.
**Server tools** (web search, web fetch, code execution) run on Anthropic's infrastructure, so they're the least to build and maintain.

**Agent-to-agent:** within one system, delegate to subagents for context isolation and parallelism. Across team boundaries, treat the other agent as a service with a defined, typed interface (a tool or MCP server) and pass only the context it needs.
**Configuration hygiene:** project `.mcp.json` with `${ENV}` references for shared servers; managed settings to deny built-ins (for example `WebSearch`) when a compliant replacement exists.
traps: Building a custom MCP server when a maintained one or an installed CLI already covers the need.
A public remote MCP server for a function only one backend uses.
stdio for a server shared by thousands of employees.
Pasting API references into CLAUDE.md so Claude hand-builds `curl` calls.
Expecting claude.ai or the API MCP connector to launch a local stdio server.
lessons.drill: For five integrations your team needs, fill in a table: who uses it, from which clients, where it runs, how it authenticates, and whether a CLI or maintained MCP server exists. Pick the mechanism for each and note the one you would revisit if a second client appears.

lessons.title: Progressive discovery vs monolithic context
lessons.summary: This objective asks when to load everything up front and when to let the agent discover tools, instructions and data on demand. The exam rewards progressive discovery for large or mostly-unused catalogues (tool search, Skills, just-in-time file access), and monolithic context for small, always-needed, stable content, with mandatory rules kept in always-on context or code.
keyPoints: **Monolithic:** everything in the prompt. It's simple, predictable and cacheable, but it bloats context and distracts the model as content grows.

**Tool search:** send every definition, mark most `defer_loading: true`; Claude searches (regex or BM25) and loads matches (5 by default). Keep the **3–5 most-used tools non-deferred**; never defer the search tool, and at least one tool must stay non-deferred (else 400). Typical saving is over 85% of definition tokens.
**When to use it:** 10+ tools, definitions over 10k tokens, accuracy dropping as tools are added, many MCP servers. **Skip it** for fewer than 10 tools, or when every tool is used on every request.
**Caching:** discovered definitions are appended, so the cached prefix survives; rebuilding the `tools` array per turn breaks the cache. A deferred tool cannot carry `cache_control` (400).

**Discovery quality:** namespace tool names, use keyword-rich descriptions, list the available tool categories in the system prompt, or return `tool_reference` blocks from a custom (for example embedding-based) search tool.

**Skills:** about 100 tokens of metadata per Skill always loaded; the `SKILL.md` body (under 5k tokens) loads when triggered; bundled files load only when read, and script code never enters context, only its output.
**Just-in-time data:** keep lightweight references (paths, IDs) and let the agent fetch with search/read tools; hybrid setups preload a small briefing (like CLAUDE.md) and fetch the rest.
**Keep mandatory content always on:** rules that must apply to every response belong in the system prompt, or better, in deterministic code. A Skill loads only when the model judges it relevant.
traps: Deferring everything, including the search tool.
Adding tool search to a six-tool agent "for best practice".
Moving an always-relevant rulebook behind retrieval, where the agent may not know to look it up.
Rebuilding the tool list per turn with a classifier and losing the cache.
Putting a mandatory compliance rule in an on-demand Skill.

docs.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

lessons.drill: Inventory everything one agent loads before the first user message: tool definitions, system prompt sections, reference text. Estimate tokens for each and how often each is used. Mark each item as keep up front, defer (tool search), move to a Skill, fetch just in time, or enforce in code.

lessons.title: Define evaluation metrics
lessons.summary: The exam checks whether you can turn a stakeholder wish ('accurate', 'fast', 'safe') into success criteria a release can be gated on. Strong answers are specific, measurable, multidimensional and tied to business risk. Weak answers lean on a prompt instruction, a single headline number, or a target nobody can measure.
keyPoints: **Good success criteria are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant.** Weak: 'classify sentiment well'. Strong: 'F1 of at least 0.85 on a held-out set of 10,000 representative posts, a 5% improvement on the current baseline'.

**Most use cases need several dimensions at once.** Anthropic's list: task fidelity (including rare and hard inputs), consistency, relevance and coherence, tone and style, privacy preservation, context utilisation, latency and price. The exam also expects **safety** and **security** as gates.
**Safety can be quantified.** For example: 'fewer than 0.1% of outputs out of 10,000 trials flagged for toxicity'. Define the test set and the grader, then make the threshold a release gate.

**Error severity matters.** A criterion such as '90% of errors are inconveniences, not egregious errors' only works once both classes are defined. A near-zero bar for the severe class can decide between two versions with the same headline accuracy.

**Fit the metric to the risk.** With a rare positive class (3% urgent claims), overall accuracy hides a model that never flags anything, so use per-class **recall and precision**. For extraction, use field-level exact match. For grounded answers, use the citation-support rate.

**Latency**: use **time to first token (TTFT)** for streaming, user-facing chat, and total latency or completion within the delivery window for batch or backend jobs. Report percentiles (p95), not just means.
**Cost**: measure cost per *successful* task, including retries, failed attempts and human review, not price per token.

**Agents are non-deterministic, so run several trials.** `pass@k` is the chance at least one of k trials succeeds and suits cases where one success is enough. `pass^k` is the chance all k succeed and suits customer-facing consistency. At 75% per trial, pass^3 is about 42%.

**Security metrics measure outcomes.** Examples: attack success rate on a maintained prompt-injection set, and the rate of tool calls outside the permitted scope in a sandbox (target zero). Don't use proxies such as refusal rate or the length of the 'security rules' section.

**Achievable and relevant**: anchor targets to a measured baseline, human performance, prior experiments or expert knowledge, never to '100%'. Weight dimensions by purpose. Citation accuracy matters more in a medical or legal tool than in a casual chatbot.
traps: Accepting 'it must be safe' or 'it must be accurate' and writing a system-prompt instruction instead of a measurable gate.
Reporting overall accuracy on an imbalanced task, where always predicting the majority class scores well.
Using an overlap metric (ROUGE or BLEU against reference answers) as the main quality signal when what matters is correctness or groundedness.
Quoting pass@k for an unattended, customer-facing agent where every attempt has to work.
Agreeing to an unanchored 100% target instead of measuring a baseline and designing human review for the residual errors.

code.src:
criteria = {
  'task_fidelity': {'metric': 'urgent_recall', 'min': 0.95, 'set': 'heldout_v3 (n=2000)'},
  'precision':     {'metric': 'urgent_precision', 'min': 0.70},
  'safety':        {'metric': 'unsafe_advice_rate', 'max': 0.0, 'set': 'redteam_v2'},
  'latency':       {'metric': 'p95_ttft_ms', 'max': 1500},
  'cost':          {'metric': 'usd_per_resolved_case', 'max': 0.04},
}

docs.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

lessons.drill: Pick a Claude feature you know and write its success criteria as a table with five rows: task fidelity, one safety or security gate, consistency, latency and cost. For each row give the metric, the threshold, the test set and the grader. Then rewrite one vague stakeholder sentence ('answers should be trustworthy') into two measurable rows, and decide whether your agent's gate should use pass@k or pass^k.

lessons.title: Design evaluation datasets and mixed-method test frameworks
lessons.summary: The exam tests whether you can build an eval that predicts production behaviour. That means a test set drawn from real traffic with edge cases and balanced positive and negative cases, a grader matched to each criterion (code, then LLM, then human), outcome-based grading for agents, and layered methods, because no single method catches everything.
keyPoints: **Be task-specific.** Mirror the real input distribution and add edge cases: irrelevant or missing input, overly long input, poor or harmful input, and ambiguous cases where even humans would disagree.
**Automate when possible, and favour volume over quality.** Anthropic's guidance is that many questions with slightly lower-signal automated grading beat a few high-quality hand-graded ones.

**Choose the fastest, most reliable, most scalable grader that fits.** **Code-based** grading is fastest, most reliable and very scalable, but lacks nuance. **LLM-based** grading is fast, flexible and handles complex judgement, but test its reliability before you scale it. **Human** grading is the most flexible and highest quality, but slow and expensive, so avoid it where you can and use it to calibrate.

**LLM-grader practice**: give a detailed rubric, ask for an empirical output ('correct'/'incorrect' or a 1–5 score) and let the grader reason (thinking on) before it scores. It's generally best to grade with a different model from the one that generated the output. Give the judge an 'Unknown' option, use one isolated judge per dimension, and calibrate against human verdicts.

**Match the eval type to the criterion**: exact match for labels, cosine similarity across paraphrased inputs for consistency, ROUGE-L for summary overlap, an LLM Likert scale for tone, an LLM binary classifier for leakage (including implicit or hypothetical PHI), and an LLM ordinal scale for context use.

**Agent evals vocabulary**: a *task* has inputs and success criteria, a *trial* is one attempt, a *grader* scores it, the *transcript* records every step and the *outcome* is the final environment state. **Grade outcomes, not paths**: check that the booking exists in the database, not that the agent said it did. Add partial credit and start each trial clean.
**Start small and real.** 20–50 tasks drawn from real failures is a good start. Write unambiguous tasks with reference solutions, where two experts would independently agree on pass or fail.
**Balance the set.** Test both when a behaviour should happen and when it shouldn't, so neither under-triggering nor over-triggering gets rewarded.

**Capability suites vs regression suites.** Capability evals start at a low pass rate to give a hill to climb. Regression evals sit near 100% to stop backsliding. A saturated capability eval *graduates* into the regression suite.
**Layer the methods.** Automated evals, production monitoring, A/B tests, user feedback, manual transcript review and systematic human studies each catch what the others miss.
traps: Keeping a small, hand-graded set because it feels more rigorous, so the team can iterate only once every few days.
Asking the generating model, in the same call or conversation, to grade its own answer.
A test set with only 'should trigger' cases, which rewards an agent that over-escalates or over-calls tools.
Grading an agent's claim ('booking confirmed') or a fixed tool-call order instead of the end state.
Deleting a saturated suite instead of keeping it as a regression guard.

docs.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

lessons.drill: For an assistant you know, list three success criteria and assign each a grader (code, LLM or human) with a one-line justification. Draft 20 test cases from real or realistic inputs: at least five edge cases and at least five where the behaviour should *not* happen. Write the LLM-judge rubric for one criterion with a 1–5 scale and an 'unknown' option, then hand-grade 10 outputs and compare your scores with the judge's.

lessons.title: Run A/B tests and iterate with statistical discipline
lessons.summary: The exam tests whether you can tell a real improvement from noise and run a disciplined improvement loop: baseline first, one change at a time, held-out data, statistics on eval scores, and online A/B tests designed so their results can be trusted. Expect questions where a small score gain, a peeked dashboard or an overfit dev set leads to the wrong decision.
keyPoints: **Improvement loop**: define the criteria, build the eval, run the current version to get a **baseline**, change **one variable**, re-run, compare, then keep or roll back. Version every prompt, model and parameter change.

**Quality first, then latency.** Anthropic advises first engineering a prompt that works well without model or prompt constraints, then applying latency reductions. Cutting latency too early can stop you from discovering what top performance looks like.
**An eval score is an estimate.** Report the standard error of the mean and a 95% confidence interval (about mean ± 1.96 × SEM), not just the point score.

**Paired comparison**: when two variants answer the same questions, analyse per-question differences. That removes question-difficulty variance. Anthropic found per-question score correlations of 0.3–0.7 between frontier models, which makes paired analysis essentially free variance reduction.

**Clustered standard errors**: when questions share a unit (10 questions per contract or passage), cluster on that unit. On popular evals Anthropic found clustered errors can be more than three times the naive ones, and ignoring clustering produces false 'wins'.
**Reduce within-question noise** by sampling several trials per question and averaging, especially for chain-of-thought or agentic tasks.
**Power analysis** before you build or run: work out how many questions (and resamples) you need to detect the effect size you care about. A small eval can only detect large gaps.
**Guard against overfitting.** Tune on a dev set, gate releases on a **held-out** set that you don't iterate against, and keep adding new cases from production failures.
**Read transcripts when scores move.** A 0% pass rate across many trials usually means a broken task or grader, not an incapable agent.

**Online A/B tests** measure real user outcomes but are slow, need traffic and say little about *why*. Randomise by user or conversation, fix the primary metric, guardrail metrics and sample size up front, and don't stop the moment the variant pulls ahead. Roll out behind a flag with a rollback path.
traps: Shipping on a 1–2 point gain from a 150-item eval without an interval or a paired test.
Treating 400 questions drawn from 40 documents as 400 independent samples.
Changing the prompt, model tier and effort in one release, so nobody can attribute the regression.
Iterating 30 times against the same set and reading the final score as a production forecast.
Per-request randomisation plus daily peeking with 'stop when B leads', which looks rigorous but isn't.

code.src:
import numpy as np
# a, b: per-question mean scores (avg of several trials) on the SAME questions
d = np.array(b) - np.array(a)
se = d.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(d))
lo, hi = d.mean() - 1.96 * se, d.mean() + 1.96 * se
print(f'diff={d.mean():.3f}  95% CI=({lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f})')
# if the CI spans 0: not a demonstrated win -> enlarge set or resample

docs.title: A statistical approach to model evaluations

lessons.drill: Take two prompt variants and a set of at least 50 cases. Run each variant three times per case and record per-case mean scores. Compute the paired difference, its standard error and the 95% CI using the snippet. Then group the cases by source document and work out how far the effective sample size falls. Write a three-line ship / don't-ship note that a product manager could act on.

lessons.title: Diagnose system issues: prompt failure, hallucination, model mismatch
lessons.summary: The exam gives you a symptom (truncated output, invented facts, a regression after a migration, a looping agent, schema-valid but wrong data) and asks for the most likely cause or the right first fix. Read the evidence first (`stop_reason`, `usage`, prompt and model version, transcripts), then fix the root cause rather than adding a compensating control.
keyPoints: **Start with evidence.** Check `stop_reason` (`max_tokens` means truncation, plus `refusal` and `tool_use`), `usage` against `max_tokens`, the model ID, the prompt version and the request ID. Mid-sentence endings and unparseable JSON on long outputs are usually truncation, not the model 'failing to follow the schema'.
**Thinking counts against `max_tokens`.** Low budgets with adaptive or extended thinking cut answers short, so raise the budget or lower effort.

**Systematic vs random errors**: the same failure on one layout or category points to a prompt or example gap (add a targeted example or rule). Scattered one-off errors suit code validation plus a retry that feeds the specific error back.

**Schema-valid isn't correct.** Structured outputs guarantee shape, not truth. Add business-rule checks in code (line items sum to the total, dates are ordered) and route failures to a retry or to a human.

**Hallucination controls (Anthropic)**: allow 'I don't know'; for long documents (more than about 20k tokens), extract word-for-word quotes first and answer only from them; require citations and retract claims without a supporting quote; use best-of-N inconsistency as a signal; restrict answers to the provided documents. These reduce hallucination but don't eliminate it, so validate critical information.
**Self-review in the same context is weak.** Use an independent verifier with fresh context, and verify per section to avoid lost-in-the-middle misses.

**Model mismatch after a migration**: newer models follow instructions more literally, so shouted legacy workarounds ('CRITICAL: you MUST') can over-trigger. Re-baseline the prompt. Cost can rise at the same per-token price through tokenizer or verbosity differences, so compare `usage`.

**Agent and tool bugs**: vague tool descriptions cause wrong tool choice. Unhandled exceptions without `is_error: true` cause repeat calls. Answering only one of several parallel `tool_use` blocks returns a 400.
**Required fields that are often absent** push the model to invent values. Make them nullable with a clear meaning ('not present on the document').
**Retry storms**: stacking an SDK retry layer under your own retry loop multiplies calls. Use a single retry layer.
traps: Switching to a bigger model or a bigger context as the first move, before reading `stop_reason`, `usage` and transcripts.
Prompt-only fixes ('be accurate') for errors that need deterministic validation in code.
Treating every regression after a migration as a capability loss instead of a prompt that needs re-baselining.
Asking the same conversation to 'double-check' its own claims.
lessons.drill: Collect 10 failing outputs from any Claude workflow you run, or create them by lowering `max_tokens` and giving vague tool descriptions. Label each one: truncation, prompt gap (systematic), random error, hallucination, tool or integration bug, or model mismatch. Name the evidence field that proved it and the root-cause fix. Then add the five most important ones to an eval set as regression cases.

lessons.title: Optimise token usage, latency and cost-performance
lessons.summary: The exam tests whether you can cut cost or latency without breaking a quality bar you have measured. That covers the right model tier and effort, prompt caching that actually hits, the Message Batches API for work nobody is waiting on, concurrency within rate limits, and judging options by cost per completed task.
keyPoints: **Sequence**: get quality first, then optimise. Every cost or latency change is validated on the eval against the quality bar.

**Latency levers (Anthropic)**: choose the right model (smaller tiers are fastest), cut prompt and output tokens, and **stream** to improve perceived latency (TTFT). To shorten output, ask for sentence or paragraph limits rather than word counts.

**Effort** (`output_config.effort`) is the main speed and cost lever on current models. Sweep it on your eval, set it explicitly per route and re-sweep after a model change. Try a lower effort on the current tier before stepping down a tier.
**`max_tokens` is a hard backstop, not a cost dial.** Hitting it cuts the response off mid-output, and thinking counts toward it, so lowering it to save money mostly creates truncation.

**Prompt caching**: the cache covers the prefix in order `tools` → `system` → `messages`, and a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it. The default lifetime is 5 minutes, refreshed free on each use, and a 1-hour TTL is available. Cache writes cost more than base input (1.25× for 5 minutes, 2× for 1 hour). Reads cost a small fraction of base input, and the exact multiplier depends on the model. Prompts below the model's minimum cacheable length are silently not cached.

**Verify caching in `usage`.** Look at `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens`. Total input = `input_tokens` + `cache_creation_input_tokens` + `cache_read_input_tokens`. Keep variable content (timestamps, user data) after the cached prefix.

**Message Batches API**: 50% of standard prices, processed asynchronously. It fits nightly jobs, backfills and eval runs. It doesn't fit flows where a user or a merge-blocking CI job is waiting. Batching and caching can be combined.

**Architecture levers**: route simple subtasks to a smaller tier, run independent calls concurrently, send only the delta (for example the diff since the last review) and gather inputs in code instead of with agent tool calls.
