**Throughput**: size concurrency to your rate limits (requests and input or output tokens per minute) with a token-aware limiter instead of firing everything and retrying 429s.
**Judge by cost per completed task**: (total spend including failed attempts and retries) ÷ successful outcomes. A pricier configuration that succeeds more often can be cheaper overall.
traps: Cutting `max_tokens` to save money and getting truncated, unparseable output.
Putting a timestamp or user ID at the top of the system prompt, so every request writes a new cache entry.
Using batches for interactive or blocking work because they're cheaper.
Dropping to the smallest tier before trying effort, caching and batching on the current one.
Comparing options on price per token instead of cost per completed task.

code.src:
resp = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL, max_tokens=8000,                       # generous backstop
    output_config={'effort': 'medium'},                  # swept on eval
    system=[{'type': 'text', 'text': STABLE_RULES,
             'cache_control': {'type': 'ephemeral'}}],  # stable prefix first
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': f'{today}\n{doc}'}],  # variable last
)
u = resp.usage
hit_ratio = u.cache_read_input_tokens / (u.input_tokens + u.cache_creation_input_tokens + u.cache_read_input_tokens)

lessons.drill: On a 30-case eval, run one route at two effort levels and with and without a cached system prompt. Record pass rate, mean input and output tokens, the cache-read ratio, p95 latency and cost per completed task in one table. Recommend a configuration, then list which of your organisation's workloads could move to the Batches API and which can't (someone is waiting).

lessons.title: Monitor system performance with logging and observability
lessons.summary: The exam tests whether your monitoring would catch the failures LLM systems actually have. Most quality regressions, truncations, cache misses and drift still return HTTP 200. Expect questions on per-request log fields, agent traces, quality sampling, org-level usage and cost reporting, Claude Code telemetry, and logging sensitive data safely.
keyPoints: **Per-request record**: request ID (`request-id` header, `_request_id` in the SDKs), model, prompt version, `usage` (input, output, cache creation and cache read tokens), latency (TTFT and total), `stop_reason` and error status. Give Anthropic support the request ID for a failing call.

**Quality monitoring**: HTTP dashboards miss quality drops. Sample production traffic into rubric or LLM-judge scoring tagged by prompt version and segment, watch the `stop_reason` mix and output length, and feed failures back into the eval set.

**Agent traces**: link every model call and tool call for one user request under a trace or session ID, with tool names, inputs and results (redacted) and per-step tokens and latency, so a run can be replayed as a transcript.

**Drift**: when inputs change (a new product line, a new language or document type), segment-level quality can fall while the overall average looks flat. Track the input-category mix and quality per segment.

**Org-level usage and cost**: the Admin API usage and cost report endpoints need an Admin API credential; workspace API keys don't work. For new integrations Anthropic recommends the **Usage and Cost Analytics API**. Usage can be bucketed by `1m`, `1h` or `1d` and grouped by model, workspace, API key, service tier and more. The cost report is in USD with **daily** buckets only. Data typically appears within about 5 minutes.

**Cache health**: track the share of input served from cache (`cache_read_input_tokens` over total input) per prompt version. A sudden drop after a release usually means something variable has entered the cached prefix.

**Claude Code OpenTelemetry**: `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1` plus `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER`, `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER` and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`. Metrics include `claude_code.token.usage` and `claude_code.cost.usage`. Prompts are **redacted by default** (`OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1` turns them on), and tool details are off unless `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1`. Enforce the settings org-wide through the managed settings `env` block, because a repository's `.claude/settings.json` exporter variables are ignored.

**Sensitive data**: log metadata by default. Capture content only redacted or sampled, in an access-controlled store with defined retention, especially for PHI or PII and third-party observability platforms.
**Alerts**: spend against budget, 429 and 5xx/529 rates, p95 latency, the truncation (`max_tokens`) rate, the cache-hit ratio and sampled quality per prompt version.
**Monitoring is reactive.** It finds problems after users do, so pair it with pre-release evals and A/B tests (the 'Swiss cheese' model).
traps: Error-rate and latency dashboards only, so quality regressions return 200 and go unseen.
Logging every prompt and response in full to a third-party tool by default in a regulated workload.
Calling the cost report with workspace keys, or expecting minute-level cost buckets.
Putting Claude Code telemetry variables in a repo's `.claude/settings.json` and expecting org-wide enforcement.
Per-call logs with no trace ID linking the steps of an agent run.

code.src:
log.info('llm_call', extra={
  'trace_id': trace_id, 'step': step, 'request_id': msg._request_id,
  'model': msg.model, 'prompt_version': PROMPT_V, 'stop_reason': msg.stop_reason,
  'in': msg.usage.input_tokens, 'out': msg.usage.output_tokens,
  'cache_read': msg.usage.cache_read_input_tokens,
  'cache_write': msg.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens,
  'ttft_ms': ttft, 'total_ms': total, 'segment': request_category,
})  # content: redacted/sampled only

lessons.drill: Write the log schema and the alert list for one Claude service: fields, which ones may hold content and how they are redacted, retention, and five alerts with thresholds. Then call the usage report endpoint (or read the Console Usage page) grouped by model at `1h` buckets, and compute your cache-read ratio for the last day.

lessons.title: Implement guardrails and safety controls
lessons.summary: The exam asks where a control must live so that it holds when the model is wrong or manipulated. Expect scenarios where a stronger prompt is tempting but the professional answer is a deterministic control at the execution layer (tool handler, hook, permission rule, egress allowlist) with the prompt kept as one layer among several.
keyPoints: **Layered guardrails**: input screening (often a fast, low-cost tier as a classifier) → system-prompt policy → least-privilege tools with checks in code → output filtering (DLP/regex for account numbers and similar) → monitoring and audit. Design assuming any single layer can fail.

**Prompts guide, code enforces.** Ordering rules (verify identity before refund), limits (refund caps) and forbidden paths belong in the tool handler, an Agent SDK or Claude Code **hook** (a `PreToolUse` hook can block a call), or permission rules, not only in instructions the model may skip.

**Least privilege**: give each agent only the narrow tools its job needs (`get_order_status(order_id)` rather than `run_sql` or a general shell), with scoped, read-only credentials where possible. Removing a capability beats guarding it.

**Untrusted content is data.** Tool results, retrieved chunks, emails and web pages can carry indirect prompt injection. Delimit them (XML tags) and say they are data, but rely on structural limits on what a fooled model can do.
Break the **lethal trifecta** in any single step: untrusted input + access to private data + an outbound channel (email, HTTP, rendered Markdown images).

**Authorisation from the session, never from model input**: the handler derives user or tenant from the authenticated request and checks ownership. An ID the model passes is a claim, not a credential.
Handle `stop_reason: "refusal"` explicitly: don't parse the turn as success, don't run its tool calls, show a safe message and log it.

**Claude Code**: permission rules are evaluated deny → ask → allow; Bash rules match command text only, so pair them with the **sandbox** (OS-level filesystem and network isolation). Admins enforce policy through managed settings.
Tune an over-blocking screen with clearer policy definitions and borderline few-shot examples, and route uncertain cases to a stronger model or a human rather than loosening the screen blindly.
traps: Choosing 'make the system prompt more emphatic' as the fix for a rule the agent sometimes skips.
Putting `tenant_id` in a tool's input schema and calling it authorisation.
Treating logging or after-the-fact review as prevention.
Believing a `curl`/`wget` deny rule is network isolation.
Assuming a more capable model is a security boundary.
lessons.drill: Take one agent you run (or a toy with `read_notes`, `fetch_url` and `issue_refund`). List every rule that currently lives only in the prompt. For each, write where it should be enforced (handler, hook, permission rule, egress allowlist) and implement the two riskiest. Then plant an injected instruction in a note and confirm the code-level controls hold even when the model follows it.

lessons.title: Identify risks, limitations and failure modes
lessons.summary: This objective tests whether you can name how an LLM system actually fails in production and trace a symptom to its root cause. The professional answer usually makes a hidden failure visible (typed errors, explicit statuses, stopping conditions) instead of masking it with retries, a bigger model or a softer prompt.
keyPoints: **Model-level limits**: hallucination (fluent but unsupported claims), knowledge cut-off and stale facts, run-to-run variation, poorly calibrated self-reported confidence, and susceptibility to injected instructions.

**System-level failure modes** cause more incidents than the model: tools that swallow errors and return success, `null` meaning both 'no match' and 'service down', timeouts reported as empty results, and truncated outputs (`stop_reason: "max_tokens"`) parsed as complete.

**Silent failure is the worst failure.** Make tools return typed errors (transient vs permanent, retryable or not) and make 'could not check' a first-class result, distinct from 'checked and found nothing'.
**Agents compound errors**: a wrong early step propagates. Add stopping conditions (iteration and cost caps), detect repeated identical failing calls, and checkpoint for human input when blocked.

**Hallucination mitigations** from the docs: allow the model to say it doesn't know, ground answers in extracted quotes from supplied sources, and verify claims with citations; retract claims without support.

**Refusals** (`stop_reason: "refusal"`) and **ambiguous inputs** are expected outcomes: handle them as states in the workflow, not crashes, and ask rather than guess when a lookup returns several matches.

**Distribution shift**: new document layouts, suppliers, languages or product lines arrive after launch. Schemas need an escape value (`other` plus detail) and evals need refreshing from production samples.
Run a **pre-mortem / failure-mode table** per component: failure, detection signal, blast radius, mitigation, owner. Prioritise by impact × likelihood, not by what is easiest to fix.
traps: Treating a confident tone or self-reported confidence as evidence of correctness.
Adding blind retries to a permanent error (bad credentials, lapsed licence).
Reporting 'no results found' when the search tool actually timed out.
Upgrading the model to fix a failure caused by a tool contract or missing data.
Letting an agent loop without iteration or spend limits.

code.src:
{
  "status": "error",
  "error_type": "upstream_unavailable",
  "retryable": true,
  "checked": false,
  "message": "Vendor DB timed out after 10s; vendor match NOT evaluated"
}

lessons.drill: Draw your system's pipeline and, for each tool and model call, fill in a failure-mode table: how it fails, what the caller currently sees, whether that is distinguishable from success, and the blast radius. Fix the top row by changing the contract (typed error or explicit status), then write one eval case that would have caught it.

lessons.title: Apply human-in-the-loop validation
lessons.summary: The exam tests where human review adds value, how it is enforced, and how it is targeted. Strong answers put the approval gate in code at the point of execution, route by observable risk rather than the model's self-rated confidence, give reviewers the evidence they need, and keep sampling what is auto-accepted.
keyPoints: **Gate at execution**: for irreversible or high-impact actions (payments over a threshold, deletes, deploys, external messages) the tool returns 'pending approval' and acts only after an authorised person approves. A prompt saying 'ask the user first' is not a gate.

**Meaningful review**: the reviewer needs authority to change or reject the output and the information to judge it. A one-click approve screen with no evidence invites rubber-stamping (automation bias).
**Structured handoff**: give the human a summary (who, issue, facts established, what was tried, why escalated, recommended next step) rather than a raw transcript.

**Route on observable signals**: validation failures, computed-vs-stated mismatches, policy gaps, explicit requests for a human, high-impact fields. Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; calibrate any score against labelled data first.
**Field-level routing** beats document-level averages: one wrong amount can hide inside a high average confidence.
**Sample the auto-accepted stream** (stratified by segment) so confidently wrong outputs are measured; keep a sampling floor even when a segment looks good.
Prioritise review queues by **risk and impact**, and size human capacity to the volume the routing rule actually produces.
**Close the loop**: reviewer corrections become labelled data for recalibrating thresholds, few-shot examples and new eval cases.
In unattended runs (CI, batch) there is nobody to ask: make 'needs human decision' an explicit output status instead of letting the agent pick an interpretation.
traps: Implementing approval as a system-prompt instruction.
Escalating on sentiment or on the model's own confidence score.
Reviewing only low-confidence items, so confident errors are never seen.
Replacing a required human approver with an LLM judge.
Removing review because overall accuracy is high without a per-segment breakdown.

docs.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

lessons.drill: Pick one workflow with a human step. Write down: which actions are gated in code, what the reviewer sees, what triggers review, and what sample of auto-accepted items is checked. Simulate a week of volume and compute queue size per reviewer. Change one trigger from a self-rated score to an observable signal and re-estimate.

lessons.title: Ensure regulatory compliance
lessons.summary: Compliance questions test the architect's controls, not vendor paperwork trivia: data minimisation, residency, retention, access control, audit trails, DPIAs, human review and due diligence on every processor in the data path. Expect distractors that move responsibility into a prompt or assume a vendor arrangement covers everything.
keyPoints: **Map the data flow first**: every place personal or regulated data goes (prompts, logs, caches you run, vector indexes, eval sets, third-party tools and MCP servers) and who processes it. Each processor in the path needs its own review.

**Data minimisation**: send only the fields the task needs; redact or pseudonymise before the prompt is built and re-link results in your own system. Enforce it in code with a pre-send check, not with an instruction.

**Residency** is set by platform and region choice and by the API's data residency controls (per-request inference geography plus workspace-level allowed and default geos), never by a prompt. On Amazon Bedrock and Google-managed Vertex AI the cloud provider is the data processor and its own controls apply.

**Zero Data Retention** is enabled per organisation and covers **eligible** features only; features that store files, jobs or container state are typically not eligible. Under ZDR the API does **not** block an ineligible feature, so the architect must restrict which features the application uses.

**HIPAA readiness** on the Claude API (with a signed BAA) blocks non-eligible features with a 400 error. The docs warn not to put PHI in JSON schema definitions used by structured outputs or `strict: true` tools, because compiled schemas are cached separately from message content.

Third-party integrations (tools, websites, external MCP servers) are outside Anthropic's data arrangements: do vendor due diligence, sign the appropriate agreements, minimise what they receive, or host the capability yourself.
**Retention and erasure**: set TTLs for every store you own, and tag derived artefacts (chunks, embeddings, eval samples, logs) with a subject key so deletion requests reach all of them.

**Audit trail** for regulated decisions: request ID, pinned model ID, prompt/template version, retrieved document IDs and versions, tool calls, output, and the human reviewer's action, in an access-controlled, append-only store with a defined retention.

**GDPR DPIA**: high-risk processing (for example, automated assessment of people or large-scale special-category data) requires a data protection impact assessment **before** processing starts; involve the DPO early.
traps: Writing 'do not store data' or 'keep data in the EU' into the system prompt.
Assuming an organisation-level ZDR or BAA covers every feature and every third-party tool.
Encrypting a store and calling that erasure.
Logging full prompts forever 'for audit' in conflict with minimisation and retention rules.
Answering with a claim about which certifications a vendor holds instead of the architect's own controls.
lessons.drill: Draw the data-flow diagram for one Claude feature you own. Mark every store and every processor. For each, write: which personal data enters, the lawful purpose, retention TTL, who can read it, and how an erasure request reaches it. Then list the API features the app uses and check each one against the eligibility table for your data arrangement.

lessons.title: Address ethical AI: bias, fairness, transparency
lessons.summary: This objective tests whether you can measure and reduce unfair outcomes and be honest with the people affected by a system. Expect scenarios on counterfactual bias testing, disaggregated evaluation, AI disclosure, meaningful human review of high-stakes recommendations, and traceable explanations rather than post-hoc rationalisation.
keyPoints: **Measure before you fix.** Anthropic's discrimination research generated many decision prompts and **systematically varied demographic information** in otherwise identical cases to expose outcome differences; careful prompting reduced both positive and negative discrimination. Use the same counterfactual pattern, including proxies (names, postcodes, language).
**Disaggregate evaluations**: report quality per language, region, user group and document type. A strong aggregate score can hide a segment the system fails.

**Minimise sensitive inputs**: remove protected attributes and close proxies the decision doesn't need, then re-run the counterfactual suite; keep it as a regression gate on every prompt or model change.

**High-risk uses** under Anthropic's Usage Policy (for example legal, medical, finance, credit, insurance, housing, employment, education, public benefits): a qualified person must meaningfully review the AI recommendation with authority to change it, and the affected person must be told AI was used.
**AI disclosure**: consumer-facing chatbots and agents must disclose that users are interacting with AI, at least at the start of each session or in the interface.
**Transparency in agents**: show planning steps and sources. Explanations should be generated **with** the decision and tied to published criteria and cited evidence, not asked for after the fact.
**Honest claims**: report measured performance with its scope (dataset size, segments covered, date), label AI-generated content, and provide a path to a human and to contest a decision.
Bias work is lifecycle work: diverse eval data at design, counterfactual tests before launch, segment monitoring and complaint review in production.
traps: Deleting the protected attribute and declaring the system fair without testing proxies.
Publishing one aggregate accuracy figure as proof of fairness.
Giving an AI persona a human name without telling users it is AI.
Treating a reviewer who can only click 'approve' as meaningful human review.
Asking the model afterwards 'why did you decide this?' and presenting that as the explanation.

docs.title: Evaluating and mitigating discrimination in LM decisions

lessons.drill: Take 30 cases from a decision-support prompt you own. Create variants that change only a name, a postcode or the writing style. Run them, compute the score gap per attribute, and pick the largest. Change the prompt (explicit criteria, remove the unnecessary attribute) and re-run to see whether the gap shrinks without hurting overall accuracy.

lessons.title: Structured discovery and requirement gathering
lessons.summary: The exam checks that you can turn a vague business ask into measurable success criteria, real data, named stakeholders and hard constraints before you choose a model or pattern. The right answer usually means asking a sharper question or getting a baseline, not building something.
keyPoints: **Start with the problem, not the model.** Find out the business outcome, who owns it, today's process and what it costs. 'Build an agent' is a proposed solution. The requirement is something like 'cut refund handling time without raising wrong refunds'.

**Success criteria must be specific, measurable, achievable and relevant** (Anthropic's eval guidance). 'Accurate' becomes something like '>= 0.85 F1 on a held-out labelled set'. Most systems need several criteria at once: task fidelity, consistency, tone, privacy, latency and price.
**Baseline the current process** (handle time, error rate, cost per case, backlog) before you design. Without a baseline nobody can show ROI later, and 'is it better?' turns into a matter of opinion.

**Collect real, representative samples early**, including messy edge cases, ambiguous inputs and cases where experts disagree. Curated 'happy path' examples hide the hard part of the problem and inflate feasibility estimates.

**Map the stakeholders**: the business owner, end users, people who consume the output downstream, compliance, legal, privacy and security approvers, and the operations team that will run it. Approvers who show up late are the most common cause of late redesigns.

**Surface hard constraints up front**: data residency and the platform choice (Claude API vs Bedrock, Vertex AI or Foundry), retention and ZDR eligibility of the features you plan to use, throughput against rate limits, cost ceiling, audit needs, and which actions can't be reversed.

**Quantify asymmetric error costs.** Ask what a false negative costs compared with a false positive, and which actions need human approval. The answers set thresholds, review rules and how much autonomy the system gets.
**Check feasibility with a time-boxed spike** against a small labelled set before committing to targets. Achievable targets come from your own measurements, not public benchmarks.
**Prefer the simplest solution that meets the criteria.** Discovery may show that a single call, a deterministic rule or no LLM at all is enough. Agents are for steps you can't predict in advance.
traps: Building a prototype first and asking stakeholders whether it 'feels good enough'. That is not an acceptance criterion.
Treating compliance or the operations team as sign-off steps at the end instead of discovery participants.
Taking a feasibility target from a vendor benchmark or leaderboard instead of a spike on the customer's own data.
Asking which model or framework the stakeholder prefers as a discovery question. That is a design choice, not a requirement.
Accepting curated sample data that leaves out the edge cases production will be full of.

docs.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

lessons.drill: Take the request 'Use Claude to speed up our supplier-onboarding reviews.' Write a one-page discovery plan: 6 questions for the business owner, the 4 stakeholder groups you would interview and why, the baseline metrics you would collect, the sample data you would ask for (how many items, which edge cases), and three measurable success criteria with numbers. Mark which answers could change the architecture.

lessons.title: Communicating architectural decisions and trade-offs
lessons.summary: You present the same decision differently to executives, compliance and engineering, but always with measured evidence and honest residual risk. Expect questions where the right option frames a trade-off in the audience's units (cost per outcome, risk, effort) and the distractors overpromise, bury the bad news or argue from benchmarks.
keyPoints: **Translate to the audience's units.** Executives want cost per resolved case, time saved and risk compared with the baseline. Compliance wants data flows, controls, residual risk and audit evidence. Engineers want interfaces, failure modes and operational load. Tokens and per-token prices are inputs to the numbers, not the message.

**Present options, not a single answer.** Give 2–3 viable options with quantified trade-offs (quality on your eval, p95 latency, cost per task at projected volume, operational complexity) and a clear recommendation with its reasoning.
**Compare on cost per completed task**, including retries and human rework. A cheaper tier that fails more often can cost more overall. Show the whole cost, not the token price.

**Be honest about residual error.** LLM systems have a measured, non-zero error rate. Say what it is, how it was measured (sample size, how representative), and which controls limit the impact (grounding with citations, validation, human review on high-risk paths). Never promise 'zero hallucinations'.

**Explain mechanisms in plain terms**: streaming improves *perceived* latency (time to first token), not total time. The Batches API halves cost but gives up immediacy (most batches finish within an hour, up to 24 h). A bigger context window adds cost and latency and doesn't guarantee better answers.
**Tie every claim to evidence**: your eval results, load tests and pilot data. Public benchmarks are context, not proof for this workload.
**Deliver bad news early, with options**: if the eval misses the target, say so with the data and offer choices (narrow the scope, add human review, extend the timeline). Don't quietly lower the bar.
**Record the decision and the alternatives you rejected** (an ADR) so the reasoning survives staff changes and can be revisited when the facts change.
traps: Leading an executive briefing with per-million-token prices or model names instead of business outcomes.
Telling compliance that a system-prompt instruction 'prevents' a risk. Explain the deterministic controls instead.
Citing leaderboard rankings as the reason to pick a model for this workload.
Presenting one option as inevitable, which hides the trade-offs the stakeholder is entitled to choose between.
Reporting a point estimate from 40 eval items as if it were a guarantee.
lessons.drill: For one of your Claude features, write three 5-sentence briefs on the same decision (for example routing to a smaller tier): one for a CFO (cost per outcome, risk), one for a compliance lead (data flow, controls, residual risk) and one for the engineering team (interfaces, failure modes, on-call impact). Every number must trace back to an eval or a load test.

lessons.title: Feedback loops, expectation alignment and SLAs
lessons.summary: This objective checks that you agree measurable targets before launch, set SLAs from measured distributions with headroom and with dependencies taken into account, and turn stakeholder and user feedback into eval cases and controlled changes instead of reacting to anecdotes.
keyPoints: **Agree success and exit criteria before a pilot**: the metrics, thresholds, sample size, duration and who decides. Then a single bad demo output is a data point you triage, not a reason to roll back.

**Set SLAs from measurement**: load-test at the projected peak, read the p50/p95/p99 distribution, add headroom, and state the measurement window and method. Never set an SLA from a demo or a vendor's typical speeds.
**Quality SLOs are statistical**: 'at least 95% of sampled responses pass the rubric each week', measured with a defined grader. 'The model will never be wrong' is not a target you can commit to.

**Account for dependencies.** Your availability can't exceed your upstream's unless you design fallbacks (queueing, retry with backoff, a degraded mode, a cached answer or human handoff). Write down what is excluded and what degraded behaviour looks like.

**Match the latency promise to the need**: if consumers can wait a day, agree an asynchronous SLA and use the Message Batches API (50% cheaper, results within 24 h). Don't build real-time capacity nobody needs.

**Close the feedback loop**: capture explicit feedback (ratings, corrections) and implicit signals (escalations, edits, retries), triage and label them, add failures to the regression eval set, fix, re-evaluate, and release behind a flag.
**Explicit feedback is biased and sparse.** Complement it with randomly sampled grading of production traffic, and segment by cohort, intent and prompt version.
**Manage scope changes through change control**: estimate the impact of every new request on evals, cost, latency and timeline, then let the owner prioritise.
**Set user expectations in the product**: say what the assistant can and can't do (no live browsing, no memory between sessions unless built in), where it may be wrong, and how to escalate.
traps: Promising a p95 latency from a few demo calls on an idle system.
Committing to 99.99% availability with a single upstream model dependency and no fallback.
Rolling back a launch because an executive saw one bad answer, when the agreed metrics are within threshold.
Collecting thumbs-down ratings into a dashboard that nobody turns into eval cases.
Accepting 'just add three more languages' without re-running evals and re-estimating cost.

docs.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

lessons.drill: Draft an SLO sheet for a Claude summarisation service: one latency SLO (percentile, window, how it's measured), one quality SLO (rubric, grader, weekly sample size), one availability SLO with exclusions and degraded-mode behaviour, plus an error budget and an escalation path. Then design the feedback loop that turns a user correction into a regression eval case.

lessons.title: Architecture documentation and implementation guidance
lessons.summary: You're tested on writing documentation that keeps decisions auditable and makes teams self-sufficient: ADRs with context, alternatives and consequences; data-flow views for compliance; runbooks for operators; and short reference implementations that encode the platform's conventions.
keyPoints: **An ADR records context, the decision, the alternatives considered and the consequences** (good and bad), plus a status and a date. 'We use Sonnet' is not an ADR. 'Sonnet-tier for drafting because it met the 92% rubric target at a third of the Opus-tier cost per task; trade-off: weaker on X; revisit if Y' is.
**ADRs are append-only.** When a decision changes, write a new ADR that supersedes the old one and mark the old one 'Superseded by ADR-NNN'. Don't rewrite history.

**Document the 'why' with evidence**: link the eval run, the load test or the cost model that justified each threshold (for example a human-review confidence cutoff). Auditors and future maintainers need the reasoning, not just the setting.

**For compliance reviews, draw the data flow**: the source systems, what is redacted, which platform and region processes the request (Claude API, Bedrock, Vertex AI, Foundry), what is logged and for how long, which tools can read or write what, and where the trust boundaries are.

**Platform choice has documented consequences**: partner-operated platforms such as Amazon Bedrock set their own model retirement schedules, and feature availability can differ between platforms. Record these in the ADR.

**Implementation guidance is code, not prose**: a reference client or gateway that pins the model ID in configuration, logs `request_id`, model, prompt version, `usage`, `stop_reason` and latency, retries 429/529 with backoff, and uses structured outputs for JSON. Teams copy what works.
**Tool and MCP contracts are documentation the model reads.** Clear names, parameter descriptions, examples and actionable error messages improve agent behaviour as well as human understanding.

**Runbooks map symptoms to actions**: 429 or 529 spikes, a rise in `stop_reason: max_tokens`, more refusals, cost anomalies, and model deprecation notices. Each entry names the owner and the rollback step.

**Tailor the view to the audience**: a context diagram for executives, component and sequence views for engineers, data flow and controls for compliance. It is one model of the system with several views.
traps: Editing an old ADR in place when the decision changes, which loses the audit trail.
A 60-page wiki as the only implementation guidance, with no runnable reference code.
Documenting 'the system prompt tells the model not to send data outside the EU' as a residency control.
Telling teams to set `temperature` to 0 everywhere: current models reject sampling parameters with a 400 error.
Leaving the model ID, the prompt version and the eval evidence out of the architecture record.

code.src:
# ADR-014: Route ticket summarisation to the Haiku tier
Status: Accepted (supersedes ADR-009) | Date: 2026-10-02
Context: 1.2M tickets/month; ADR-009 used the Sonnet tier at $X/month.
Decision: Haiku tier, pinned ID in config `SUMMARY_MODEL`.
Alternatives: Sonnet tier (baseline); Batches API (rejected: agents need it live).
Evidence: eval run #318: 94.1% vs 95.0% rubric pass; p95 1.1 s vs 2.4 s.
Consequences: -61% cost per ticket; weaker on multi-thread tickets ->
  route those to Sonnet tier. Revisit if pass rate < 93% for 2 weeks.

lessons.drill: Write two ADRs for a Claude system you know: the original platform choice (Claude API vs a cloud platform) and a later one that supersedes a model-tier decision. Each needs context, decision, at least two alternatives, the evidence, consequences and a revisit trigger. Then write a 10-line runbook entry for 'stop_reason max_tokens rate tripled overnight'.

lessons.title: Supporting lifecycle phases
lessons.summary: The exam treats a Claude system as a product with a life cycle: discovery, design, handoff to an operating team, monitoring, iteration and eventually migration or retirement. Expect questions on handoff packages, change control for prompts and models, and planned model migrations.
keyPoints: **Handoff is a deliverable**: named owners, an on-call runbook, dashboards and alerts, the eval suite with its thresholds, prompt and model version history, rollback steps, and known limitations. Run a period of shadowing or joint on-call before the transfer.

**Every change is a deploy**: a prompt, the model ID, a tool schema, effort or `max_tokens`. Version it, gate it with regression evals, release it behind a flag or a percentage split, and keep a one-step rollback.

**Model lifecycle**: Active, then Legacy, then Deprecated (still works, has a retirement date and a recommended replacement), then Retired, after which **requests fail** and are not redirected. Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice before retiring publicly released models.
**Find every place a model is used**: the Claude Console Usage page can export a CSV broken down by API key and model. Pair it with a code search for model IDs and assign each use an owner.

**Platform schedules differ**: dates on Anthropic's deprecations page apply to Anthropic-operated platforms. Partner-operated platforms (Amazon Bedrock, Google-managed Vertex AI) set their own retirement schedules, so check theirs.

**Migrate early, with evals**: test the replacement well before the retirement date. Compare quality, format compliance, refusals, latency and token usage and cost per task. Re-tune the prompts (remove workarounds written for the old model), then canary with rollback triggers.

**Iteration loop**: production failures feed the eval set, prompts or tools change, the change goes through the regression gate and a staged release, then you monitor. Watch quality drift that still returns HTTP 200 (`stop_reason` mix, refusals, rubric scores).

**Decommissioning is a phase too**: tell users and give them a timeline, remove traffic, revoke API keys and tool or MCP credentials, apply the retention policy to logs and stored outputs, and archive the ADRs and eval results.
traps: Assuming a retired model ID is routed automatically to its successor.
Using the dates on Anthropic's deprecations page for a workload that runs on Amazon Bedrock.
Handing the system over as 'the repo plus a README' with no eval suite, alerts or owners.
Moving 100% of traffic to a new model the day it is announced, without a canary.
Leaving API keys and MCP server credentials active after a feature is shut down.

docs.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

lessons.drill: Pretend the model your service uses was just deprecated. Within 15 minutes, write the migration plan: how you find every use (Console usage export plus code search), the owner of each use, the eval comparison table you'll fill in (quality, schema-valid rate, refusals, p95 latency, cost per task), the canary percentage and rollback triggers, and the date by which 100% of traffic is moved, well before retirement.

lessons.title: Configure Claude Code for teams
lessons.summary: Expect questions on putting each configuration in the right scope (managed, project, local, user), what enforces versus what merely guides, and how an organisation rolls out models, permissions, telemetry, MCP servers and skills consistently. The right answer uses managed settings for policy, committed project files for team conventions, and personal files for preferences.
keyPoints: **Settings precedence** (highest first): managed → command line (`--settings`) → project local `.claude/settings.local.json` → shared project `.claude/settings.json` → user `~/.claude/settings.json`. List keys such as `permissions.allow` **merge** across scopes rather than override.

**Managed settings** (server-managed from the admin console, MDM/OS policy, or a `managed-settings.json` file) carry org policy that users can't override. A managed `model` is only a default; `availableModels` / `deniedModels` are the locks. `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` makes managed settings the only source of permission rules (user, project and local allow/ask/deny rules are ignored).

**Permissions** evaluate deny → ask → allow; a local allow can't beat a project or managed deny. In a committed project file, deny and ask rules apply at once, while allow rules wait until each developer trusts the folder. `bypassPermissions` and `auto` as `defaultMode` don't take effect from project or local files.

**Guidance vs enforcement**: CLAUDE.md, skills and prompts are guidance. Anything that must always or never happen belongs in hooks (command/http hooks are deterministic), deny rules, the sandbox, or managed settings.

**Where things live**: team conventions in committed `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/` (path-scoped); repeatable procedures in `.claude/skills/`; reviewers and specialists in `.claude/agents/`; project MCP servers in `.mcp.json` at the repo root (one-time approval per developer); cross-repo distribution via plugins and a marketplace.
**Personal preferences** go in `~/.claude/settings.json`, `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` or `CLAUDE.local.md` — never in shared files, and they never reach CI or teammates.

**Telemetry for adoption and cost**: enable OpenTelemetry (`CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1` plus exporter settings) through managed settings' `env`. Repository settings can't set the exporter variables. Prompt content is redacted unless explicitly enabled.
**Model and effort defaults** can be set per scope; switching model mid-session re-reads the conversation uncached. Subagents can run a cheaper model (`model: haiku`) for simple jobs.
**Verify a rollout** with `/status` (active setting sources, including managed), `/permissions`, `/context` and `claude doctor`.
traps: Putting an org-wide security rule in a project CLAUDE.md ('never read .env') instead of a managed deny rule.
Expecting a developer's local allow to override a project deny, or a committed allow rule to apply before the folder is trusted.
Setting a managed `model` and believing developers can't pick other models (that needs `availableModels`).
Committing personal sandbox paths or API endpoints into `.claude/settings.json`.
Defining MCP servers under `mcpServers` in `settings.json` or inside `.claude/` instead of `.mcp.json` at the repo root.
lessons.drill: Draft a rollout plan for a 50-engineer team: list five settings and say for each whether it belongs in managed, project, local or user scope and why. Then create a test repo with a committed deny rule and a local allow rule for the same command, run `/permissions` and `/status`, and confirm which rule wins.

lessons.title: Improve developer workflows with AI-assisted tooling
lessons.summary: Questions describe a team adopting Claude Code (or the API) and ask which workflow change raises quality or throughput: give Claude a check to run, plan before broad changes, review with fresh context, isolate parallel work, and automate in CI with narrow permissions and budgets. Distractors trust 'done' without evidence or let the generator review itself.
keyPoints: **Give Claude a check to run**: tests, typecheck, linter or a fixture diff, with the exact command in CLAUDE.md. To *enforce* it, use a `Stop` hook that exits 2 so Claude keeps working until the check passes; ask for evidence (command + output), not 'all tests pass'.

**Explore → plan → implement**: plan mode (`Shift+Tab` or `--permission-mode plan`) blocks edits until you approve, which is worth it for cross-cutting or unfamiliar changes and wasteful for a one-line fix.
**Spec first for fuzzy work**: have Claude interview you and write `SPEC.md`, then build in a fresh session from the spec, and review against it.

**Independent review**: a reviewer that never saw the generating conversation (a fresh subagent, `/code-review`, or a separate CI session) catches what the author's reasoning hides. Give a reviewer subagent read-only tools (`Read, Grep, Glob`) so the limit is enforced, and scope it ('report correctness gaps, skip style').
**Parallel work without collisions**: separate git worktrees per session (`claude --worktree <name>`), so concurrent edits land on separate branches.
**Context hygiene**: `/clear` between unrelated tasks; delegate broad exploration to subagents; after two failed corrections, clear and write a better prompt rather than a third correction.

**Automation**: `claude -p` in CI or scripts with `--output-format json` (or `--json-schema`), narrow `--allowedTools`, `dontAsk` permission mode, and caps (`--max-turns`, `--max-budget-usd`, job timeouts). Never `bypassPermissions` outside an isolated container.
**Cost-aware habits**: subagents add tokens; use a cheaper model for simple subagent jobs and lower effort for quick iterative steps; check `/usage` to see which skills or subagents consume the most.
**Measure the workflow change** with team metrics (PR cycle time, review findings, rework, cost per merged PR from telemetry), not anecdotes.
traps: Letting the session that wrote the code review its own diff.
Running two Claude sessions on the same checkout so their edits collide.
Using plan mode for every trivial fix, or skipping it for a multi-module migration.
Letting Claude edit the tests it must satisfy instead of locking them (deny rule) and iterating on the implementation.
Adding 'IMPORTANT' to CLAUDE.md for a rule that has to hold every time instead of a hook.
lessons.drill: In a sample repo, add a `Stop` hook that runs the typecheck and exits 2 on failure, plus a read-only `reviewer` subagent in `.claude/agents/`. Ask Claude for a change that breaks a type, watch the hook send it back, then have the reviewer compare the diff to a short spec. Note what each control caught.

lessons.title: Support debugging and operational issue resolution
lessons.summary: The exam gives a symptom — an ignored instruction, a hook that never fires, an MCP server with no tools, a spike of API errors, rising cost — and asks for the first diagnostic step or the root cause. Good answers inspect what actually loaded or what the API actually returned before changing prompts or models.
keyPoints: **Claude Code: inspect what loaded.** `/context` (what fills the window: memory files, skills, MCP tools), `/status` (active settings sources, including managed), `/permissions` (resolved rules), `/hooks`, `/mcp`, `/memory`, `/skills`; `claude doctor` prints settings and installation diagnostics without a session; `/doctor` proposes fixes.

**Isolate the cause**: `claude --safe-mode` turns off your customisations (CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP); a clean `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` with `--setting-sources user` excludes your own config. If the problem persists, look at managed settings or environment variables.
**If an instruction loaded but is ignored**, it's the wording or a conflict (vague, contradicted, buried in a long file), not loading; if it must hold every time, move it to a hook or deny rule.

**Common config faults**: hook `matcher` is case-sensitive and a string (`"Edit|Write"`), hooks live under `hooks` in settings files; project MCP config is `.mcp.json` at the repo root and needs one-time approval; relative paths in MCP `command`/`args` resolve from the launch directory; subdirectory CLAUDE.md loads only when Claude touches that directory. `claude --debug` shows hook and MCP evaluation.
**API triage order**: HTTP status/type → `stop_reason` → `usage` vs `max_tokens` → the exact request (roles, tool_use/tool_result pairing) → only then prompt or model choice.

**Status codes**: 400 malformed or unsupported parameter (fix, don't retry); 401/403 credential or permission; 404 wrong or retired model ID; 413 payload too large; 429 your rate limit (honour `retry-after`); 500 transient; 529 service overloaded. Retry 429/5xx/529 with exponential backoff and jitter; the SDKs already retry these by default.

**Integration-bug signatures**: truncated tool JSON with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`; a 400 about unanswered `tool_use` IDs after parallel calls; repeated identical tool calls when a handler returns an empty string instead of `is_error: true`.

**Log the request ID** of failing calls for support escalation, and use OpenTelemetry metrics (cost, tokens by type including cache reads, sessions) to spot regressions such as a cache-hit collapse after a prompt change.
traps: Switching to a bigger model to fix truncated JSON when `stop_reason` is `max_tokens`.
Treating 529 overload as your rate limit, or rotating API keys to escape 429s.
Wrapping a blanket retry loop around an SDK that already retries, multiplying attempts and retrying permanent 4xx errors.
Adding more emphasis to CLAUDE.md before checking with `/context` that the file loaded at all.
Pasting a multi-megabyte log into the session instead of grepping it or delegating analysis to a subagent.
lessons.drill: Break three things on purpose in a test repo: a lowercase hook matcher, an MCP server with a relative script path, and a CLAUDE.md placed in a subdirectory. For each, find the fault using only `/hooks`, `/mcp`, `/context` and `claude doctor`, and write down which command revealed it.

questions.stem: The research system's lead agent runs on the Agent SDK. For simple fact questions ("What year was the company founded?") it still spawns eight subagents and runs 40+ searches, and on obscure topics it sometimes runs for an hour chasing sources that don't exist. Which change BEST addresses both problems?
options: Move the lead agent to the most capable model tier so it can judge question complexity on its own
Add a `Stop` hook that sends the lead back to work until the report cites at least ten distinct sources
Remove subagents and answer every question in one agent loop with no turn limit, so research on hard topics is never cut off early
Add effort-scaling rules to the lead's prompt and enforce `max_turns` and `max_budget_usd` limits in the harness
explanations: A stronger model may judge complexity a little better, but nothing bounds the runaway case and nothing tells it how much effort each question type deserves.
This forces even more work on simple questions and could loop forever when ten sources don't exist.
This removes the over-spawning but makes the runaway problem worse: with no limit, nothing stops a loop chasing nonexistent sources.

Correct. Scaling rules (simple fact: one agent and a few calls; broad comparison: several subagents) address over-spawning; Anthropic's research system embedded such rules because agents struggled to judge appropriate effort, and hard turn/budget caps in the harness stop the runaway loops regardless of what the model decides.

questions.stem: In the research system, the coordinator runs a `market-size` subagent and a `regulatory-impact` subagent in parallel. The regulatory analysis needs the market-size figures to estimate exposure, so its section often contains invented placeholder numbers. A developer proposes letting the two subagents message each other mid-task. What should the architect do instead?
options: Let both subagents append to a shared scratch file as they work, so each can read the other's latest figures
Merge the two subagents into one with both tool sets, so it has the market figures in its own context
Run `market-size` first, then pass its condensed figures into the `regulatory-impact` brief
Keep both in parallel and tell `regulatory-impact` in its prompt to estimate market size itself when needed
explanations: Concurrent writes to a shared file create a race: the regulatory worker may read before the figures exist, and the coordinator no longer controls what each worker sees.
This works for two workers but discards the specialization and context isolation that justified separate subagents; it doesn't scale to the general dependency problem.

Correct. A real dependency means the subtasks are sequential. Routing the first result through the coordinator keeps hub-and-spoke control and gives the second worker the exact inputs it needs in its brief.
This duplicates work and produces figures that may contradict the market-size worker's, leaving the coordinator to reconcile two estimates.

questions.stem: The research team is splitting responsibilities between the coordinator and its search/analysis subagents. Which TWO responsibilities should stay with the coordinator? (Select TWO.)
options: Running each individual web search and reading the full source pages
Decomposing the research question into subtasks and deciding which can run in parallel
Extracting quotes and publication dates from each source document
Synthesizing worker findings into the report and resolving contradictions between workers
Retrying a failed page fetch inside a worker's own search loop
explanations: This is worker execution. Doing it in the coordinator floods its context with raw pages, which is what delegation is meant to avoid.
Correct. Decomposition and scheduling need the whole question in view; that is the coordinator's job.
Per-source extraction is narrow, parallelizable worker work.
Correct. Only the coordinator sees all workers' results, so only it can merge them and reconcile conflicting findings.
Retrying a fetch is local to the worker's own tool loop; escalating every transient failure to the coordinator adds latency and noise.

questions.stem: The research coordinator splits a question into five independent sub-questions, but it starts each search subagent only after the previous one has returned. Reports are good, but each takes about 25 minutes. Which change MOST directly cuts the run time?
options: Switch every subagent to the most capable model tier so that each one finishes its searches faster
Merge the five sub-questions into one subagent so there is only a single round trip
Launch the five independent subagents in parallel, then synthesize once all have returned
Add an evaluator subagent that reviews each worker's output before the next one starts
explanations: A larger model is usually slower per call, and it doesn't remove the serial waiting that dominates run time.
One worker doing five sub-questions serially is no faster and loses context isolation between them.
Correct. Independent subtasks don't need to wait for each other; running them concurrently makes total time roughly that of the slowest worker.
This adds a step to every worker and makes the run longer.

questions.stem: Spot checks of the research system's reports show that about 8% of claims cite a source that doesn't actually support them. The synthesis subagent writes the report from the search workers' findings. Which design change BEST reduces unsupported citations?
options: Add a separate citation-check step that maps each claim to source text, with one bounded revision
Double the number of search subagents so the synthesis step has more sources to cite from
Have each search subagent re-read the final report and confirm every claim that cites one of its own sources
Add "double-check every citation before you finish" to the synthesis subagent's prompt
explanations: Correct. A dedicated evaluator with a clear criterion (does the cited text support the claim?) is the evaluator-optimizer pattern, much like the separate citation agent in Anthropic's research system. Capping revisions prevents loops.
More sources don't fix mis-attribution; they give the synthesizer more material to mis-cite.
Search workers have already returned and have no view of the full report; restarting them all is costly and leaves no one in charge of the outcome.
Self-review in the same context tends to confirm its own work, and nothing enforces that the check happens.

questions.stem: An analyst asks the research system: "For the ten largest grid-battery suppliers in Europe, summarize each one's capacity plans and recent regulatory issues." The coordinator immediately spawns ten subagents, each briefed "Research one of the ten largest European grid-battery suppliers." Several workers pick the same companies and two well-known suppliers are missing. What is the BEST orchestration?
options: Spawn twenty subagents with the same brief so overlap is more likely to cover all ten suppliers
Run one subagent to identify the ten suppliers first, then fan out one subagent per supplier in parallel
Run a single agent that researches all ten suppliers one after another in its own context
Keep the ten parallel subagents and have each one post its chosen company to a shared list so the others avoid it
explanations: Redundancy wastes tokens and still can't guarantee coverage, because no worker knows the definitive list.
Correct. Identifying the list is a dependency for the per-supplier work, so it runs first; the per-supplier subtasks are then independent and can run in parallel with distinct scopes.
This avoids duplication but is slow and piles ten companies' research into one context.
Workers coordinating through a shared list race each other and still don't agree on which ten are the largest.

questions.stem: The CI pipeline uses `claude -p` to propose fixes for failing builds. The team wants an evaluator-optimizer loop so weak fixes get improved before a PR is opened. Which design applies the pattern correctly?
options: A separate reviewer scores the fix on explicit criteria and feeds failures back, with a round cap and human fallback
Run five independent fix attempts and open a PR for whichever produced the largest diff
After generating the fix, ask the same session to "review your fix critically and improve it" and repeat until it says the fix is good
Loop generator and reviewer until the reviewer reports zero findings, with no limit, so only perfect fixes ship
explanations: Correct. Evaluator-optimizer needs an independent evaluator, clear criteria (for example tests pass, no public API change) and an iteration cap with a fallback.
This is voting with a meaningless selection criterion; diff size says nothing about correctness.
The generator critiquing itself in the same context tends to approve its own reasoning, and the stop condition is the model's own say-so.
A reviewer asked to find problems will nearly always find something, so an uncapped loop burns budget and may never end.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline handles three document types (invoices, purchase contracts, customs forms). Each type has its own schema and extraction prompt, and an existing classifier labels the type with 99% accuracy. An engineer proposes a coordinator agent that reads each document and dynamically spawns whichever extraction subagents it thinks are needed. What should the architect recommend?
options: The coordinator agent as proposed, because dynamic delegation adapts better to unusual or mixed documents than a fixed classifier
A routing workflow: classify, dispatch to that type's prompt and schema, and send low-confidence labels to review
One general extraction prompt with all three schemas merged, so no classification step is needed
A coordinator agent plus an evaluator subagent that re-extracts every document to confirm the first result
explanations: Dynamic orchestration adds cost, latency and variance for a decision that a classifier already makes reliably.
Correct. The categories are known in advance and classification is reliable, which is exactly what routing is for: predictable, cheap and auditable.
A merged schema invites cross-type confusion and fields being filled from the wrong document type.
This doubles the cost of every document on top of an orchestration layer the problem doesn't need.

questions.stem: The support-resolution agent handles multi-turn conversations with customers. The team is deciding where subagents help. Which TWO tasks are good candidates for delegating to a subagent? (Select TWO.)
options: Searching three years of a customer's order history and the knowledge base, where only the conclusion matters to the conversation
Asking the customer a clarifying question about which of two orders they mean
Issuing a refund the main agent has already verified and approved
Running a fraud-pattern analysis with read-only tools, isolated from the refund and account-change tools
Summarizing the current conversation so the main agent can remember it
explanations: Correct. Verbose, self-contained research whose output can be a short summary is a textbook use of a subagent's isolated context.
The clarifying question belongs in the live conversation; a subagent has no direct channel to the customer.
A single, already-decided tool call gains nothing from delegation and adds latency.
Correct. A subagent with a restricted tool set enforces separation: the analysis can't trigger refunds or account changes.
A fresh subagent doesn't see the conversation, so it can't summarize it unless the whole history is passed in, which defeats the point.

questions.stem: In the research system, the user and the coordinator spend several turns narrowing a question to "EU lithium-refining capacity announced since 2024, excluding pilot plants." The coordinator then delegates with the Agent tool prompt "Research the refining question we discussed." The subagent returns a generic global overview. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
options: A non-fork subagent sees only its brief; put the exact question, scope and exclusions in the Agent prompt
The subagent lacks the coordinator's tools; give it the same tool list as the coordinator
The subagent ran out of turns; raise its `maxTurns` so it can keep exploring until it discovers the intended scope
The subagent's model tier is too small to infer the scope; set `model` to a more capable tier
explanations: Correct. The parent conversation isn't visible to a non-fork subagent; the Agent tool's prompt string is the only channel from parent to subagent.
Tools aren't the gap; the subagent searched fine, just for the wrong question.
More turns spent on an unscoped question produce a longer generic overview.
No model can recover constraints that were never sent to it.

questions.stem: The research coordinator's context keeps hitting compaction partway through large jobs. Logs show each search subagent returns its full working notes, including the raw text of every page it read, often 30,000+ tokens per worker. What change BEST fixes this?
options: Disable compaction on the coordinator so that none of the worker output is ever summarized away
Move the coordinator to a model with a larger context window so that every worker's full output fits without compaction
Have subagents return their full notes but ask the coordinator to ignore everything except the conclusions
Subagents save full text to storage and return a short structured result: claims, source refs, dates, gaps
explanations: Without compaction the coordinator simply runs out of context.
A bigger window postpones the problem and worsens attention dilution on the content that matters.
Telling the model to ignore tokens doesn't remove them from the context; the cost and dilution remain.

Correct. Only a subagent's final message enters the parent's context, so make it condensed. Writing full material to storage and passing references keeps detail available without bloating the coordinator.

questions.stem: The research coordinator is rewriting the template it uses to brief search subagents. Which TWO elements MUST each brief include? (Select TWO.)
options: The full transcript of the coordinator's conversation so far, so the worker has all possible context
The specific sub-question with scope boundaries (time range, regions, exclusions)
A note that the worker can read the coordinator's history if it needs more detail
The required output format, e.g. claims with source URL and publication date
The tool lists of the other subagents, so the worker knows who else is searching
explanations: This bloats the worker's context with mostly irrelevant material and sends data the worker doesn't need.
Correct. Without a clear objective and boundaries, workers duplicate each other, leave gaps and drift.
False premise: a non-fork subagent cannot see the parent's history at all.
Correct. A common output format lets the coordinator merge results and preserves provenance.
Other workers' tool lists don't help a worker do its own task; non-overlapping scope does.

questions.stem: The research coordinator has the two subagents below. When users ask it to analyze academic PDFs that search workers have already saved, it usually delegates to `web-searcher`, which runs new searches instead. What is the BEST fix?

code.src:
agents={
  "web-searcher": AgentDefinition(
      description="Helps with research.",
      prompt=SEARCH_PROMPT, tools=["WebSearch", "WebFetch"]),
  "paper-analyst": AgentDefinition(
      description="Research helper.",
      prompt=ANALYST_PROMPT, tools=["Read", "Grep"]),
}

options: Rename the subagents to `a-web-searcher` and `b-paper-analyst` so the coordinator considers them in the intended order
Rewrite both descriptions to state when to use each: saved PDFs go to paper-analyst, new sources to web-searcher
Remove `web-searcher` and let `paper-analyst` handle both searching and analysis
Raise `paper-analyst` to a larger model tier so the coordinator trusts it with more work
explanations: Ordering by name isn't how delegation is chosen; Claude matches tasks against descriptions.
Correct. `description` is the main signal for automatic delegation. Vague, overlapping descriptions make selection near-random; explicit when-to-use criteria fix routing.
This collapses a useful separation of tools and context to avoid writing two good descriptions.
The model tier of a subagent doesn't affect which one the coordinator picks.

questions.stem: The research system's `synthesizer` subagent should only read the findings files that workers saved and write the report. In practice it often launches new web searches and adds unvetted sources. Its definition is below. What is the BEST fix?

code.src:
"synthesizer": AgentDefinition(
    description="Writes the final report from saved findings files.",
    prompt="Read findings/*.json and write a cited report.",
    model="opus",
)

options: Add "Do not search the web; use only the findings files" in capitals to the synthesizer's `prompt`
Remove `WebSearch` from the coordinator's `allowed_tools` so that no agent in the run is pre-approved to search
Ask the coordinator to remind the synthesizer in every brief that it must not search
Add `tools=["Read", "Glob"]` to the definition; an omitted `tools` field inherits every available tool
explanations: A prompt instruction is probabilistic; the tool stays available and will still be used sometimes.
`allowed_tools` controls auto-approval, not availability, and changing it also affects the search workers that need the tool.
Same weakness as a prompt rule, repeated in every brief.
Correct. With `tools` omitted the subagent gets every tool available to subagents. An explicit list removes web tools from its session entirely, which is a deterministic restriction.

questions.stem: In the research system, search subagents have saved 30 source documents to disk (about 2 million tokens in total). The coordinator now needs an analysis subagent to answer one sub-question from them. How should the coordinator pass the material?
options: Paste all 30 documents into the analysis subagent's brief so it has complete information
Summarize each document to a single line first and pass only those 30 lines to the subagent
Pass the sub-question, the file paths with a one-line note on each, and the output format
Fork the coordinator's conversation into the subagent so it inherits everything the coordinator has seen
explanations: 2M tokens won't fit in a context window, and even a fraction of it dilutes attention.
One-line summaries throw away the detail the analysis needs, and the subagent can't recover it.
Correct. The subagent reads only what it needs. Lightweight references plus just-in-time reading keep the brief small while giving the subagent access to full detail.
The coordinator's conversation doesn't contain the documents' full text either, and it would bring along unrelated history.

questions.stem: On the internal developer platform, a `repo-explorer` subagent helps engineers understand unfamiliar services. Its prompt ends with "Report everything you read so nothing is lost." Engineers say the main session becomes slow and unfocused after each exploration, because the result includes thousands of lines of pasted source. Which change BEST fixes this?
options: Replace the subagent with direct file reads in the main session so nothing has to be summarized
Run the main session on a larger-context model so the explorer's full output fits comfortably alongside the conversation
Have it return a concise summary: key files with paths and line ranges, the flow, and open questions
Have the main session run `/compact` after every exploration to shrink the pasted source
explanations: Reading everything in the main session puts the same volume of content into the main context, which is worse.
A larger window doesn't stop the noise from diluting attention and raising cost.
Correct. The subagent's final message is all that returns to the parent; asking for a condensed, referenced summary preserves isolation, and the engineer can open specific files by path when needed.
Compacting afterwards treats the symptom; the bloat is still sent and paid for each time.

questions.stem: The support-resolution agent delegates knowledge-base and public-web research to a `kb-researcher` subagent that has `WebFetch`. A review finds that the coordinator pastes the whole case into each brief, including the customer's address, payment method details and account notes. The research only needs the product and the symptom. What should the architect change?
options: Keep the full case but tell `kb-researcher` in its prompt never to include personal data in URLs or queries
Remove `WebFetch` from `kb-researcher` so it can only search the internal knowledge base
Pass only what the research needs (product, version, symptom, error codes), not the whole case
Encrypt the brief before passing it so the subagent's tools can't read the personal fields
explanations: This leaves the data in a context with outbound web access and relies on the model following an instruction.
This breaks a legitimate capability instead of fixing what is sent.
Correct. Because a subagent sees only what you pass it, brief contents are a data-minimization control. Sending only task-relevant fields removes the exposure.
The subagent must read its brief to work; encryption isn't a meaningful control here.

questions.stem: The support-resolution agent's system prompt says: "Always call `verify_identity` before calling `issue_refund`." An audit finds that about 3% of refunds were issued in conversations where verification never succeeded. What is the BEST fix?
options: Repeat the rule at the end of the system prompt with IMPORTANT, since instructions at the end get more attention
Add few-shot examples showing the agent calling `verify_identity` first in several different refund conversations
Run a nightly job that finds refunds without verification and claws them back from the customer's account
Have the `issue_refund` handler check server-side state for successful verification, else return an error
explanations: Emphasis can lower the failure rate but can't guarantee the order; a 3% miss rate on money movement needs a deterministic control.
Examples also shape behavior probabilistically; the refund still executes whenever the model skips the step.
Detecting violations after money has moved is remediation, not prevention, and creates a bad customer experience.
Correct. A prerequisite enforced in the tool handler runs every time. The error message also tells the agent what to do next.

questions.stem: The support-resolution team needs a guarantee that no refund is issued before the customer's identity is verified in the same conversation. Which TWO implementations provide that guarantee? (Select TWO.)
options: Add a required `identity_verified: boolean` parameter to `issue_refund` and reject calls where the model passes `false`
In the `issue_refund` handler, check a verified flag stored server-side for the authenticated conversation and refuse if it's missing
Leave `issue_refund` out of the agent's tool list until `verify_identity` returns success, then have the harness add it
Add a `PostToolUse` hook on `issue_refund` that alerts the fraud team when no verification preceded the refund
Put the verification rule first in the system prompt and add a red-team test suite that checks the agent follows it
explanations: The model fills in that parameter itself, so it can simply pass `true`. A gate must read state the model can't write.
Correct. The check reads state set only by the verification tool's own code path, so the model can't bypass it.
Correct. Tool gating by the harness makes an unverified refund impossible: the tool doesn't exist for the model until the prerequisite is met.
A `PostToolUse` hook runs after the refund has already been issued; it detects, it doesn't prevent.
Tests measure how often the prompt is followed; they don't enforce it in production.

questions.stem: When the support-resolution agent escalates a case, human agents receive the raw 60-120 turn transcript and spend several minutes reconstructing what happened; some re-ask the customer for information already verified. The team adds an `escalate_to_human` tool with a required input schema. Which THREE fields belong in that schema? (Select THREE.)
options: Customer and order identifiers, plus which identity checks have already passed
The agent's sentiment score for the customer, so humans can prioritize angry customers first
A summary of actions taken and their results (lookups, refunds attempted, policy checks)
The full list of tools available to the agent during the conversation
The reason for escalation and a recommended next step
The model tier and temperature used for the conversation
explanations: Correct. Identifiers and verified status let the human act immediately without re-verifying the customer.
A sentiment score doesn't tell the human what to do, and sentiment is a weak routing signal compared with the actual issue.
Correct. What was already tried, and what happened, prevents duplicate actions and repeated questions.
The agent's tool list is configuration, not case information; it doesn't help the human resolve the case.
Correct. Why the agent stopped (policy gap, customer request, failed action) plus a suggested next step makes the handoff actionable.
Model settings are operational metadata for engineers, not for the human resolving the case.

questions.stem: The support-resolution agent calls `check_refund_eligibility(order_id, amount)` before `issue_refund`. Investigations show a few approvals where the model passed a lower `amount` than the real order total (it paraphrased a customer's claim), so a large refund slipped under the auto-approval limit. Which change BEST closes this gap?
options: Add a system-prompt rule that the amount must be copied exactly from the order lookup result
Lower the auto-approval limit so that small mistakes in the amount matter less
Have a second model call review each eligibility request and confirm the amount looks consistent with the conversation
Change the tool to take only `order_id`; the handler fetches the real total and applies the limit to it
explanations: Still probabilistic; the model can paraphrase or mistype again.
This shrinks the impact but leaves the root cause: policy is still evaluated on a number the model chose.
A reviewing model reduces but doesn't remove errors, and it adds latency and cost to every refund.
Correct. Values that decide policy should come from the system of record, not from model-supplied input. Removing the parameter makes the error impossible.

questions.stem: In the extraction pipeline, an agent has tools `extract_fields`, `validate_document` and `write_to_erp`. The prompt says to write only after validation passes, but logs show occasional ERP writes of documents that were never validated. What is the BEST fix?
options: Remove `write_to_erp` from the agent; pipeline code writes to the ERP only after validation passes
Add a `PostToolUse` hook on `write_to_erp` that logs any write made without a prior validation
Strengthen the prompt and add a few-shot example of the correct three-step order
Ask the agent to output `validated: true` in its final JSON and write only when it does
explanations: Correct. When the order is fixed, the side effect belongs in deterministic code. The model extracts; the pipeline decides when to write.
Logging after the write detects the problem instead of preventing it.
A better prompt lowers the error rate but can't guarantee the order of an irreversible side effect.
The model sets that flag itself, so it's no stronger than the prompt rule.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline sends some documents to human reviewers. Reviewers say many routed items look fine while some bad extractions never reach them, and each item takes long to check because they must re-read the whole document. Which TWO changes BEST improve the handoff? (Select TWO.)
options: Route by code rules: validation failures, or field confidence below a threshold calibrated on labeled data
Ask the extraction model at the end of each document whether it is confident, and route the ones where it says no
Include the extracted values, the specific fields that failed and why, and the page/region each value came from
Attach the model's full reasoning transcript so reviewers can follow how it reached each value
Send every document to review in arrival order so reviewers see a representative sample
explanations: Correct. Deterministic, calibrated routing catches the failures that matter and stops sending clean items.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, which explains both symptoms: confident errors slip through and good items get flagged.
Correct. A focused package lets reviewers check specific fields at specific locations instead of re-reading the document.
A long transcript adds reading time; reviewers need the values and their sources, not the reasoning.
Reviewing everything defeats the purpose of automation and doesn't make individual reviews faster.

questions.stem: In the extraction pipeline, an extraction agent hands each processed invoice to a reconciliation agent by writing a prose summary ("Total is about 12.4k EUR, due next month, two line items…"). The reconciliation agent sometimes misreads amounts and dates. What is the BEST fix?
options: Define a typed handoff schema (amounts with currency, ISO dates, nulls, source refs) validated in code
Instruct the extraction agent to write more detailed prose that spells out every number precisely
Merge the extraction and reconciliation agents into one agent so that no handoff between stages is needed at all
Have the reconciliation agent re-extract the invoice itself and compare with the prose summary
explanations: Correct. A structured contract validated in code makes the handoff unambiguous, and a failed validation stops bad data at the boundary.
Prose is still ambiguous and can't be validated mechanically.
This removes the boundary but loses the separation of concerns, and the reconciliation logic still needs structured inputs.
Doubling the extraction work papers over an interface problem instead of fixing the interface.

questions.stem: A CI job runs `claude -p` to fix failing tests and then pushes the branch. CLAUDE.md says "Always run the full test suite before you finish." Sometimes the job pushes changes that still fail. Which design BEST guarantees nothing is pushed unless tests pass?
options: Put the test rule at the top of CLAUDE.md in capitals and repeat it in the `-p` prompt
Withhold push from Claude; after `claude -p` exits, the pipeline runs the tests and pushes only on success
Run Claude with `--dangerously-skip-permissions` so it can always run the test suite without being blocked by prompts
Request `--json-schema` output with a `tests_passed` boolean and push only when Claude reports `true`
explanations: Stronger wording still relies on the model choosing to follow it.
Correct. The pipeline's own test run is the gate, and withholding push from Claude means the required step can't be skipped.
Skipping permissions doesn't make the model run tests, and removes guardrails for an unattended job.
Structured output guarantees the format, not the truth: `tests_passed` is the model's own claim.
