questions.stem: The research system's policy is that every report passes a citation-verification step before delivery. The lead agent has the verifier as one of its subagents and is told to call it last. Under time pressure it sometimes delivers without verifying. What should the architect do?
options: Give the lead a larger turn budget so it doesn't run out of time before verifying
Move the instruction to call the verifier to the start of the lead's system prompt
Make verification a fixed step in orchestration code: always run the verifier, deliver only if it passes
Have the lead include a `verified: true` field in its output and have the delivery service reject reports without it
explanations: Time pressure is one trigger, but the step is still optional for the agent.
Position may help a little, but the lead can still skip it.
Correct. A mandatory step belongs in the deterministic part of the system, not in the agent's discretion.
The lead writes that field itself, so it's no guarantee the verifier ran.

questions.stem: The research system currently decomposes every question into the same four subagent tasks: background, market data, regulation, outlook. For questions like "How do EU and US battery-recycling rules differ?" the market and outlook sections come back thin or irrelevant, while the key comparison is spread across sections. What is the BEST change?
options: Add two more fixed sections (comparison and risks) so that the template covers more of the question types users ask
Keep the four sections but have the synthesis step drop any that come back thin
Have the lead decompose each question into sub-questions that fit its shape, guided by example decompositions
Run the four-section template twice with different search engines and merge the results
explanations: A bigger fixed template still forces every question into the same shape and adds more empty sections.
This hides the symptom; the comparison the user asked for is still never directly researched.
Correct. Open-ended questions vary in shape, so the subtasks should be chosen per question (orchestrator-workers) rather than fixed in advance as in a prompt chain.
Running the wrong decomposition twice doubles cost without fixing it.

questions.stem: Asked "What are the main risks of deploying solid-state batteries in passenger EVs?", the research lead splits the work into three subagents: thermal runaway, dendrite formation and manufacturing cost. Each returns strong findings, but reviewers note the report misses supply-chain and regulatory risk entirely. What is the BEST fix?
options: Run two subagents on each of the three subtopics and keep the more detailed answer
Have the lead first map the question's dimensions, then check its subtasks against that map before delegating
Give each subagent a larger search budget so it goes deeper into its subtopic
Move the synthesis step to the most capable model tier so it can recognize and fill in the missing risk areas itself
explanations: Redundancy on the same narrow topics doesn't add the missing ones.
Correct. This is over-narrow decomposition: the subtasks were good but didn't span the question. A scoping pass plus a coverage check catches missing dimensions before work is delegated.
Deeper research inside the same three boxes still leaves the gaps.
The synthesizer has no researched material on the missing risks, so it would have to invent or omit them.

questions.stem: The research lead is being tuned to split questions into parallel subagent tasks. Which TWO principles should its decomposition follow? (Select TWO.)
options: Make subtasks independent so no subagent has to wait for another's result
Create as many subtasks as possible, since more subagents always produce a more thorough report
Give each subtask a distinct, non-overlapping scope and a common output format
Split by tool, one subagent per search engine, regardless of the question
Let subagents agree among themselves who covers which part of the question
explanations: Correct. Independent subtasks can run in parallel; dependencies force sequencing.
Each subagent adds tokens and coordination; effort should scale with the question's complexity.
Correct. Distinct scopes avoid duplicated work and a shared format lets the coordinator merge results.
The split should follow the question's structure, not the tool inventory.
Coverage decisions belong to the coordinator; self-organizing workers duplicate and miss work.

questions.stem: In the research system, a fact-check step sends the same claim-verification prompt for each key claim to three independent model calls and accepts the verdict that at least two agree on. Which pattern is this?
options: Parallelization, voting variant: the same task run several times with the results aggregated
Prompt chaining with a programmatic gate between the calls
Orchestrator-workers, because a central model decides the subtasks at runtime
Evaluator-optimizer, because one call grades the output of another
explanations: Correct. Voting runs the same task several times for higher confidence; sectioning would split different subtasks.
The calls don't consume each other's output in sequence.
The subtasks here are identical and fixed in code, not chosen at runtime.
No call critiques or revises another's output; they vote independently.

questions.stem: An analyst gives the research system 25 analyst reports on one company and asks it to find where they contradict each other. A single pass over all 25 misses many contradictions; giving each report to its own subagent produces good summaries but no contradictions at all. Which decomposition BEST fits?
options: Per-report passes that extract claims with source and date, then a cross-report pass comparing claims by topic
Per-report subagents only, each told to mention anything in its report that might conflict with the other reports
One pass over all 25 reports with a much more detailed prompt listing contradiction types
Split the reports into five batches of five and look for contradictions within each batch
explanations: Correct. Local passes produce comparable structured claims, and an integration pass across them finds the cross-document conflicts.
A worker that sees one report can't know what other reports say.
One giant pass dilutes attention across 25 documents; more prompt detail doesn't fix that.
Contradictions between reports in different batches are never compared.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline must pull 40 fields from 300-page supply contracts. A single extraction call over the whole contract misses fields, and it sometimes takes the payment terms from the original clause even though a later amendment replaced them. Which approach is BEST?
options: Ask the model to read the contract twice in the same call before answering
Use a larger-context model so the whole 300-page contract fits more comfortably into a single extraction call
Make all 40 fields required in the schema so the model can't skip any
Extract per section with page references, then consolidate in a pass that applies amendment precedence
explanations: Rereading in one call doesn't change the decomposition or resolve the amendment problem.
Fitting more text in the window doesn't fix diluted attention or teach precedence.
Required fields force the model to fill gaps, inviting fabricated values where a field is absent.
Correct. Section-level passes keep attention focused, and a consolidation pass sees all candidate values so it can resolve conflicts such as amendments overriding originals.

questions.stem: To raise accuracy, an engineer changes the invoice-extraction pipeline from one structured call per invoice to 40 separate calls, one per field. Accuracy on individual fields improves slightly, but cost rises sharply and a new class of errors appears: subtotals, tax and totals that don't add up, and line items assigned to the wrong currency. What should the architect recommend?
options: Keep the per-field calls and add an LLM review call that checks all 40 answers for consistency before saving
Revert to one call per invoice with no other changes, accepting the earlier field accuracy
Group related fields per call (header, line items, totals) and check arithmetic and currency in code
Keep per-field calls but run each one three times and take the majority answer
explanations: This adds a 41st call on top of an already over-fragmented design, and the review is probabilistic.
This gives up the accuracy gain instead of fixing the decomposition.
Correct. The split was too fine: fields that depend on each other lost shared context. Grouping related fields restores consistency, and deterministic checks catch arithmetic mismatches cheaply.
Voting triples an already high cost and still doesn't give any call the context to keep fields consistent.

questions.stem: The CI review job runs `claude -p` once over a 60-file pull request. Its comments are shallow, it misses obvious bugs in some files, and it rarely catches broken call sites between modules. Which decomposition BEST addresses this?
options: Split the PR into two halves of 30 files and review each half in one pass
Increase `--max-turns` so the single pass has more time to look at everything
Per-file review passes, then a separate cross-file pass on changed interfaces and their call sites
Run the same single-pass review three times and merge all comments
explanations: Two big passes are still diluted and still can't see cross-half interactions.
More turns don't fix attention spread across 60 files in one context.
Correct. Focused per-file passes catch local bugs, and an integration pass finds problems that only show up across files.
Repeating a diluted pass repeats its blind spots and multiplies noise.

questions.stem: A nightly CI job must migrate about 400 service files from a deprecated logging API to a new one. Each file can be changed independently, and each service has its own tests. Which TWO practices BEST fit this job? (Select TWO.)
options: Build the target list with a deterministic search, then run one scoped `claude -p` per file
Send all 400 file paths to a single `claude -p` session and ask it to migrate them one after another
Pilot the prompt on a handful of files, fix the instructions, then run the full batch
Let each invocation decide which other services also need changes and edit those too
Use `--dangerously-skip-permissions` so no invocation stalls on a permission prompt
explanations: Correct. Independent items fan out cleanly: a deterministic work list plus one non-interactive run per file with the same instructions and a narrow `--allowedTools`.
One session over 400 files accumulates context and degrades long before it finishes.
Correct. Problems in the prompt show up on a few files cheaply; at 400 files they multiply.
Overlapping, self-expanding scope creates conflicting edits between runs.
Unattended runs should get a narrow allowlist with a non-prompting mode, not blanket bypass.

questions.stem: A developer asks Claude Code in one prompt to "add multi-currency support" to a billing service. The result touches the schema, services, API and UI at once, and half of it doesn't work. How should the work be decomposed instead?
options: Write a much longer single prompt that lists every file to change
Spawn four parallel subagents (schema, services, API, UI) and merge their changes at the end
Ask Claude to review its own large change and fix what it finds
Split it into ordered steps (schema, services, API, UI) and check tests after each step
explanations: More detail in one shot still produces one large, unverified change.
The layers depend on each other; parallel workers would build on interfaces that don't exist yet.
Self-review of a sprawling change in the same context finds little.
Correct. This is prompt chaining with gates: each step builds on a verified previous step, so problems surface early and stay small.

questions.stem: A developer asks Claude Code to change a core `Account` model (new required field, renamed method) and update its 40 call sites across the codebase. To go faster, they have Claude spawn ten subagents immediately, each taking four call sites. Several subagents guess the new method signature differently and edit the shared model file in conflicting ways. What is the BEST approach?
options: Do all 40 call sites sequentially in the main session to avoid any parallelism
Spawn one subagent per call site so that each one has a smaller, more focused task
Make the shared model and interface change first, then fan out the independent call-site updates
Keep the ten subagents but tell them to coordinate through comments in the model file before editing it
explanations: Safe but unnecessarily slow; only the shared core needs to be sequential.
Smaller tasks don't solve the missing dependency; forty workers would guess the interface forty ways.
Correct. Dependency-ordered decomposition: once the shared interface exists, the call-site updates really are independent and safe to parallelize.
Workers editing and messaging through a shared file recreates the conflict.

questions.stem: On the internal developer platform, an "explain this repository" tool reads every file of an unfamiliar 2,000-file monorepo in sequence before answering. It is slow and its answers are vague. Which decomposition BEST fits the task?
options: Read every file again, but in a fixed alphabetical order so nothing is missed
Embed the whole repository in the prompt of a larger-context model
Ask one subagent to read the whole repository end to end and return a single summary of what it found
Map the structure first with Glob/Grep, deep-dive per subsystem in subagents, then synthesize
explanations: Ordering doesn't change the problem: everything still lands in one diluted pass.
2,000 files rarely fit, and when they do, attention is spread too thin for a useful answer.
One subagent reading everything has the same dilution problem in a different window.
Correct. Breadth-first mapping finds where to look, focused deep dives keep each context clean, and a synthesis step combines the findings.

questions.stem: A large research job runs ten subagents over about 40 minutes. When subagent 7 hits an unrecoverable error, the whole job restarts from zero, repeating the work and cost of the first six. What should the architect change?
options: Persist the plan and each finished subagent's result; on failure, resume and rerun only unfinished subtasks
Retry the entire job automatically up to three times so that transient failures have a chance to clear on their own
Run all ten subagents inside one context so there is only one thing that can fail
Switch to a more reliable, larger model tier so subagents fail less often
explanations: Correct. Checkpointing state outside the context window lets a long run resume where the error occurred instead of restarting, as Anthropic's research system does.
Repeating the whole job repeats the wasted work and can fail again at the same point.
This removes isolation and still loses everything when that context fails.
Errors can't be eliminated; the design has to tolerate them.

questions.stem: Last week a research session produced a market analysis. Three of its key sources have since been updated, and an analyst now asks for a refreshed report. The old session still exists and can be resumed. What is the BEST approach?
options: Resume the old session and ask it to update the report, since it already holds all of the earlier context and reasoning
Start fresh, seeded with a summary of prior findings (with source dates) and the sources to re-verify
Fork the old session and ask the fork to refresh the report, keeping the original intact
Start a fresh session with only the original question so nothing stale can leak in
explanations: The resumed context is full of out-of-date tool results that the model may keep relying on.
Correct. When the old context is stale, a fresh session with a summary keeps what is still valid and makes clear what must be rechecked.
A fork carries the same stale history; it only protects the original session.
This throws away valid prior work and repeats all the research.

questions.stem: A customer returns three days after a 150-turn support conversation about a damaged shipment. The agent had verified their identity, agreed a partial refund amount and promised a replacement. The old session can be resumed, but it is long and mostly about troubleshooting steps that are no longer relevant. What is the BEST way to continue?
options: Resume the full 150-turn session so the agent has every detail of the earlier conversation
Fork the old session so the original stays intact while the agent continues in the copy
Start a new session with no history and ask the customer to explain the issue again
Start a new session seeded from the persisted case record and a short summary
explanations: Resuming carries a long, mostly irrelevant history, which costs more and risks key facts getting lost in the middle.
A fork has exactly the same long history; it only protects the original.
This discards commitments the company made and frustrates the customer.
Correct. Durable case facts (verified status, agreed amount, promised actions) kept outside the context window are the reliable source; a fresh session seeded with them is focused and accurate.

questions.stem: An engineer on the internal platform has corrected Claude Code twice about how the team's auth middleware works, and the third attempt is still wrong. The session is long and contains both failed attempts. What does Anthropic's guidance recommend?
options: Correct it a third time with more emphasis, in capitals, on the parts it keeps missing
`/clear` and start again with one better prompt that includes what was learned
Run `/compact` so the failed attempts are summarized and keep correcting
Fork the session so the failed attempts are preserved for later reference
explanations: A third correction mostly adds to a context that already contains two failed attempts for Claude to keep re-reading.
Correct. A fresh context plus a prompt that folds in the lessons usually works better than continuing to correct.
Compaction carries a summary of the failed attempts forward.
A fork keeps exactly the context that is causing the problem.

questions.stem: The extraction pipeline runs Agent SDK workers in short-lived containers. When validation fails, the pipeline sends a correction request ("`total` doesn't match the line items; recheck page 3") to whatever worker is free, using `resume` with the original session ID. These retries usually fail with a session-not-found error. Which design is the MOST robust and simplest?
options: Use `continue_conversation=True` on the retry so whichever worker is free picks up the latest session
Raise `max_turns` on the first run so corrections never need a second request
Skip resume: send a fresh request with the document, the extracted JSON and the validation errors
Resume with `fork_session=True` so the retry gets its own copy of the session
explanations: A new container has no sessions on disk, so there is nothing to continue.
The first run doesn't know about the validation failure that happens afterwards in pipeline code.
Correct. Session files are local to the host that wrote them. Passing the captured results into a fresh request avoids shipping transcripts around; the docs note this is often more robust.
Forking still needs the original session file on that machine.

questions.stem: The research system's lead agent runs multi-hour jobs and its context regularly approaches the limit, after which it loses track of its own plan and redoes finished work. Which THREE practices BEST address this? (Select THREE.)
options: Have the lead save its research plan and progress to external memory so it can reload them after its context is truncated
Move the lead to a model with a larger context window and keep all worker output in context
Have subagents write full findings to storage and return only condensed results with references
Disable compaction so that nothing in the lead's context is ever summarized away
When a phase completes, hand off to a fresh agent with a clean context, passing state through stored notes
Ask subagents to return their full transcripts so the lead never loses any detail
explanations: Correct. Anthropic's research lead saves its plan to memory because context can be truncated; reloading it restores direction.
A larger window delays the problem and worsens attention dilution.
Correct. Condensed returns plus references keep the lead's context small without losing detail.
Without compaction the lead simply runs out of context.
Correct. Fresh contexts with a stored-state handoff are how long-running agents continue past context limits.
Full transcripts accelerate the context overflow they are meant to prevent.

questions.stem: In a multi-agent research system, a due-diligence task requires reviewing 40 contracts and producing a risk memo. Running everything in one loop, the agent's context fills with full contract text and tool output, and by contract 25 its analysis gets noticeably worse. Which design change BEST addresses this?
options: Raise `max_tokens` so the model has more room to reason over the contracts
Delegate contracts to subagents that return short structured risk summaries
Ask the agent in the prompt to "forget" contracts once it has finished them
Move all 40 contracts into a cached system prompt so they are cheaper to resend on each turn and always available to the agent
explanations: `max_tokens` limits output length; it does not relieve input context pressure.
Correct. Subagents isolate the reading-heavy work so the coordinator's context grows by summaries, not transcripts.
The model cannot remove content from its own context; the harness must manage what is sent.
Caching reduces cost, not context load; the window still fills with all the text.

questions.stem: In the team's Claude Code workflow, to speed up a small refactor (renaming a function and updating its four call sites in two files), a developer configures the main agent to spawn five subagents, one per edit. The job now takes longer, uses several times more tokens, and two subagents made conflicting edits to the same file. What is the BEST recommendation?
options: Raise the concurrency limit so all subagents finish sooner
Keep the five subagents but also give each one Bash access so they can take file locks before editing shared files
Do this coupled task in the main agent; save subagents for independent, context-heavy work
Pass the parent's full conversation transcript to each subagent so they coordinate
explanations: More concurrency increases the risk of conflicting edits and does nothing for cost.
This adds more machinery to a task that does not benefit from delegation.
Correct. Subagents add tokens and coordination cost and do not share state; small, interdependent edits are better done in one context.
This erases the context-isolation benefit and still does not prevent concurrent conflicting writes.

questions.stem: A support-resolution agent currently performs every action through a general `bash` tool, including sending customer emails with `curl` to the mail API. The team now needs to require human approval before any email is sent and to log the recipient and subject. What is the BEST design change?
options: Add a system prompt rule telling Claude to ask for approval before sending email
Remove network access from the bash tool so emails cannot be sent at all
Keep the bash tool and match `curl` commands to the mail API with a regular expression that triggers an approval prompt
Promote email sending to a dedicated `send_email` tool with typed recipient, subject and body arguments the harness can gate and log
explanations: Instructions are not an enforced approval gate.
That blocks the required capability rather than gating it.
Fragile: the same action can be expressed many ways in shell, and recipient/subject are buried in an opaque string.
Correct. A dedicated tool gives the harness an action-specific hook with structured arguments; an opaque bash command string is hard to gate reliably.

questions.stem: A report-generation pipeline asks Claude to write a report outline, runs a code check that the outline covers five required sections, and only then asks Claude to write the full report from the approved outline. Which pattern from "Building effective agents" is this?
options: Prompt chaining, with a programmatic gate that checks the outline before the drafting step runs
Orchestrator-workers, because one call produces the plan the next call executes
Evaluator-optimizer, because the outline is checked before drafting
Routing, because the outline decides which prompt runs next
explanations: Correct. Sequential LLM calls where each consumes the previous output, with a code check as the gate.
An orchestrator decides subtasks dynamically and delegates them to workers; this flow is fixed in code.
Evaluator-optimizer loops an LLM critic and generator; this is a single deterministic check on the way through.
Routing classifies an input and dispatches it to one of several specialized paths; here every input follows the same fixed sequence.

questions.stem: The support-resolution system first classifies each incoming message as billing, technical outage, or general question. Billing messages go to a prompt with refund tools, outages to a prompt with network-status tools, and simple general questions to a smaller, cheaper model. Which pattern is being used?
options: Routing: classify first, then dispatch to a specialized prompt, tool set or model
Parallelization (sectioning), because each category is handled by a separate prompt
Orchestrator-workers, because the classifier delegates to specialized workers
Prompt chaining, because classification happens before the answer is written
explanations: Correct. Classify, then send to a specialized follow-up path or model; this also enables cost savings by sending easy queries to smaller models.
Sectioning runs independent subtasks of the same input at the same time; here each input takes exactly one path.
An orchestrator breaks one task into dynamic subtasks and synthesizes results; a classifier picking a single path is routing.
Chaining sends every input through the same sequence; routing chooses among different downstream paths.

questions.stem: In the CI pipeline, a security reviewer runs the same pull request through three differently worded vulnerability-review prompts at the same time and flags the PR if any reviewer reports a high-severity issue. Which pattern is this, and what is its main benefit?
options: Routing; each prompt specializes in one class of vulnerability
Prompt chaining; each review builds on the previous review's findings
Evaluator-optimizer; the reviewers critique the code and the developer revises it until all three pass
Parallelization (voting), for higher recall and confidence
explanations: All three prompts look at the same task and the PR is not dispatched to only one of them.
The reviews are independent and simultaneous, not sequential.
No generator is revising the code in a feedback loop here.
Correct. Voting runs the same task several times for diverse outputs; aggregation rules (here, any-flag) trade false positives against misses.

questions.stem: The support agent must screen each customer message for policy violations without adding latency to the reply. The team runs a guardrail classification call and the main response call at the same time and suppresses the reply if the guardrail flags the message. Which pattern does this implement?
options: Routing, since the guardrail decides whether the response is shown
Parallelization (voting): two calls vote on whether the reply is safe
Parallelization (sectioning) of independent subtasks within one request
Evaluator-optimizer: the guardrail evaluates and the main call optimizes
explanations: The guardrail is not choosing among specialized handlers; both calls always run.
Voting runs the same task multiple times; here the two calls do different jobs.
Correct. Anthropic gives exactly this guardrail-alongside-response example for sectioning.
There is no feedback loop in which the response is revised based on the evaluation.

questions.stem: In the team's Claude Code workflow, a feature applies a requested API change across the codebase. The number and identity of the files that must change are unknown until the codebase is inspected, and the edits must be combined into one coherent pull request. Which pattern fits BEST?
options: Prompt chaining, with one step per file in alphabetical order
Routing, sending each file to the most capable model for its language
Parallelization (sectioning), splitting the repository into fixed directory chunks that are edited in parallel and then concatenated
Orchestrator-workers: a central model inspects the code, decides which files need edits, delegates them and synthesizes one change
explanations: Chaining needs a fixed sequence known in advance; here the files are not known until inspection.
Routing picks one path per input; it does not plan or synthesize a multi-file change.
Fixed chunks are predefined subtasks; they ignore which files actually need changes and still require coherent synthesis.
Correct. The defining feature is that subtasks are determined at runtime, as in Anthropic's multi-file coding example.

questions.stem: In the research system, a `brief-writer` subagent turns each finished report into a two-page executive brief. Editors grade briefs against a written rubric (faithful to the report, neutral tone, plain language). In a pilot, briefs that got specific rubric-based critique and one or two rewrites scored clearly higher than first drafts. Which pattern should the architect build into this step?
options: Parallelization (sectioning): have separate subagents write each section of the brief, then concatenate them
Routing: send short reports to a fast model and long reports to a more capable one
Evaluator-optimizer: an evaluator critiques each draft against the rubric, with capped revisions
An autonomous agent with web search that gathers extra sources to strengthen each brief
explanations: Sectioning speeds up independent parts but gives no feedback loop, and separately written sections tend to read unevenly.
Routing picks a handler per input; it provides no critique-and-revise cycle, which is what the pilot showed adds value.

Correct. Anthropic names the conditions for evaluator-optimizer: clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement that provides measurable value. Both hold here; capping revisions keeps cost bounded.
The brief must be faithful to the finished report; new outside sources add cost and risk content the report doesn't support.

questions.stem: A document-extraction pipeline processes 50,000 invoices per day. Each invoice needs the same steps: extract fields, validate totals against the purchase order, and flag mismatches. Auditors require predictable, explainable behaviour and stable cost per invoice. Which architecture is MOST appropriate?
options: An autonomous agent with file and database tools that decides for each invoice how to proceed
A multi-agent supervisor with separate extraction, validation and reporting agents
An evaluator-optimizer loop that iterates on every invoice until a grader is satisfied
A workflow: structured-output extraction, then code-based validation and flagging, calling the model only where judgment is needed
explanations: Autonomy adds cost, latency and variance to a fully specified process, and makes audits harder.
Over-engineered for a fixed, known sequence; coordination overhead and cost rise with no benefit.
Every invoice paying for multiple iterations breaks the cost goal; validation can be done in code.
Correct. The steps are known in advance, so a predefined code path is cheaper, faster and more auditable than an agent.

questions.stem: A product manager wants to replace the support team's reliable rules-based refund process with an autonomous Claude agent. Which TWO conditions are strong reasons to stay with a workflow or a single call instead? (Select TWO.)
options: The task can be fully specified in advance as a fixed sequence of steps
Each completed task is worth far more than the extra tokens and latency an agent uses
Mistakes cannot be caught or rolled back before they reach customers (no tests, review or undo)
The number of steps varies widely and cannot be predicted ahead of time
The environment returns clear ground-truth feedback, such as test results, after each step
explanations: Correct. If the path is known, a predefined workflow is simpler, cheaper and more predictable.
High value per task supports, rather than argues against, an agent.
Correct. Low recoverability of errors is a key reason not to grant autonomy.
Unpredictable step counts are what agents are good for.
Environmental feedback is what lets agents self-correct, so it favours an agent.

questions.stem: An internal-platform team plans a hierarchical multi-agent system (a supervisor, a retrieval agent and an answer agent) to answer employee questions about an 80-page HR handbook. No prototype or evaluation set exists yet. What should they do FIRST?
options: Build the full supervisor architecture now but use Haiku-tier models for every agent so that the cost of the extra calls stays low
Start with an autonomous agent that can browse the intranet, since it can discover answers the handbook lacks
Fine-tune a model on the handbook so no retrieval or agents are needed
Prototype one well-prompted call with the relevant content, measure it on a small eval set, then add complexity
explanations: This still commits to the most complex design before knowing whether it is needed.
Adds scope, cost and risk without evidence that it is needed.
Costly and slow to iterate; it also skips the step of measuring a simple baseline.
Correct. Anthropic's guidance is to find the simplest solution first; one call with retrieval and examples often suffices.

questions.stem: In the multi-agent research system, the coordinator delegates with briefs like "research the semiconductor shortage". Logs show workers duplicating each other's searches, some drifting into unrelated topics, and the lead struggling to merge their free-form outputs. What is the MOST effective fix?
options: Let the workers read each other's full transcripts in real time so they can see what others have searched and avoid overlapping work
Replace the workers with a single agent that does all research sequentially
Give each worker a specific objective, scope boundaries, tool guidance and an output format
Add an evaluator agent that rejects duplicate findings after they are produced
explanations: This defeats context isolation, multiplies tokens, and still does not define who owns what.
This may avoid overlap but gives up parallelism and context isolation for broad research instead of fixing the briefs.
Correct. Workers see only their brief; vague delegation causes duplication and drift, and a fixed output format makes synthesis reliable.
This catches waste after paying for it rather than preventing it.

questions.stem: A five-step extraction chain generates structured regulatory-filing records. Step 3 (converting extracted data to a specific JSON schema) fails validation in about 5% of runs, and the current code restarts the whole chain on any error, wasting tokens and time. What is the BEST improvement?
options: Add a code gate after step 3 that validates its output and retries only that step, feeding back the validation error, with a retry cap
Raise the temperature on step 3 so that retries produce different outputs
Run the entire chain three times in parallel for every filing and keep whichever run finishes successfully first
Convert the chain into an autonomous agent that decides on its own how to recover
explanations: Correct. Gates between chain steps catch errors early, and targeted retries with feedback avoid re-running successful steps.
Sampling changes do not make outputs schema-compliant; use structured outputs plus validation and a targeted retry instead.
Triples cost on every filing to address a 5% failure in one step.
Replacing a predictable workflow with an agent adds variance; the failure is localized to one step.

questions.stem: The CI code-review job makes three independent model calls per pull request (security, performance, style), one after another, then a fourth call to summarize. End-to-end latency is 40 seconds and the target is under 20. Which TWO changes MOST directly reduce latency without lowering review quality on the hard checks? (Select TWO.)

code.src:
sec = await ask(SECURITY, diff)
perf = await ask(PERF, diff)
style = await ask(STYLE, diff)
return await ask(SUMMARY, sec + perf + style)

options: Chain the reviews so each one receives the previous reviewer's findings
Set every call to the maximum effort level
Run the three independent reviews concurrently (for example with `asyncio.gather`) before the summary call
Add an evaluator-optimizer loop to the summary step
Route the simple style check to a smaller, faster model while keeping the more capable model for security
explanations: Chaining is sequential by definition and keeps latency high.
Higher effort typically increases latency.
Correct. Sectioning independent subtasks means latency is set by the slowest call rather than the sum.
Extra iterations add latency.
Correct. Routing easy subtasks to a faster tier cuts latency while preserving quality where it matters.

questions.stem: An autonomous data-cleanup agent on the developer platform occasionally loops for hours, repeatedly re-running the same failing query and running up a large bill. Which TWO safeguards BEST address this? (Select TWO.)
options: A spend or token budget for the run, enforced by the harness
Removing error details from tool results so the agent stops trying once a tool fails
Switching to a model with a larger context window so the loop has more room
A hard cap on iterations or turns, after which the run stops and reports partial progress
Raising the effort level so the agent thinks harder before each retry
explanations: Correct. A budget cap (such as `max_budget_usd` in the Agent SDK) bounds cost even when the agent keeps going.
Hiding errors removes the ground truth the agent needs to change strategy.
More context lets the loop run longer; it does not stop it.
Correct. Stopping conditions such as a maximum iteration count are a standard agent guardrail.
May help some cases but is not a safeguard and can increase cost per iteration.

questions.stem: The support-resolution system's routing step sends tickets to refund, technical or account handlers. About 8% of tickets are ambiguous (for example, a refund request caused by a technical fault) and get misrouted, and the refund handler then issues wrong refunds. What is the BEST improvement?
options: Replace routing with a fully autonomous agent that has every tool from all three handlers
Add more few-shot refund examples to the refund handler's prompt
Add an "uncertain" route to a general handler or human, and evaluate the router on labelled tickets
Remove the router and send every ticket to all three handlers in parallel, then merge their answers and actions into one response
explanations: Loses the separation of concerns and gives one agent broad refund powers, increasing risk.
This tunes the downstream handler, not the misclassification that sends tickets there.
Correct. Routing works when categories are distinct; an explicit fallback path and a measured classifier handle the ambiguous cases safely.
Triples cost for every ticket to fix 8% of them and creates conflicting actions.

questions.stem: The support-agent team is debating its architecture. According to Anthropic's "Building effective agents", what distinguishes an agent from a workflow?
options: In an agent, the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use; in a workflow, LLMs and tools follow predefined code paths
An agent uses tools, while a workflow cannot call tools
An agent always uses multiple models, while a workflow uses a single model
An agent runs on Anthropic's infrastructure with a managed sandbox, while a workflow always runs on the customer's own servers
explanations: Correct. This is Anthropic's definition.
Workflows can call tools along predefined paths.
Model count is not the distinction; both can use one or many models.
Hosting location is unrelated to the definition.

questions.stem: In the research system's report-polishing step, an evaluator-optimizer loop refines the executive-summary headline. The evaluator prompt says only "make it better". Logs show the loop often runs to its 10-iteration cap, flip-flopping between two phrasings, and quality ratings do not improve after the first revision. What is the BEST action?
options: Raise the iteration cap to 25 so the loop has time to converge
Use the same prompt for generator and evaluator so they agree faster
Give the evaluator explicit criteria and a pass threshold, keep a low cap, or drop the loop
Run five evaluators in parallel each round and average their scores, so that a single noisy evaluator cannot stall the loop
explanations: Without criteria, more iterations just extend the oscillation.
Agreement is not quality; the evaluator still has no criteria.
Correct. Evaluator-optimizer only works with clear criteria and measurable improvement from feedback.
Adds cost without fixing the underlying lack of criteria.

questions.stem: A developer-platform team is designing an orchestrator-workers system that migrates logging calls across hundreds of repositories. Which THREE design choices are sound? (Select THREE.)
options: Have every worker receive the orchestrator's full transcript so they all share the same knowledge
Require the orchestrator to fix the full list of subtasks in code before inspecting any repository
Give each worker an isolated context and have it return a concise summary of what it changed and what it could not do
Let each worker spawn unlimited sub-workers to maximize parallelism
Use a cheaper, faster model for the reading-heavy per-repo workers and a more capable model for planning and synthesis
Cap concurrency, nesting depth and total spend for the run
explanations: This removes the main benefit of isolation and multiplies token cost.
Predefining subtasks turns this into parallelization and loses the orchestrator's main advantage: deciding the work at runtime.
Correct. Isolation keeps the orchestrator's context small, and condensed reports make synthesis tractable.
Unbounded nesting is a classic runaway-cost failure mode.
Correct. Matching model tier to subtask difficulty is a standard cost lever in hierarchies.
Correct. Fan-out can grow quickly; limits such as maximum concurrent subagents, spawn depth and a budget bound cost and rate-limit pressure.

questions.stem: In the multi-agent research system, the search subagent has two tools: `search` ("Searches documents.") backed by the firm's internal index of peer-reviewed papers, updated quarterly, and `web_search` ("Searches the web."). For questions about events from the last few weeks, the subagent keeps querying `search`, finds nothing recent, and the final report says the topic has no coverage. Which change BEST addresses the root cause?
options: Force `tool_choice` to `web_search` whenever the user's question mentions the current year
Add a rule to the coordinator's system prompt listing phrases such as "this month", "latest" or "recent" that should make every subagent use web search instead of the internal index
Merge both into a single `search` tool that sends every query to both backends and returns the union of the raw results
Rename the internal tool `papers_search` and rewrite both descriptions to say what each one covers and when to prefer it
explanations: Forcing a tool on a keyword heuristic removes judgment entirely and misfires on questions that mention a year but need peer-reviewed sources.
A keyword list in another agent's prompt is brittle and sits at the wrong layer; the subagent still sees two indistinguishable tools.
Sending every query to both backends doubles result volume and mixes sources with different trust levels, which hurts provenance, without making the choice clearer.
Correct. The descriptions are the main signal Claude uses to choose between tools; stating coverage, recency and when to use each removes the ambiguity at the source.

questions.stem: In the invoice extraction pipeline, the extractor agent first calls `list_vendors` (which pages through all 4,000 vendors) to find a match, then calls `lookup_vendor(vendor_id)`, which returns the full vendor record of about 180 fields. Each invoice now uses tens of thousands of tokens and matching accuracy falls on long invoices. The extractor only needs the canonical vendor ID, legal name, tax ID and default currency to fill the schema. Which THREE changes are MOST appropriate? (Select THREE.)
options: Move the pipeline to a model tier with a larger context window so that the full 180-field vendor records fit without trimming
Return only the fields the extraction step uses (vendor ID, legal name, tax ID, default currency) by default
Replace `list_vendors` with a search tool that takes a name or tax ID and returns the top few candidate vendors
Remove the vendor ID from results, because opaque IDs are where the model makes mistakes
Add a `response_format` option so the agent can request the detailed record only when it actually needs more fields
Base64-encode each vendor record to reduce the number of tokens it occupies
explanations: A bigger window treats the symptom; the irrelevant fields still dilute attention and cost tokens on every call.
Correct. Returning only high-signal fields keeps context small and focused on what the next step needs.
Correct. Search beats list: the agent should never page through every vendor to find one match.
The canonical vendor ID is required to write the extracted record; removing it breaks the downstream step. The fix for confusing IDs is to pair them with readable names, not to drop them.
Correct. A concise/detailed switch keeps the default lean while still allowing the full record when a case needs it.
Base64 does not reduce tokens for the model and makes the content unreadable to it.

questions.stem: Every MCP tool behind the support-resolution agent returns `{"error": "Request failed"}` with `isError: true` on any failure. Logs show two patterns: the agent retries `issue_refund` several times when the refund was blocked by policy, and it escalates to a human whenever `get_order` times out, even though the same call usually succeeds seconds later. Which TWO changes BEST address this? (Select TWO.)
options: Add an `error_category` (transient, validation, business_rule, permission) and a `retryable` flag to every error result
Add a system-prompt rule: "Always retry a failed tool up to three times before escalating."
Make each error message state the next step, e.g. "retry in a few seconds", "fix field X" or "do not retry; escalate"
Return HTTP 500 for every failure so that the MCP client's transport layer retries the request automatically before the model ever sees it
Move the agent to a larger model tier so that it can infer the real cause of each failure from the surrounding conversation
explanations: Correct. Category and retryability tell the agent whether another attempt can possibly help, which separates the timeout case from the policy case.
A blanket retry rule makes the policy case worse (three identical refused refunds) and still treats all failures the same.
Correct. Actionable messages give the agent the next step for each case instead of leaving it to guess.
Transport-level errors hide the tool-level detail from the model and would retry the policy refusal too.
The model cannot infer what the tool never reported; the error result is uninformative regardless of model size.

questions.stem: In the research system, a subagent's `fetch_journal_articles` tool hits a publisher API that returned 401 for most of last week after a licence lapsed. The tool caught the 401 and returned an empty article list as a normal result. The synthesis step then wrote that "no peer-reviewed evidence was found" in that journal. What is the BEST fix?
options: Tell the coordinator in its system prompt to treat any empty result from that journal as suspicious and to mention possible gaps in the report
Drop the journal from the subagent's sources until the licence is renewed
Retry the 401 inside the tool until the publisher starts accepting the credentials again
On auth failures return `isError: true` with an access-failure message; return an empty list only when a search truly found nothing
explanations: A prompt heuristic cannot tell a real empty search from a failed one; the tool must report the difference.
Removing the source hides the coverage gap instead of reporting it, and the report still overstates what was checked.
A 401 from an expired licence will not fix itself on retry; this burns time and budget.
Correct. "Could not check" and "checked, found nothing" must be distinguishable so the coordinator can report the gap or try another source.

questions.stem: In the extraction pipeline, `lookup_vendor` returns `{"vendor": null}` both when no vendor matches and when the vendor database is unreachable. Pipeline code sends every invoice with a null vendor to the new-vendor onboarding queue. During a 40-minute database outage, 900 invoices from existing vendors were misrouted. Which TWO changes BEST prevent this? (Select TWO.)
options: Return a transient, retryable `isError` result when the database is unreachable, and keep a successful `{"vendor": null}` for a real no-match
Add a prompt instruction telling the extractor to look more carefully and double-check its reasoning whenever the vendor lookup comes back null
Return `isError: true` for both the no-match and the unreachable case, so that no invoice is ever routed to onboarding automatically again
During outages, serve the vendor list from a cache without marking the data as possibly stale, so the pipeline keeps running at full speed
Have pipeline code park invoices whose lookup failed with a retryable error for re-processing, instead of routing them as no-match
explanations: Correct. Separating "could not check" from "checked, no match" is the core fix.
The extractor cannot distinguish the two cases from identical output, so double-checking adds cost without information.
A real no-match is a valid answer; treating it as an error stalls legitimate onboarding and conflates the two cases again.
Unflagged stale data swaps one silent failure for another.
Correct. Once errors are classified, deterministic routing in code can hold retryable failures rather than misrouting them.

questions.stem: A CI job runs `claude -p` to check database migrations through an MCP tool `check_migration`, then gates the merge on Claude's verdict. The tool's handler catches connection failures and returns "No issues found." During a database maintenance window, a destructive migration passed review and shipped. What is the MOST important fix?
options: Lower `--max-turns` so the job finishes before connection problems can affect it
Return `isError: true` saying the check could not run, and gate the merge on a structured field that records whether the check ran
Add "be extra careful with destructive migrations" to the CI prompt
Run the review job twice in parallel against the same database and allow the merge only when both runs independently report that the migration has no issues
explanations: Turn limits do not change what the tool reports; the false "no issues" would still be returned.
Correct. The tool must never report success on failure, and the pipeline should gate on an explicit "check ran" signal so an unverifiable run fails.
The model was told there were no issues; a more careful prompt cannot detect a failure the tool disguised as success.
Two runs against the same unreachable database will both receive the same false success.

questions.stem: The support-resolution agent was given every tool the company's MCP servers expose: 48 tools across billing, shipping, CRM administration, marketing campaigns and internal analytics. It regularly picks the wrong tool (for example a marketing contact lookup instead of the CRM customer lookup), and tool definitions consume a large share of each request. What is the BEST change?
options: Move the agent to the largest available model tier, which is better at choosing correctly among many similar-looking tools from different servers
Add a long section to the system prompt that explains, tool by tool, when each of the 48 tools should and should not be used
Scope the agent to the tools support resolution needs, split by role into specialists with a few tools each, and drop admin and marketing tools
Set `tool_choice` to `any` so the agent always commits to a tool rather than hesitating between them
explanations: Selection accuracy degrades with large tool sets regardless of tier, and the definitions still cost context on every request.
More prompt text adds context and leaves 48 overlapping tools in place; it treats the symptom.
Correct. A scoped tool set per role improves selection, cuts context and removes tools the agent should never use.
Forcing a call does nothing to help the agent pick the right tool, and current models reject forced `tool_choice` with a 400.

questions.stem: In the multi-agent research system, the coordinator was given `web_search`, `web_fetch` and the tool for delegating to subagents. Transcripts show it often runs searches and fetches pages itself instead of delegating, so its context fills with raw pages and synthesis quality drops on long questions. What is the BEST change?
options: Tell the coordinator in its prompt to delegate all searching and to avoid fetching pages itself
Raise the coordinator's context budget so the raw pages it fetches and its working synthesis both fit comfortably in one window
Remove search and fetch from the coordinator and give them only to the search subagents
Force `tool_choice` to the delegation tool on every coordinator turn
explanations: A prompt instruction may help, but the tools remain available and the coordinator will still reach for them.
More context postpones the problem and keeps irrelevant raw content in the coordinator's window.
Correct. Scoping tools by role keeps the coordinator on decomposition and synthesis and keeps raw content in subagent contexts.
Forcing delegation every turn stops the coordinator from ever writing its synthesis, and current models reject forced `tool_choice` modes.

questions.stem: The research system's synthesis subagent was given web search and fetch "just in case" it finds a gap. Reviewers find that final reports now cite sources the analysis subagents never vetted, and some claims have no traceable citation. What should the architect do?
options: Keep the tools but add a prompt rule that the synthesis subagent may only search when a claim is unsupported
Move synthesis into the coordinator so a single agent both searches and writes the report
Add a second synthesis subagent that independently re-checks every citation the first one added from its own searches before the report is published
Remove search and fetch from the synthesis subagent; it works from the vetted findings it is given and reports gaps back to the coordinator
explanations: The permission remains and so does the behaviour; a prompt rule does not scope the tool set.
Merging roles gives one agent even more tools and context, which is the opposite of scoping.
Adding a checker treats the symptom and adds cost while unvetted sources keep entering.
Correct. Least-privilege tool sets keep each stage in its role, and returning gaps keeps the coordinator in charge of further research.

questions.stem: The research system's own harness calls the Messages API with tools from seven MCP-backed services, 160 tools in total. Tool definitions alone take about 50k tokens per request, and subagents often choose a near-duplicate tool from the wrong service. Which TWO changes BEST address this? (Select TWO.)
options: Add the tool search tool and mark most tools `defer_loading: true`, keeping the few most-used tools loaded
Mark every tool, including the tool search tool, `defer_loading: true` so nothing loads up front
Give each subagent only the services and tools its role needs instead of the full catalog
Raise `max_tokens` so subagents have more room to reason about which tool to choose
Move all 160 tool descriptions into the system prompt and keep only short tool names and schemas in the `tools` array
explanations: Correct. Tool search loads only the definitions Claude needs, which cuts context and keeps selection accurate with large catalogs.
At least one tool, normally the search tool itself, must stay non-deferred; deferring everything is rejected with a 400.
Correct. Role-scoped tool sets shrink each agent's choice to what it actually uses.
Output budget does not change how many definitions crowd the context or how similar they are.
The descriptions would still occupy the context, and separating them from the tool definitions makes selection harder.

questions.stem: A search subagent in the research system needs to run about a dozen independent queries per sub-question. Transcripts show exactly one search per turn and 12 sequential turns. Its request configuration was copied from another service:
options: Change `tool_choice` to `{"type": "any"}` so the subagent must call a tool on every turn
Split the work into twelve subagents, one per query, so that the coordinator can run all of the queries concurrently
Lower `max_tokens` so each turn finishes faster
Remove `disable_parallel_tool_use` so Claude can request several independent searches in a single turn
explanations: Forcing a call does not let the agent issue more than one per turn while parallel use is disabled.
Twelve subagents add coordination overhead to work a single agent can parallelise with tool calls.
Shorter turns do not reduce the number of sequential turns.
Correct. `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` caps Claude at one tool call per response; removing it lets independent searches go out together.

questions.stem: To "let it finish the job", the extraction agent was also given `update_erp` and `email_vendor` tools. Occasionally it posts a record to the ERP before the pipeline's validation and human-review steps have run, and a few vendors received emails about invoices that were later rejected. What is the BEST fix?
options: Add a prompt rule that the agent must complete every validation step and wait for human review before it calls `update_erp` or `email_vendor`
Remove `update_erp` and `email_vendor` from the extractor; pipeline code posts and notifies only after validation and review pass
Add a hook that logs every `update_erp` and `email_vendor` call so the audit trail is complete
Lower the model's temperature so it follows the intended order more consistently
explanations: A prompt rule is probabilistic; the premature posts are exactly the failures it would not prevent.
Correct. An extraction step should only extract; side-effecting actions belong in deterministic code after the checks.
Logging records the problem but does not stop it.
Sampling settings do not enforce ordering or remove the capability.

questions.stem: The team wants Claude Code to read GitHub issues and pull-request review threads while it implements features. A developer proposes writing a custom stdio MCP server that wraps the dozen GitHub REST endpoints the team uses. What should the tech lead recommend?
options: Build the custom server as proposed, since a server tailored to the team's dozen endpoints will be smaller and easier to reason about
Add a maintained, existing GitHub MCP server to the project `.mcp.json`, with the token supplied through `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`
Paste the GitHub REST API reference into CLAUDE.md so Claude can construct `curl` calls through Bash when it needs issue data
Have each developer run `claude mcp add` at local scope with their own token pasted into the command
explanations: A custom wrapper duplicates a maintained integration and becomes the team's code to secure and keep current.
Correct. Adopting an existing server for a common system is the default; project scope shares the configuration and env-var expansion keeps the token out of git.
A large API reference in CLAUDE.md costs context every session and replaces a typed integration with ad hoc shell calls.
Local scope works for one person but is not shared, so every developer has to configure it by hand and setups drift.

questions.stem: The platform team wants Claude Code's web lookups to go through the company's licensed enterprise search provider instead of the built-in WebSearch tool, for compliance logging. Which approach BEST meets this?
options: Set an environment variable that points the built-in WebSearch tool at the enterprise provider's API endpoint
Connect an MCP server exposing the provider's search as a tool, and deny `WebSearch` in managed or project settings
Add a CLAUDE.md instruction asking Claude to prefer the enterprise provider whenever it searches
Write a skill that tells Claude to send each query to the provider's search URL with WebFetch and parse the results
explanations: The WebSearch backend is not configurable; there is no setting that redirects it.
Correct. A different search backend comes in through an MCP tool, and a deny rule on `WebSearch` keeps lookups on the compliant path.
A preference in CLAUDE.md neither provides the integration nor guarantees the built-in tool is not used.
WebFetch runs an extraction prompt over a single page; it is not a search integration, and nothing stops the built-in search from being used.

questions.stem: The support agent uses the Agent tool to hand order investigations to a subagent that calls several order and shipping tools. The parent agent then tells customers "your refund amount has been confirmed" without quoting the amount, because it never sees the order records the subagent looked up. What is the BEST change?
options: Give the parent the same order and shipping tools so it can repeat the lookups itself after the subagent finishes
Run the subagent directly inside the parent's context so that all of its intermediate tool calls and outputs are visible to the parent agent
Define the subagent's output so its final message includes the facts the parent needs (order ID, amount, dates, status) in a fixed structure
Increase the parent's context window so the subagent's tool outputs fit alongside the conversation
explanations: Duplicating every lookup wastes calls and undoes the reason for delegating.
Sharing the whole intermediate transcript defeats the context isolation a subagent provides; the parent needs the facts, not the raw calls.
Correct. The parent sees only the subagent's final result, so that result must carry the specific facts in a predictable shape.
The subagent's intermediate outputs never reach the parent, whatever the parent's window size.

questions.stem: The support-resolution agent has a `lookup_order` tool whose description is just "Order tool." In testing, when customers ask "where is my package?", Claude often answers from earlier conversation text or asks for details it could get from the tool, rather than calling it. What should the architect do FIRST?
options: Force the tool with `tool_choice` on every request so Claude can never answer an order question without calling it.
Rewrite the description to state what it returns and when to call it (order status, shipping, contents).
Increase `max_tokens` so Claude has room to plan tool calls.
Add the customer's full order history to the system prompt so Claude has the data without needing the tool.
explanations: Forcing a call on every turn would also fire on unrelated questions such as greetings or return policy, and forced tool_choice is rejected on some newer models. It hides a description problem rather than fixing it.
Claude decides whether to call a tool mostly from its description. Saying when to call it is the highest-leverage fix and the documented first step.
max_tokens limits output length. It has no effect on whether Claude thinks the tool applies.
Preloading order history goes stale and bloats every request. It works around the tool instead of making it usable.

questions.stem: An internal scheduling assistant on the developer-productivity platform exposes `list_users`, `list_events`, and `create_event`, mirroring the REST API one-to-one. Transcripts show Claude paging through hundreds of users and events to find a free slot, using tens of thousands of tokens per booking. Based on Anthropic's guidance on writing tools for agents, which TWO changes are MOST appropriate? (Select TWO.)
options: Return the raw JSON for every user and event, including internal IDs and all fields, so Claude has maximum information.
Add more granular endpoints such as `get_user_by_id` and `get_event_by_id` so Claude has more options.
Replace the chain with a higher-level `schedule_event` tool that finds common availability and books the meeting.
Remove pagination from `list_users` so Claude gets everyone in one call instead of many round trips.
Replace `list_users` with a `search_users` tool that returns only people matching a name or email query.
explanations: Low-signal fields and opaque IDs waste tokens and lead to mistakes. The guidance is to return meaningful, concise context.
Adding more thin endpoint wrappers spreads the work across even more calls, the opposite of consolidation.
Consolidating a multi-step workflow into one purpose-built tool is a core recommendation. It saves tokens and removes chances for intermediate errors.
One unpaginated dump floods the context window. The guidance is pagination and filtering with sensible defaults.
Search beats list for agents. Returning only relevant matches keeps context small, as in the article's search_contacts vs list_contacts example.

questions.stem: An internal CRM tool on the developer-productivity platform returns records like `{"owner": "5f2c9e1a-...", "acct": "a91e77d0-...", "stage": 3}`. Claude often passes the wrong ID in follow-up calls and sometimes makes up IDs. Which change is MOST likely to improve accuracy?
options: Base64-encode the UUIDs to save tokens.
Add a system prompt instruction telling Claude to carefully double-check every UUID against earlier results before using it.
Return readable names/labels, plus a `response_format` option that includes full IDs only when needed.
Enable `strict: true` on the follow-up tools so that only well-formed UUID strings can ever be passed as arguments.
explanations: Encoding makes the IDs even less meaningful to the model and doesn't help it pick the right one.
Claude has nothing to check the IDs against. The problem is that the data is uninterpretable, not a lack of care.

The guidance is to resolve opaque identifiers into semantically meaningful values. That measurably improves precision and reduces hallucinated IDs. A concise/detailed switch saves tokens while still exposing IDs when needed.
Strict mode enforces schema shape, not meaning. A well-formed but wrong UUID still passes.

questions.stem: An internal SRE assistant's `search_logs` tool sometimes returns about 40k tokens of raw log lines. After a few calls the agent's answers get worse and the context fills up. What is the BEST change to the tool?
options: Move the most recent hour of logs into the system prompt on every request so the tool needs to return far less data.
Silently truncate every result to its first 2,000 characters so the context window can never be flooded by one call.
Increase `max_tokens` on each request.
Add filters and a default limit with pagination; when truncating, say so and suggest how to narrow.
explanations: This puts a large, ever-changing blob into every request and breaks prompt caching. The tool itself should return focused results.
Silent truncation leaves Claude reasoning from partial data without knowing it. If you truncate, say so and give guidance.
max_tokens controls output length, not how much tool output lands in the input context.
Pagination, filtering, and truncation with sensible defaults are the recommended way to make tool output token-efficient. Telling the agent how to narrow the search steers it toward better queries.

questions.stem: The support-resolution agent, built on the SDK Tool Runner, has an `issue_refund` tool. Compliance requires a human to approve any refund over $500 before money moves. Declined refunds must not execute, and Claude should be able to tell the customer what happened. Which approach BEST meets these requirements?
options: Add "Always ask the user for explicit confirmation before issuing any refund over $500" to the system prompt.
Set `strict: true` with `"maximum": 500` on the amount field so Claude is structurally unable to request larger refunds.
Drop the Tool Runner and hand-write the agent loop, because the runner executes tools automatically and cannot support approval gates.
Gate inside the run function (or on the yielded call): over $500, get approval; if declined, return "not approved".
explanations: A prompt instruction is a request, not a control. Claude might not ask, and the approval would come from the customer rather than a compliance reviewer.

Strict mode doesn't support numeric constraints like maximum (the raw API rejects the schema; the SDKs strip it and check client-side), and blocking large refunds outright isn't the requirement. They need approval, not prohibition.
This is a common misconception. The runner supports human-in-the-loop gates, so a manual loop isn't required.

Approval belongs in code that runs before the side effect. The Tool Runner supports gating in the run function or intervening on the yielded message, and returning a declined result keeps Claude informed.

questions.stem: An internal engineering assistant has only a `bash` tool. It sends email by running `curl` against the company mail API. Security now requires every outbound email to be shown to the user for confirmation and recorded in an audit log with recipient, subject, and body. Which approach BEST meets this?
options: Add a regex blocklist to the bash handler that rejects any command containing `curl` or the mail API's hostname.
Promote email to a dedicated `send_email(to, subject, body)` tool the harness can gate and log.
Add a second shell tool, `bash_email`, used only for email.
Instruct Claude in the system prompt to print each email for the user's review before sending it with curl via bash.
explanations: Blocklists on shell strings are easy to bypass (wget, python -c, encoded commands), and they don't provide confirmation or structured audit data.
A dedicated tool gives the harness typed arguments it can intercept, show for confirmation, and audit. That's the documented reason to promote an action out of bash.
Another shell-string tool still gives the harness an opaque command, so it can't reliably render or audit the email fields.
Prompt instructions can be skipped. The harness still sees only an opaque command string.

questions.stem: On the team using Claude Code, engineers keep pasting a 30-page internal API style guide into Claude Code sessions. It's only needed when someone designs or reviews an HTTP endpoint. The repo's CLAUDE.md is already about 180 lines. What is the BEST way to give Claude this guide?
options: Append the full guide to CLAUDE.md.
Package it as a skill whose description says when to use it, with details in referenced files.
Build an MCP server with a `get_style_guide` tool that returns the full document whenever Claude decides it needs it.
Add a PreToolUse hook that injects the full guide into context before every file edit Claude makes in the repo.
explanations: CLAUDE.md loads in full every session. A 30-page guide would cost context on every request, and the docs suggest keeping CLAUDE.md short.
Skills use progressive disclosure: only the description is in context until the task matches, then the body and referenced files load. That fits occasional reference material.
MCP is for connecting to external systems. Wrapping a static document in a server adds infrastructure without benefit over a skill.
This adds the guide's cost to every edit, including unrelated ones. Hooks are for deterministic automation, not on-demand knowledge.

questions.stem: The platform team wants Claude to read and update its internal ticketing system from three places: engineers in Claude Code, support staff in Claude Desktop, and a custom triage bot built on the Agent SDK. The ticketing API needs per-user OAuth. Which approach BEST meets the requirements?
options: Write a skill with step-by-step curl instructions for the ticketing REST API and share it with each team that needs it.
Define the same custom tools separately in each of the three apps.
Build one MCP server for the ticketing system and connect it from each client.
Create a Claude Code plugin with a hook that periodically syncs tickets into local files that Claude can read and edit.
explanations: Skills provide knowledge, not a connection or auth. Each user would have to handle credentials in shell commands, and that's fragile and insecure.
This works but duplicates and maintains the same integration three times, which is what MCP avoids.
MCP is the reusable-integration choice: build the connection and auth once in a standard server, and every MCP-capable client (Claude Code, Desktop, Agent SDK) can use it.
A Claude Code plugin doesn't help Desktop users or the SDK bot, and syncing to local files adds staleness and auth problems.

questions.stem: In an engineer's Claude Code session on the platform, they ask which of 200 services still call a deprecated endpoint. Answering means grepping and reading dozens of files, and the output is filling the main conversation even though only the final list matters. What is the BEST approach?
options: Delegate it to a subagent, which returns only a summary.
Write a skill describing exactly which grep commands to run and how to read the results for this kind of investigation.
Connect a code-search MCP server so Claude can query the whole repository through dedicated search tools instead of grep.
Add "keep answers concise" to CLAUDE.md.
explanations: Subagents isolate context. The file reads and searches happen in the subagent's window, and the main conversation gets only the findings.
A skill adds instructions to the main context. The grep output would still land in the main conversation.
Better search tools may help, but their results still enter the main context. Nothing isolates the intermediate work.
Conciseness affects Claude's replies, not the tool output that is filling the context.

questions.stem: The team's repo CLAUDE.md says "Never modify files under `db/migrations/applied/`". Claude still edits those files now and then during refactors. The team needs a guarantee that it never happens. What should they do?
options: Move the rule into a dedicated skill whose description mentions migrations, so it loads whenever migrations come up.
Add a PreToolUse hook (or permission deny rule) blocking edits to that path.
Restate the rule in capitals in CLAUDE.md.
Create a migrations subagent and instruct Claude to delegate any work touching migrations to that subagent instead.
explanations: A skill is still an instruction Claude may or may not apply. It isn't enforcement.
Hooks and permission rules are enforced by the harness, so they hold every time. Instructions in CLAUDE.md or skills are requests the model interprets.
Emphasis may reduce violations but can't guarantee them.
Delegation is also an instruction-level choice. Nothing stops the main agent from editing the files directly.

questions.stem: A team using Claude Code adds 30 custom Agent Skills and worries about filling the context window. Which statement correctly describes how skill content is loaded?
options: Every SKILL.md loads in full at session start.
Skills load only when a user types `/skill-name`; Claude cannot select or load a skill on its own from the task.
Each skill always runs in its own separate context window, like a subagent, so skills never consume main-context tokens.
Only names and descriptions load up front; bodies load on trigger, and extra files only if read.
explanations: Full bodies aren't preloaded. Having many installed skills costs little until they're used.
By default Claude can load a skill automatically when its description matches the task. disable-model-invocation turns that off.
Skill content normally loads into the current context. Only skills configured with context: fork run in a subagent.
This is progressive disclosure: metadata (about 100 tokens per skill) is always present, instructions load on trigger, and resources and scripts load or run as needed.

questions.stem: The platform's analytics team wants Claude Code to answer business questions against their Postgres warehouse. It has to follow team conventions: which of the 2,000 tables are canonical, fiscal-calendar rules, and standard metric definitions. Which TWO components together BEST meet this? (Select TWO.)
options: A skill that documents the canonical tables, fiscal-calendar rules, metric definitions, and example query patterns.
A PostToolUse hook that rewrites any SQL Claude writes to use canonical table names.
The full warehouse schema for all 2,000 tables pasted into CLAUDE.md.
An output style that formats every answer as a Markdown table.
An MCP server that provides query tools against the warehouse, with the connection and credentials handled by the server.
explanations: A skill teaches Claude how to use those tools well. Skill + MCP is the documented pairing, and the skill loads only when the task needs it.
Deterministically rewriting SQL can't capture semantic rules like metric definitions, and silently changing queries is risky.
A 2,000-table schema in CLAUDE.md costs context on every request, even unrelated ones.
Formatting is unrelated to querying correctly or following team conventions.
MCP supplies the external connection and tools. That is its purpose.

questions.stem: One internal Python backend on the platform calls the Messages API and needs Claude to use one internal function, `get_account_tier(account_id)`, which lives in the same codebase. No other app or client will ever use it. What is the MOST appropriate way to expose it?
options: Wrap it in a remote MCP server, deploy it on a public HTTPS endpoint, and attach it with the MCP connector.
Define it as a custom tool in the `tools` array and run it in your loop (or with the SDK Tool Runner).
Upload an Agent Skill whose instructions explain how to call the function.
Put every account's tier in the system prompt so no tool is needed.
explanations: This adds deployment, public exposure, and auth with no reuse to pay for it. MCP is worth it when several clients share the integration.
When one application owns a capability, a client tool is the simplest fit: the function runs in-process with direct access to your code and data.
On the API, skills run in a sandboxed code-execution container with no network, so a skill can't call into your backend.
That data goes stale, grows with your account count, and is sent on every request.

questions.stem: A research agent's news-gathering step has to answer questions about events after the model's training cutoff and cite sources. The team wants the least engineering and maintenance effort. What should they use?
