Stream responses so text appears as it is generated, and track time to first token as the user-facing latency metric
explanations: Batch processing is asynchronous and would make the wait far longer for an interactive tutor.
A hard cap cuts explanations off mid-sentence and changes the answers.
A smaller tier may lower quality, which the stem rules out, and still needs evals.
Correct. Streaming improves perceived responsiveness without changing the answer, and time to first token measures what students experience.

questions.stem: A national agency is contracting an internal platform team to provide a Claude-based document-summarisation service to several departments. The agency asks the architect to draft the performance SLA. Which THREE elements belong in it? (Select THREE.)
options: A p95 latency target for a defined document size, set from load tests on representative documents
A guarantee that summaries will contain no hallucinated statements of any kind
An average latency target only, since percentile figures are too hard for the departments' non-technical managers to interpret
A minimum quality score on a fixed, versioned eval set, re-run whenever the prompt or model changes
An availability target plus defined behaviour on overload or outage, such as queuing with status updates and notification
A fixed number of output tokens per summary, used as the measure of summary quality
explanations: Correct. Percentile latency for a defined workload, grounded in measurement, is a promise the team can meet and monitor.
No LLM system can guarantee zero errors; an SLA should commit to a measured quality threshold and the controls around it.
Averages hide the tail that users experience; SLAs should use percentiles.
Correct. Quality needs an objective, repeatable measure, re-checked on each change so regressions are caught.
Correct. Departments need to know availability and what happens on failure, not just the happy path.
Length is not quality; a token count says nothing about faithfulness or usefulness.

questions.stem: An insurance carrier receives an email from Anthropic saying the model ID used by its claims-summary, broker-chat and fraud-triage services is deprecated, with a retirement date about two months away. Each service team owns its own API keys. What is the BEST plan?
options: Find every caller via the usage export by API key and model, run each service's evals on the recommended replacement early, and migrate service by service
Keep the current model until close to the retirement date, then change the model ID in all three services together in a single coordinated release
Move all three services to the most capable tier now, since a stronger model should absorb any behaviour differences without further prompt work
Ask Anthropic for an extension for the deprecated model and revisit the migration next year
explanations: Correct. Anthropic's deprecation guidance is to find usage (the Console usage export breaks it down by API key and model), test replacements well before retirement, and migrate as soon as possible. Rolling out one service at a time limits the blast radius.
Requests to retired models fail, and switching every service at the deadline leaves no time to find behaviour changes, so any regression lands in production all at once.
A bigger tier is not a migration plan. It changes cost and latency without evidence, and it still needs evals because prompts tuned for the old model can behave differently.
Nothing promises an extension. Planning around one leaves all three services exposed to failing requests on the retirement date.

questions.stem: A legal-tech SaaS runs contract-clause extraction on an Opus-class model at high effort. Finance wants a 35% cost cut. An engineer proposes a cascade: a Haiku-class model handles each contract first and escalates to a Sonnet-class model, then to the Opus-class model, when its self-reported confidence is low. There is a labelled eval of 400 real contracts. What should the architect do FIRST?
options: Build the cascade behind a feature flag, route 10% of production traffic through it, and compare its monthly cost with the current setup
Move all traffic to the Sonnet-class model, since mid-tier models usually handle extraction well
Sweep effort on the current model against the eval, measure cost per correct contract, and require any cascade to beat that whole curve
Lower `max_tokens` on the current model so each response costs less
explanations: This tests a complex design in production before the simplest lever has been measured, and it relies on self-reported confidence, which is not calibrated against the eval criteria.
This is a guess based on general tier traits. Without measuring on the 400-contract eval, the team can't tell whether accuracy holds or whether the failures cost more than the savings.

Correct. Anthropic's guidance is that tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models, and that a multi-model setup must beat the single model's whole score-versus-spend curve. Recording cost per correct contract keeps failures in the comparison.
`max_tokens` is a hard output cap. Lowering it truncates extractions instead of making the model work more efficiently, which trades cost for failures.

questions.stem: A public-sector agency is choosing between one Opus-class agent at reduced effort and an Opus-class orchestrator that hands work to cheaper Sonnet-class or Haiku-class workers. Which TWO workload characteristics MOST favour the orchestrator-with-cheaper-workers design? (Select TWO.)
options: The work fans out across many independent documents whose total size is larger than one context window
Each step depends on the conclusions of the previous step in a single reasoning chain
Most items are routine, but a long tail of costly cases drives the total spend
The whole task fits comfortably in one context window and finishes in a few turns
Every worker would need the orchestrator's full conversation history to do its part
explanations: Correct. Independent pieces that together exceed one context window are where delegation came out ahead in Anthropic's measurements. Each worker handles one piece in its own context.
A dependent chain can't be split cleanly. Anthropic found the orchestrator's model alone at lower effort did better for this shape of work.
Correct. Routine work with a long cost tail is the other situation where delegating to lower-cost models paid off, as long as accuracy is checked and not only cost.
If the work fits in one context without a long cost tail, a single model at lower effort is simpler and was measured to do better.
If workers need the full history, delegation repeats the expensive context in every call and the coordination cost cancels out the cheaper rates.

questions.stem: A retail bank's data team pairs a Sonnet-class executor that runs a reconciliation agent with an Opus-class advisor that the executor may consult on hard decisions. After two weeks, the eval score is within run-to-run noise of the executor alone, and cost per task is up about 15%. Traces show the executor consulted the advisor on 3 of 600 tasks. What is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
options: The advisor model is too weak for these decisions, so the team should move the advisor up to the top frontier tier and rerun the evaluation
The executor should be forced to consult the advisor on every turn so that the pairing gets a fair test
The eval set is too small to separate the two setups, so the team should ship the pairing to production and let live data decide
An advisor that is rarely consulted adds overhead without help; benchmark against single-model baselines at different effort levels
explanations: The advisor was almost never called, so its strength isn't the bottleneck. A pricier advisor would raise cost without changing the score.
Consulting on every turn would turn the setup into the expensive model doing most of the work, plus the cost of the executor. It also measures something other than the design the team is evaluating.
Shipping a setup that costs more with no measured gain swaps evidence for hope. The trace data already explains why the score didn't move.

Correct. Anthropic's guidance is that an advisor only helps when the executor consults it. When it rarely does, the pairing scores within noise of the executor alone. Any pairing should be judged against the executor alone and the larger model at lower effort, keeping whichever leads on cost per solved task.

questions.stem: A law firm's email-triage agent reads inbound emails from clients and third parties, labels them, and drafts replies for paralegals to review. It is connected to the firm's mail MCP server with all 22 tools enabled, including `send_email`, `forward_email` and `delete_thread`. In a red-team test, an email with hidden instructions got the agent to forward a privileged thread to an outside address. What should the architect do FIRST?
options: Add a system-prompt rule that instructions inside email bodies must never be followed, and repeat that rule after each email is inserted into the context
Add an output classifier that scans every outgoing message for privileged-document markers before the mail server is allowed to deliver it
Enable only the tools the triage role needs (read, label, create draft), so sending stays with the paralegal who reviews each draft
Move the agent to the most capable model tier, which is more resistant to instructions hidden in untrusted content such as email bodies
explanations: A prompt rule is not a security boundary; injected text can still persuade the model, and the forward tool remains available to act on it.
A classifier is a compensating control that can miss content; the root cause is that an agent reading untrusted input holds tools that can send data out.
Correct. The triage job never needs send, forward or delete. Removing them in the toolset configuration removes the exfiltration path, and the human who sends the draft is the approval step.
Stronger models resist injection better but not reliably; the agent would still hold the capability the attack used.

questions.stem: A retailer's customer-service agent has 31 tools from four internal MCP servers. A 30-day trace review shows that `find_customer` (CRM server) and `lookup_client` (loyalty server) return overlapping data and the agent alternates between them unpredictably, and that six tools were never called. Which TWO changes BEST reduce capability bloat while protecting answer quality? (Select TWO.)
options: Consolidate the overlapping customer lookups into one tool with a clear name and description, and retire the other from this agent
Add `get_customer_by_email`, `get_customer_by_phone` and `get_customer_by_id` so that the agent always has an exact-match lookup available
Keep all 31 tools but add a paragraph per tool to the system prompt that explains when to prefer each one over the similar ones
Remove the never-called tools from this agent's configuration, then re-run the evaluation suite to confirm no task depended on them
Raise the model's effort level so that it reasons for longer about which of the similar-looking tools is the right one to call
explanations: Correct. Overlapping tools with similar purposes confuse selection; Anthropic's tool-writing guidance favours fewer, clearly distinct tools.
More granular near-duplicates add to the overlap problem and the token cost of definitions.
Prose about 31 tools costs more tokens and leaves the overlap in place; it treats the symptom.
Correct. Unused tools cost context on every request and add choices; pruning them and re-running evals confirms the change is safe.
More reasoning may help slightly but leaves duplicate and unused tools in the agent's context on every request.

questions.stem: A fintech's operations agent runs in the company's own harness with a single `bash` tool on a host where the payments CLI is installed. Compliance now requires that every refund above $500 is approved by a human and recorded with its amount, account and reason in an audit log. Engineers propose detecting refund commands by parsing the bash command strings with regular expressions. What is the BEST design?
options: Keep the single bash tool and add a system-prompt rule that the agent must announce any refund above $500 to the user before running it
Keep bash and parse commands with regular expressions as proposed, adding new patterns to the parser whenever the payments CLI's syntax changes
Promote refunds to a dedicated `issue_refund` tool with typed fields that the harness can gate and audit; keep bash for low-risk work
Remove bash entirely and expose every payments CLI subcommand as its own dedicated tool, so that all actions are typed and auditable
explanations: Announcing is not approval, and nothing enforces the rule; the harness still sees only an opaque command string.
Regex over shell strings is brittle (aliases, scripts, flag order) and easy to bypass, so it cannot be the control compliance relies on.
Correct. A dedicated tool gives the harness typed amount, account and reason values to gate on and log; bash keeps its breadth for actions that need no gate.
This over-corrects: dozens of new tools add selection errors and definition tokens when only one action needs a gate.

questions.stem: An insurer's claims-intake assistant classifies first-notice-of-loss messages and extracts 12 fields. On a 400-item labelled eval, the current configuration (largest model tier, high effort) scores 96% field accuracy with a p90 time to finish of 11 s. The live intake form requires at least 94% accuracy and p90 under 4 s. What should the architect do?
options: Switch to the smallest model tier at its default settings, since extraction is a simple task and the speed gain is guaranteed to hold
Sweep lower effort levels and smaller tiers on the same eval, timed in one run, and pick the cheapest one that clears both thresholds
Keep the configuration and ask the business to relax the 4 s target, since accuracy matters more than speed for insurance claims
Keep the current configuration and raise `max_tokens` so that responses never need a retry, which removes the slow tail of the distribution
explanations: It may be fast enough, but nobody has checked that it holds 94% accuracy; the decision needs measurement.
Correct. Measuring each candidate's accuracy and latency on the same eval in one run gives a justified choice: the cheapest configuration that meets both requirements.
The SLA comes from the product requirement; candidates that might meet both bars haven't been tested yet.
`max_tokens` is a ceiling, not a speed control; it does not shorten generation.

questions.stem: A legal-research product generates 2,500-token memos with the top Opus-tier model. Customers on a premium plan accept the quality but complain that memos take too long to finish. Responses already stream, the prompt prefix is cached, and evals show a smaller tier drops citation accuracy below the contractual bar. Fast mode is available for the current model. Which change BEST cuts time to finish while keeping the same model's quality?
options: Evaluate fast mode on the current model, which raises output speed at a premium price, and price that into the plan
Route memos to the smaller tier and add a second pass in which the large model reviews and corrects every memo's citations
Turn off streaming so that the full memo arrives as a single response, which removes the per-token transmission overhead
Lower `max_tokens` to 1,000 so generation stops sooner, and let users ask for a continuation whenever a memo is cut off
explanations: Correct. Most of the wait is output generation; fast mode runs the same model at higher output speed for a higher price, so quality is unchanged and the premium plan can absorb the cost. Confirm the gain on this workload.
Two passes add a second model call, so the total time may rise, and the smaller tier's citation errors still have to be caught.
Streaming does not slow generation; turning it off only delays when users see text.
Truncating memos trades a contractual deliverable for speed and pushes the remaining wait into extra calls.

questions.stem: A logistics company's dispatch agent takes about 40 s per task. Traces show 14 model calls per task. Most calls request two or three independent read-only lookups, but the harness runs them one after another and returns each result in its own user message. The first three lookups (shipment, carrier, weather at origin) are the same on every task. Accuracy on the eval is at target. Which TWO changes are MOST likely to cut task time without lowering accuracy? (Select TWO.)
options: Set `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` so each response requests a single lookup and the agent's reasoning stays sequential and easy to trace
Run the independent lookups from one response concurrently and return all of their results together in a single user message
Move the agent to the smallest model tier, since the work is mostly lookups and smaller tiers have the shortest time to first token
Raise `max_tokens` on every call so that the model never stops early and has to make an extra call to finish its plan
Run the three always-needed lookups before the first model call and include their results in the first user turn
explanations: This forces more sequential calls, adding time to first token for each one.
Correct. The parallel calls only save time if the harness executes them concurrently; returning all results in one message also keeps Claude making parallel calls.
A smaller tier may need more turns or lose accuracy; it has to be checked on the eval, unlike the two changes that leave the model unchanged.
Hitting `max_tokens` is not the problem shown in the traces, and the cap does not speed generation.
Correct. Prefetching predictable lookups removes calls from every task; check that the larger first turn doesn't hurt accuracy.

questions.stem: A bank's support assistant handles 50,000 conversations a day. When a customer disputes an answer, the support team gives engineering a timestamp, but engineering cannot match it to a specific Claude request or to the retrieval calls that fed it. Which change BEST fixes this?
options: Write every full prompt and response to the general application log so engineers can search the text for the customer's wording
Ask customers to attach a screenshot to each dispute so that engineers can find the right conversation by its visible content
Create a trace ID per conversation, pass it through the retrieval and model calls, and log each response's request ID against it
Add the customer's name and account number to the system prompt so the model repeats them in every answer for later search
explanations: Full text in a general log raises privacy risk for banking data and still gives no reliable join between retrieval and model calls.
Screenshots are manual and do not identify the request or retrieval results behind the answer.
Correct. A propagated trace ID links every step of the conversation, and the API request ID identifies the exact model call, including for provider support.
This puts personal data into prompts and answers and still links nothing to the retrieval calls.

questions.stem: A hospital network wants OpenTelemetry traces from its clinical-documentation assistant in its observability vendor, to debug slow and failed requests. Prompts contain patient information. The tracing integration can export metadata only (IDs, timing, status, token counts) or full prompt and response content. What should the architect recommend?
options: Export full content for all traffic, since the vendor is already approved for the hospital's operational logs and richer traces shorten debugging
Export full content but tell the model to replace patient names with initials in its responses, so that the exported traces are de-identified
Disable tracing entirely and rely on clinicians reporting slow requests, since any telemetry from a clinical system is a privacy risk
Export metadata only by default; turn on full content only for a backend whose access and retention are confirmed fit for patient data
explanations: Approval for operational logs is not approval for patient data; full content would be stored under the vendor's own access and retention settings.
Prompts would still contain patient data, and asking the model to redact is not a reliable de-identification control.
This throws away the debugging capability the team needs when a privacy-safe option exists.
Correct. Metadata is enough to debug slow and failed requests. Content export is a separate decision that depends on the backend meeting the hospital's requirements.

questions.stem: After a release of a SaaS company's contract-review assistant, cost per request rose about fivefold and time to first token doubled, with no errors and unchanged quality scores. The 30,000-token system prompt and tool definitions were not edited, except that a line with the current date and time was added at the top of the system prompt. Which monitoring signal would have flagged this at deploy time, and what is the root cause?
options: The HTTP 429 rate rising; the longer prompt exceeds the organisation's input-token rate limit, so the SDK keeps retrying
`stop_reason` shifting to `max_tokens`; the extra line pushes output past its limit, so responses are truncated and then retried
`usage.cache_read_input_tokens` falling to near zero; the timestamp changes the prefix on every request, so the cache never hits
Output tokens per request rising; the model now writes the date into every answer, which raises the cost per request
explanations: No errors were seen, and a single line does not explain a fivefold cost rise.
One line in the input does not affect output limits, and no truncation was reported.
Correct. Caching is a prefix match; a value that changes on each request at the top invalidates everything after it. Tracking cache reads per release catches this immediately.
A date in each answer adds a handful of tokens, not a fivefold cost increase and slower first tokens.

questions.stem: A payments company is defining the default per-call telemetry record for every Claude request across 20 services. Records feed a shared log index that 300 engineers can query. Which THREE fields belong in that default record? (Select THREE.)
options: The API request ID and the calling service's own trace ID for the user request
The full prompt and response text, so any engineer can replay a whole conversation
The model ID, input and output tokens, and the cache read and cache write tokens
The API key used for the call, so that usage can be attributed to the right key
The customer's name and card number, so incidents can be traced to a customer quickly
Stop reason, tool names and error flags, time to first token and total latency
explanations: Correct. These IDs let engineers join a call to its user request and to provider-side records.
Full payment conversations in a broadly readable index create a data-exposure risk; capture content only in an access-controlled tier if needed.
Correct. Model and token fields, including cache fields, explain cost and latency and expose cache regressions.
Secrets never belong in logs; attribute usage with the key's ID or the workspace instead.
Card data and names in a shared index violate data minimisation; use a pseudonymous customer reference if one is needed.
Correct. These show truncation, refusals, tool failures and where time goes.

questions.stem: A research product's multi-agent system runs for 10–30 minutes per task. About 8% of tasks end with a thin report. The logs only record the user's question, the final report and total tokens, so the team cannot tell whether a subagent got stuck, a search returned nothing, or the coordinator discarded findings. What should the architect add FIRST?
options: A second coordinator that re-runs every task whose report falls below a length threshold, then keeps the longer of the two reports
Step-level tracing of each agent's delegation briefs, tool calls and results, errors and decisions, linked under one task trace
A feedback button on the report so that customers can flag thin reports, followed by a weekly manual review of the flagged tasks
A larger model for every subagent, since thin reports usually mean the subagents could not reason well enough about their search results
explanations: Re-running doubles the cost and hides the failure instead of explaining it.
Correct. Anthropic credits full production tracing with diagnosing why its research agents failed. Agents are stateful and errors compound, so the step-level path is what reveals the cause.
Feedback flags symptoms later, but reviewers would still lack the step data needed to find the cause.
This guesses at a cause the team cannot yet see; it may not be the model at all.

questions.stem: An education platform's tutoring agent serves minors. The privacy office forbids engineers from reading conversation content in production, but the product team needs to know why session completion fell 12% after a model update. Which monitoring approach BEST satisfies both?
options: Grant two senior engineers break-glass access to read every transcript from the affected week, with each access logged and reviewed
Compare content-free signals by model version (tool-call sequences, turns per session, stop reasons, refusal rates) before and after
Wait until enough teacher complaints arrive to reveal the failure pattern, since no conversation content may be inspected directly
Send full transcripts to an external analytics vendor, which summarises the issues so that the engineers themselves never see raw text
explanations: Bulk reading of minors' conversations conflicts with the privacy rule, even with access logging.
Correct. Anthropic describes monitoring agent decision patterns and interaction structure without monitoring conversation contents; comparing these by version shows where behaviour changed.
This leaves the regression unexplained and slow to fix when content-free analysis is possible.
Sharing minors' transcripts with another processor widens exposure instead of respecting the restriction.

questions.stem: A media company's finance team wants exact monthly Claude spend per API key and per workspace, and wants to spot a leaked key quickly. The platform team proposes summing token counts from the OpenTelemetry traces it already collects, which are sampled at 10% and delivered on a best-effort basis. What should the architect recommend?
options: Raise trace sampling to 100% so the summed token counts become exact, then build the finance report from the traces
Use the provider's usage and cost reporting for spend by key and workspace, and keep traces for debugging and latency
Multiply the sampled token totals by ten and add a 5% buffer, since sampling error averages out over a whole month
Ask each service team to log its own token counts in a shared spreadsheet at month-end for finance to reconcile
explanations: Even unsampled, best-effort delivery can drop spans, and only instrumented callers appear, so a leaked key used elsewhere would be missed.
Correct. Usage and cost reports count every request by key and workspace, including ones with no spans; traces serve diagnosis.
Extrapolation cannot give exact spend and cannot reveal a leaked key's traffic.
Manual self-reporting is error-prone and blind to unauthorised use of a key.

questions.stem: A telecom runs 3 million Claude-backed support turns a day. Storing full traces (including tool inputs and outputs) for every turn would cost more than the model calls, yet engineers need complete detail when something goes wrong. Which strategy BEST balances cost and diagnosability?
options: Keep lightweight metrics for every turn, plus full traces for errors, refusals and low-scored turns and a small random sample
Keep full traces for every turn but delete them after 24 hours, so that storage stays bounded while recent issues can still be debugged
Record nothing per turn and rebuild any failing conversation on demand by replaying the user's messages against the current model
Keep full traces for a 1% random sample only, since a large enough random sample captures every failure mode in proportion to its frequency
explanations: Correct. Metrics on all traffic support alerting and trends; full detail is kept where it is most likely needed, plus a random sample for unbiased analysis.
This still pays to write every full trace, and issues found after a day can no longer be investigated.
Replays are not faithful: tool results, retrieved data and sampling differ, so the original failure may not recur.
Rare but severe failures are likely to fall outside a 1% sample; errors and flagged turns should always be kept.

questions.stem: A 40-person accounting firm wants an assistant that answers staff questions about its internal policy handbook. The handbook is about 90,000 tokens and changes a few times a year. A contractor has proposed a vector database, a chunking pipeline and an embedding service. What should the architect recommend?
options: Put the whole handbook in the prompt with prompt caching, and revisit retrieval only if the corpus outgrows that approach
Build the proposed pipeline, since retrieval is the standard architecture for any assistant that answers questions over documents
Fine-tune a model on the handbook so that the answers come from the model weights and no handbook context is needed
Split the handbook into ten sections and ask staff to choose the right section before they type their question
explanations: Correct. Anthropic suggests that a knowledge base under about 200,000 tokens can go entirely in the prompt, with prompt caching keeping repeated use fast and cheap.
Retrieval adds components to build and maintain and can miss relevant passages; it isn't needed for a corpus this small.
Fine-tuning is costly, hard to update when the handbook changes, and gives no grounding in the actual text.
This moves retrieval work onto users, who may pick the wrong section, when the whole handbook fits in context.

questions.stem: An asset manager indexes 10-K filings for an analyst assistant, embedding chunks of about 400 tokens as-is. When analysts ask 'What was Acme's revenue growth in Q2 2025?', they often get chunks from other companies' filings, because many chunks read like 'Revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter' and name neither company nor period. Which change BEST addresses the root cause?
options: Raise the number of retrieved chunks from 5 to 50 so the right company's chunk is more likely to appear among the results
Have Claude write a short chunk-specific context from the full filing and prepend it before embedding and BM25 indexing
Tell the model in the generation prompt to ignore any retrieved chunk that does not name the company asked about
Double the chunk size to 800 tokens so that more of the surrounding text is captured in each chunk's embedding
explanations: More chunks add noise and tokens; the chunks still lack the company and period, so ranking stays poor.

Correct. This is contextual retrieval: 50–100 tokens naming the company, filing and period make each chunk findable. Anthropic measured a 49% drop in top-20 retrieval failures when it was applied to both embeddings and BM25.
If the right chunk was never retrieved, discarding the wrong ones cannot produce a correct answer.
Larger chunks may still omit the company name and dilute the embedding, and they don't fix the missing context.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company plans to apply contextual retrieval to 30,000 regulatory documents averaging 8,000 tokens, each split into about ten chunks. Finance objects that sending the full document once per chunk to generate context multiplies indexing input cost roughly tenfold. Which design BEST addresses the concern?
options: Write one summary per document and prepend that same summary to all of its chunks, so each document needs only one model call
Skip contextualisation and rely on a reranker, which recovers any missing chunk context at query time at no indexing cost at all
Put each document once in a cached prompt prefix and generate every chunk's context against it, so repeats bill as cache reads
Contextualise only the first chunk of each document, since later chunks usually repeat the context that the opening establishes
explanations: Anthropic found generic document summaries gave very limited gains compared with chunk-specific context.
A reranker can only reorder chunks that were retrieved; it does not restore context missing from the index, and it adds per-query cost.
Correct. Anthropic used prompt caching so each document is loaded once and referenced for every chunk, estimating a one-time cost of about $1.02 per million document tokens.
Later chunks are exactly the ones that lose context; skipping them leaves the original failure in place.

questions.stem: A public-sector agency's benefits assistant splits policy manuals into fixed 300-token chunks with no overlap. Evaluation shows many wrong answers come from chunks that separate an eligibility rule from its exceptions in the next paragraph, and from tables split across two chunks. Which TWO changes BEST address this? (Select TWO.)
options: Chunk along the document's structure (sections, rules with their exceptions, whole tables) instead of at fixed token counts
Raise retrieval from top-5 to top-100 chunks so that both halves of each split rule are usually present in the context
Embed each full manual as a single vector so that no eligibility rule is ever separated from its listed exceptions
Add a modest overlap between adjacent chunks, then re-run the retrieval eval to tune chunk size and overlap together
Tell the model in the system prompt to assume exceptions may exist whenever a retrieved rule looks incomplete
explanations: Correct. Boundaries that follow the document's structure keep rules, exceptions and tables together.
This floods the prompt with mostly irrelevant chunks and still doesn't guarantee both halves are retrieved.
One vector per manual makes retrieval far too coarse to find specific rules.
Correct. Overlap reduces breaks at boundaries; Anthropic notes chunk size, boundaries and overlap all affect retrieval, so tune them on an eval.
Guessing about missing exceptions makes answers vaguer and less trustworthy; the retrieval defect remains.

questions.stem: An insurance carrier's underwriting assistant retrieves from 12 years of underwriting guidelines. Guidelines are reissued every year, and old versions stay in the index for audit reasons. Underwriters report answers that quote superseded rules, and many questions concern a specific state. Which indexing change BEST fixes this?
options: Add a system-prompt instruction to prefer the most recent rule whenever the retrieved chunks conflict with one another
Store state, effective-date and status metadata on each chunk, and filter to in-force versions for that state before ranking
Delete all superseded guidelines from every system, including the audit archive, so the index holds only current rules
Re-embed the corpus with a larger embedding model that separates current guidelines from superseded ones more clearly
explanations: If only superseded chunks are retrieved there is no conflict to resolve, and dates may not appear in chunk text.
Correct. Version and jurisdiction are known facts, so filtering on stored metadata excludes superseded and out-of-state rules deterministically while the archive stays intact.
Audit needs the history; the fix is to exclude old versions from live answers, not destroy them.
Embeddings capture meaning, not validity dates; near-identical yearly versions will still look alike.

questions.stem: A consulting firm is building an internal assistant over 2 million documents from client engagements. Engagement teams may see only their own clients' material. The prototype retrieves the top 20 chunks across the whole index and tells the model to 'only use documents the user is allowed to see', passing the user's team list in the prompt. What is the BEST fix?
options: Keep the prompt rule and add an output classifier that blocks any answer mentioning client names outside the user's own engagements
Store each document's access groups on its chunks and filter retrieval by the signed-in user's groups before Claude sees anything
Build a separate vector index per user, copying in every document that user can access, and rebuild every index each night
Move the access rule to the top of the system prompt and repeat it after the retrieved chunks so the model weighs it more
explanations: Restricted content still reaches the model, and a classifier can miss paraphrased leaks.
Correct. Authorisation belongs in deterministic retrieval code tied to the authenticated identity; unauthorised content never enters the context.
This enforces access but duplicates the corpus per user and leaves permissions up to a day stale; metadata filtering does the same on one index.
A prompt is not an access control; the restricted chunks are already in the model's context.

questions.stem: A SaaS company switched its help-centre RAG to a newer embedding model. To save cost, only articles created after the switch were embedded with the new model; existing vectors were kept, and queries are now embedded with the new model. Retrieval for older articles collapsed. What should the team do?
options: Re-embed the whole corpus with the new model into a new index, validate it on the retrieval eval, then switch queries
Lower the similarity threshold for older articles so that they are still returned even when their scores are lower
Embed each query with both models and average the two vectors, so that it matches old and new articles equally well
Add older article titles to the system prompt so that the model can answer questions about them without any retrieval
explanations: Correct. Queries and documents must be embedded by the same model; re-indexing the corpus and validating before cut-over restores comparability safely.
Scores between a new-model query and old-model vectors are not meaningful, so a lower threshold returns noise.
Vectors from different models live in different spaces; averaging them produces a vector meaningful in neither.
Titles alone don't contain the answers, and this sidesteps rather than fixes the broken index.

questions.stem: A law firm is choosing an embedding model for retrieval over contracts and case law. One vendor tops a public general-purpose leaderboard; another offers a legal-domain model. Anthropic does not offer its own embedding model. Which TWO steps BEST support the decision? (Select TWO.)
options: Pick the leaderboard leader, since public benchmark rank reliably predicts retrieval performance in any domain
Build a labelled set of real lawyer queries with known relevant passages and compare recall at the pipeline's top-K
Include the legal-domain model among the candidates and weigh retrieval quality against latency and cost at volume
Embed the documents with a Claude model, since one vendor for generation and embeddings keeps the vectors aligned
Choose the model with the largest embedding dimension, since more dimensions always produce better retrieval quality
explanations: General benchmarks may not reflect legal vocabulary or the firm's query patterns.
Correct. Measuring recall on the firm's own queries is the evidence the choice should rest on.
Correct. Anthropic's embeddings guide lists domain specificity, inference performance and customisation as selection factors.
Anthropic does not offer an embedding model, and generation and retrieval models don't need to share a vendor.
Dimension is a storage and speed trade-off; it does not guarantee better retrieval.

questions.stem: A manufacturer's maintenance assistant indexes equipment manuals. To give chunks context cheaply, the team prepends the same 150-token summary of each manual to every chunk from that manual. Retrieval improved only slightly. According to Anthropic's contextual retrieval findings, which change is MOST likely to improve retrieval further?
options: Lengthen the shared summary to about 600 tokens so that it covers more of each manual's subsystems and procedures
Index only the per-manual summaries instead of the chunks, and fetch the whole manual whenever its summary matches
Remove the summaries and raise the chunk size until each chunk holds an entire chapter of the equipment manual
Replace the shared summary with a short context generated for each chunk that situates it within the manual
explanations: A longer generic summary is still the same for every chunk, so it doesn't distinguish one chunk from another.
Anthropic reports that summary-based indexing performed poorly.
Chapter-sized chunks dilute embeddings and pass much more irrelevant text to the model.
Correct. Anthropic found generic document summaries gave very limited gains, while chunk-specific context cut retrieval failures substantially.

questions.stem: A health insurer's member-benefits assistant must show, for each claim in an answer, the exact passage from the retrieved plan documents that supports it. Today the prompt asks Claude to quote its sources, and auditors sometimes find quotes that do not appear verbatim in any document. Which change BEST meets the requirement?
options: Return each answer as JSON with a `quote` field per claim using structured outputs, and keep the existing prompt instruction
Lower the sampling temperature so that quoted passages are reproduced more faithfully from the retrieved documents
Pass each retrieved chunk as a document block with citations enabled, and show the returned cited text and its location
Add a second model call asking Claude to confirm each quote is accurate before the answer is shown to the member
explanations: Structured outputs guarantee the JSON shape, not that the quote text exists in a source; citations also can't be combined with structured outputs.
Sampling settings don't guarantee verbatim quotes.
Correct. The citations feature extracts `cited_text` from the provided documents, so every citation points to a real passage, and `cited_text` doesn't count toward output tokens.
A model checking a model is still probabilistic and adds latency; the citations feature solves this structurally.

questions.stem: An industrial-equipment company's support assistant uses embedding search over service bulletins. Technicians who search for exact fault codes such as 'E-4471' or part numbers often get bulletins about similar-sounding faults instead of the one that names the code. What is the BEST retrieval change?
options: Add a BM25 keyword index next to the embeddings and merge both result lists with rank fusion
Ask technicians to describe the symptom in words instead of typing the fault code into the search
Switch to a larger embedding model, which will represent fault codes and part numbers more precisely
Raise top-K from 10 to 100 so the bulletin that names the code is more likely to appear somewhere
explanations: Correct. BM25 matches exact terms such as codes; Anthropic's contextual retrieval post uses an error code as the example and combines both rankings with rank fusion.
This discards the most precise signal the technician has.
Embeddings capture meaning and often miss exact identifiers whatever the model size.
The right bulletin may still rank poorly, and the extra chunks add noise and cost.

questions.stem: A bank's policy assistant passes the top 10 chunks from hybrid search to Claude. Offline analysis shows the correct chunk is in the top 150 candidates for 97% of questions but in the top 10 for only 78%. The latency budget allows about 300 ms more per query. Which change BEST improves answer quality?
options: Re-chunk the corpus into much smaller pieces so that more distinct chunks fit within the top 10 results
Pass all 150 candidates to Claude, since a large context lets the model find the right chunk on its own
Retrieve about 150 candidates, rerank them with a reranking model, and pass the top 20 to Claude
Move generation to the largest model tier so that it answers better from the 10 chunks it receives
explanations: Smaller chunks don't fix ranking and can strip context from each chunk.
150 chunks per request raise cost and latency and bury the relevant passage in noise.
Correct. Recall is fine but ranking is weak. Anthropic's setup retrieved 150 candidates and passed the reranked top 20; confirm the reranker's added latency fits the 300 ms budget.
When the right chunk isn't in the top 10 for 22% of questions, no generator can answer those correctly.

questions.stem: A retail chain wants its analyst assistant to answer questions such as 'Which five stores had the largest drop in weekly sales versus last year?' The data is in a 40-million-row sales warehouse table. A prototype embeds each row as text and retrieves the 50 most similar rows. Answers are often wrong. What should the architect change?
options: Give Claude a read-only query tool over the warehouse, or code execution over an extract, to compute the answer
Raise top-K to 5,000 rows and use the large context window so the model sees enough data to compute the rankings
Add a reranker so that the 50 rows passed to the model are the most relevant ones for each analyst question
Embed weekly aggregates instead of individual rows so that fewer, richer chunks are retrieved for each question
explanations: Correct. Aggregates and rankings over structured data are computations; a narrow read-only query tool or code execution produces exact results.
A sample of rows still can't produce correct totals over 40 million rows, and the cost would be large.
Better ordering of 50 rows doesn't change the fact that the answer needs aggregation over all rows.
Pre-aggregation helps only the questions it anticipated, and similarity search still can't rank or compare stores.

questions.stem: A procurement team asks questions such as 'Which suppliers that failed a quality audit in 2025 have contracts renewing in the next 90 days, and what remediation did they commit to?' The answer spans audit reports, a contract register and email threads. A single top-20 retrieval on the whole question returns fragments from only one source. Which approach BEST fits this query pattern?
options: Give an agent search tools over each source so it can run successive targeted queries, each shaped by earlier results
Raise top-K to 200 on the single retrieval call so that fragments from all three sources are likely to be included
Merge the three sources into one index with larger chunks so that a single query can reach across all of them
Precompute an answer for every supplier each night and retrieve the matching precomputed answer at query time
explanations: Correct. Just-in-time, agentic retrieval lets the agent find failed suppliers, then check their contracts, then find remediation emails.
The question is multi-hop: the second lookup depends on the first result, which a bigger single retrieval can't do.
Merging indexes doesn't create the joins the question needs, and larger chunks blur retrieval.
Precomputing works only for questions anticipated in advance and goes stale.

questions.stem: A telecom's support chatbot retrieves knowledge-base articles using the customer's latest message as the search query. Follow-ups such as 'and what about for the business plan?' or 'does that apply abroad?' retrieve unrelated articles, although first questions work well. What is the BEST fix?
options: Use the entire conversation transcript, concatenated, as the retrieval query on every turn
Retrieve only on the first turn and reuse those same articles for the rest of the conversation
Ask customers to restate their full question in every message so that each query stands alone
Rewrite each follow-up into a standalone query using the conversation, then retrieve with it
explanations: A long transcript dilutes the query with earlier, unrelated topics.
Follow-ups often need different articles from the first question.
This pushes the system's problem onto customers and hurts the experience.
Correct. A standalone query carries the missing context (which plan, which feature) into retrieval; check it on recorded conversations.

questions.stem: A real-estate investment firm wants Claude to analyse one 250-page lease (about 140,000 tokens) at a time and answer questions such as whether any clause, read together with its amendments, restricts subletting. The RAG prototype retrieves eight chunks and misses interactions between distant clauses. Which approach BEST fits?
options: Put the whole lease in the prompt, document first and question last, and cache it for follow-up questions on that lease
Shrink chunks to 100 tokens so the retriever can fit more of the relevant clauses within its eight retrieved chunks
Summarise each page into two sentences and send only those summaries, which keeps every request small and cheap
Raise top-K to 30 chunks and add a reranker so that more clauses about subletting are included in each request
explanations: Correct. The lease fits in the context window, and the task needs reasoning across distant clauses. Long documents at the top with the question at the end improve quality, and caching makes follow-ups cheap.
Tiny chunks lose context and still can't guarantee every interacting clause is retrieved.
Summaries drop the exact wording that legal interpretation depends on.
More chunks help, but clauses that interact without mentioning subletting can still be missed.

questions.stem: A university's research-office assistant passes 20 retrieved grant-policy chunks to Claude. The prompt puts the user's question and instructions first, then pastes the chunks as one block of plain text with no sources. Answers often miss relevant chunks and cannot say which policy they came from. Which TWO changes BEST follow Anthropic's long-context prompting guidance? (Select TWO.)
options: Merge the 20 chunks into one condensed summary paragraph before inserting it, so that the prompt is shorter
Place the retrieved chunks first and put the question and instructions at the end of the prompt
Strip document titles and dates from the chunks to save tokens for more retrieved policy text
Wrap each chunk in its own document tags, with source and date metadata in subtags
Shuffle the chunk order on each request so that the model does not favour the chunks that come first
explanations: A merged summary loses wording and source boundaries, so answers become harder to ground and impossible to attribute.
Correct. Anthropic's guidance puts long-form data at the top and the query at the end, which can improve response quality by up to 30% in tests.
Removing metadata stops the model from attributing answers to policies.
Correct. Per-document tags with source metadata help the model separate and cite sources.
Random order adds variance without addressing structure or attribution.

questions.stem: An energy company's engineering assistant retrieves from 8,000 slide decks and scanned inspection reports. Many answers depend on charts, diagrams and tables that are images inside the files, but the pipeline extracts only the text layer and embeds it. Which change BEST addresses the failure?
options: Increase the chunk overlap so that captions near each image are always included with the surrounding text
Instruct the model to tell the user to 'see the original chart' whenever a question appears to concern a chart, diagram or table
Embed pages with a multimodal model or describe visuals at ingestion, and send retrieved page images to Claude
Switch to a larger text embedding model, which can infer the content of figures from their captions alone
explanations: Captions rarely contain the values in a chart, and scanned pages may have no text layer at all.
This admits the gap rather than closing it.
Correct. Retrieval has to see the visual content (multimodal embeddings or text descriptions), and Claude can read the retrieved page images directly.
No text model can recover information that was never extracted from the images.

questions.stem: A government tax-guidance assistant scores 71% on its answer-quality eval. The team disagrees about whether to change the retriever or the generation prompt. Which TWO analyses BEST locate the problem? (Select TWO.)
options: Measure retrieval recall: for each eval question, check whether the labelled supporting passage was in the chunks passed to Claude
Swap in the largest model tier and compare scores, since a jump would prove that retrieval is not the problem
Count the average tokens per answer, since short answers indicate that retrieval failed to return content
Rewrite the generation prompt and keep whichever version scores higher, since the prompt is cheaper to change
For failures where the supporting passage was retrieved, review how the answer used it to find generation errors
explanations: Correct. Recall on labelled questions shows how many failures start with a retrieval miss.
A score change wouldn't separate the two stages and spends money without diagnosing anything.
Answer length is a weak proxy unrelated to whether the right passage was retrieved.
Changing a component before locating the fault may optimise the wrong stage.
Correct. Failures with the right passage in context point to the generation step (prompt, layout, model).

questions.stem: A multinational's HR assistant answers policy questions for employees in 30 countries. Policies for different countries are worded almost identically, and retrieval often returns another country's leave policy. Each employee's country is known from their profile. What is the BEST retrieval strategy?
options: Filter by the employee's country (plus global policies) using chunk metadata, before ranking the results
Add the employee's country to the query text so that the embedding leans towards that country's policies
Retrieve the top 50 across all countries and ask Claude to discard any chunks from other countries
Train a separate embedding model for each country so that each country's policies cluster apart
explanations: Correct. When the scope is known, a metadata filter excludes other countries deterministically, and similarity ranking then works within the right set.
Near-identical wording means the country term barely shifts the ranking.
The prompt fills with irrelevant chunks, and the right one may not be among the 50.
Thirty custom models are costly to build and maintain, and a filter solves this directly.

questions.stem: An e-commerce platform team wants engineers' Claude Code sessions to read and update tickets in its incident tracker. The tracker ships a well-documented CLI that every engineer already has installed and signed in. A developer proposes building and hosting a custom MCP server that wraps the same operations. What should the tech lead recommend first?
options: Build the MCP server as proposed, since MCP is the only supported way for Claude Code to reach an external system
Let Claude Code use the installed CLI through Bash (with `--help` if needed) and keep MCP for systems without a CLI
Paste the tracker's REST API reference into CLAUDE.md so that Claude can build HTTP calls whenever it needs ticket data
Export every open ticket to a JSON file in the repository each morning so that Claude can read tickets without any tool
explanations: Claude Code can run CLIs through Bash; a new server adds build, hosting and maintenance work, and its tool definitions take context even when unused.
Correct. Claude Code's guidance is that a system's CLI is usually the easiest way in, with MCP for systems that lack one; the CLI also reuses each engineer's existing sign-in.
Hand-built HTTP calls duplicate what the CLI already does, and the reference loads into every session.
A daily export is stale and read-only, so Claude can't update tickets.

questions.stem: An accounting-software vendor's support agent has 35 procedure documents (refund handling, tax-form corrections, data migration and so on), totalling 140,000 tokens, pasted into the system prompt for every request. Most conversations need one procedure or none. Which change BEST reduces context load while keeping the procedures available?
options: Keep all of the procedures in the system prompt and turn on prompt caching so that the 140,000 tokens become cheap to resend
Package each procedure as a Skill, so only its name and description stay in context and the full text loads when a task matches
Condense each procedure into a single paragraph and keep those 35 paragraphs in the system prompt instead of the full text
Split the agent into 35 agents, one per procedure, and send every conversation to all 35 of them in parallel
explanations: Caching cuts cost and time to first token, but all 140,000 tokens still sit in context and can distract the model on every request.
Correct. Skills use progressive disclosure: roughly 100 tokens of metadata per Skill are always loaded, and the instructions enter context only when triggered.
Condensed procedures lose the step-by-step detail agents need to follow them correctly.
Fan-out to 35 agents multiplies cost and creates an aggregation problem for a task one agent can handle.

questions.stem: A logistics start-up's dispatch assistant has six small tools (under 1,500 tokens of definitions in total), and almost every request uses all six. An engineer proposes adding the tool search tool and deferring five of them 'to follow best practice for context efficiency'. What should the architect advise?
options: Adopt the change, since deferring tools always cuts tokens and improves tool selection, whatever the size of the tool catalogue
Adopt it, but defer all six tools and the tool search tool as well, so that the context starts out completely empty
Keep all six loaded; deferral adds search round trips and suits large catalogues, not a few tools used every time
Replace the six tools with one generic tool that takes an action name, so that only a single definition has to load
explanations: Tool search pays off for large catalogues; here it would add a search before almost every call for negligible savings.
Deferring the search tool and every other tool is rejected by the API: at least one tool must stay non-deferred.
Correct. Anthropic's docs say standard tool calling fits better with fewer than 10 tools, or when every tool is used on every request.
A generic action dispatcher weakens schemas and makes tool use harder to validate and audit.

questions.stem: A pharmacovigilance team's case-coding agent applies a 60,000-token coding rulebook to every case; any rule may be relevant to any case, and the rulebook changes quarterly. An architect proposes moving the rulebook behind a retrieval tool so that the agent fetches only the rules it thinks it needs. What is the BEST response?
options: Keep the rulebook in the prompt as a stable, cached prefix; retrieval risks missing rules the agent didn't know to look up
Adopt the retrieval tool, since progressive discovery is always preferable to loading large reference content into the prompt up front
Move the rulebook into a Skill so that it loads only when the agent decides that a case needs the coding rules
Split the rulebook between the system prompt and the user turns so that no single block exceeds 30,000 tokens
explanations: Correct. When content is needed on every request, is stable and fits comfortably, loading it up front with prompt caching is cheaper per use and avoids discovery misses.
Progressive discovery suits large, mostly-unused content; here the agent cannot know which rules apply without reading them.
Every case needs the rulebook, so on-demand loading adds a step and the risk that it is skipped.
Splitting the text doesn't change how much context is used, and it complicates caching.

questions.stem: An enterprise IT assistant has 220 tools from nine MCP servers. To save tokens, the harness runs a classifier before each turn and rebuilds the `tools` array with the 15 tools it predicts are relevant. Token use fell, but prompt-cache reads are near zero, and wrong-tool errors rise whenever the classifier misses a needed tool. Which change BEST addresses both problems?
options: Keep the classifier but have it select 60 tools per turn instead of 15, so that needed tools are missed less often
Send all 220 tools on every turn with a cache breakpoint after them, accepting the token cost in exchange for a stable cache
Run the classifier once per conversation instead of every turn, and restart the conversation whenever a needed tool is missing
Send the full catalogue with most tools deferred plus the tool search tool, so Claude appends what it needs
explanations: A different tool set each turn still changes the prefix and breaks the cache, and misses remain possible.
This restores caching but brings back the context bloat and the selection errors seen with hundreds of tools.
Restarts lose conversation state and frustrate users; the classifier's misses are still the bottleneck.
Correct. With tool search, Claude finds tools itself, and discovered definitions are appended rather than swapped, which preserves the cached prefix.

questions.stem: A bank's internal assistant uses the built-in BM25 tool search over 900 deferred tools. Logs show many misses: employees ask to 'freeze a card', but the tool is described as 'set payment instrument status to suspended'. Rewriting all 900 descriptions will take months. Which approach BEST improves discovery soon?
options: Remove tool search and load all 900 tool definitions so the model can read every description directly on each request
Raise the number of tools returned per search to 200 so that the right tool is usually somewhere in the results
Switch to the regex variant of tool search, which matches tool descriptions more loosely than BM25 does
Implement a custom search tool based on embedding similarity that returns `tool_reference` blocks for matching deferred tools
explanations: 900 definitions bring back context bloat and degrade selection well past the 30–50 tool range.
Loading 200 tools per search defeats deferral and hurts selection accuracy.
Regex is lexical too, so it won't connect 'freeze' with 'suspended'.

Correct. Anthropic documents custom tool search: return `tool_reference` blocks from your own tool, for example using embeddings, which match on meaning rather than exact words. Improve descriptions over time as well.

questions.stem: A SaaS company's agent uses tool search over 300 deferred tools. Traces show that on 90% of requests the agent first searches for and loads the same three core tools (`get_account`, `search_tickets`, `add_note`), adding a round trip. It also sometimes fails to search for billing tools at all, because it does not know they exist. Which TWO changes BEST address this? (Select TWO.)
options: Mark the three core tools as non-deferred so that they are loaded from the start of every request
Mark the tool search tool itself as deferred so that it takes no context until the agent needs it
Add a short system-prompt section listing the tool categories available through search, such as billing
Put a `cache_control` breakpoint on each deferred tool definition so that search results load faster
Raise the search result limit to 50 so that each search loads every tool that could possibly be relevant
explanations: Correct. Anthropic recommends keeping the 3–5 most frequently used tools non-deferred.
The search tool must never be deferred; Claude needs it in context to find anything.
Correct. Describing the available categories tells Claude what it can search for.
A deferred tool can't carry `cache_control`; the API returns a 400.
Loading 50 tools per search undoes the context savings and adds selection noise.

questions.stem: A pharmacy chain's patient-messaging agent must append a specific regulatory disclaimer to every outbound message. To shrink the system prompt, a developer moved the disclaimer rule into a Skill along with 20 situational procedures. Audits now find messages without the disclaimer. What should the architect do?
options: Rewrite the disclaimer Skill's description to say it applies to every message, so that it triggers more often than it does today
Leave situational procedures in Skills, but have the sending code append the fixed disclaimer to every message
Instruct the model in the system prompt to always check the list of Skills for compliance rules before writing any reply
Add the disclaimer as an example inside each of the other 20 Skills so that it appears whenever any Skill happens to load
explanations: Skills still load only when the model judges them relevant, so a broader description doesn't guarantee the rule is applied.
Correct. A fixed, mandatory text is best enforced deterministically in code; on-demand loading suits situational content, not rules that apply to everything.
This adds another probabilistic step to a requirement that must hold every time.
Messages that need no Skill would still go out without the disclaimer.

questions.stem: A retail bank's product owner writes the success criterion for a new complaint-classification feature as 'Claude should categorise complaints well and fast.' The architect has to turn it into a criterion the team can test against before launch. Which rewrite is BEST?
options: Claude should reach 100% accuracy on every complaint category, so that no complaint is ever routed to the wrong team.
At least 92% agreement with compliance-team labels on a held-out set of 2,000 recent complaints matching the production category mix, with p95 latency under 3 seconds.
Claude should categorise complaints accurately and quickly, as judged each week by the product owner reviewing a sample of outputs and confirming they look reasonable.
Use the most capable Claude model at its highest effort setting, so that categorisation quality is as high as it can be.
explanations: Not achievable or anchored to any baseline. A 100% target can't be met or verified, and it doesn't name a test set or a latency bar.
Correct. It is specific (agreement with expert labels), measurable (92%, p95 under 3 s), tied to a representative held-out set, and covers both dimensions the owner cares about.
Still vague and unmeasurable. 'Looks reasonable' to one reviewer is neither a defined scale nor a repeatable test.
This is a configuration choice, not a success criterion. It says nothing about how to measure 'well' or 'fast', and it may break any latency or cost target.

questions.stem: A hospital network is launching a patient-portal assistant that answers questions about appointments and medications. The chief medical officer's only requirement for privacy is 'it must be safe.' The architect needs a privacy criterion that can block a release. Which is BEST?
options: Add a system-prompt instruction telling Claude never to reveal protected health information, to check every answer for patient details before sending it, and always to put patient safety first.
Track the weekly number of patient complaints about privacy, and investigate whenever it rises above the previous month's level.

Zero responses judged by a calibrated binary grader to disclose another patient's health information, across a 500-query test set with explicit, hypothetical and implicit PHI cases; any failure blocks release.
Require the assistant to refuse any question that mentions a medication, which removes the risk of disclosing medical details.
explanations: An instruction is a control, not a measure. Without a test set and a threshold nobody can show the release meets the requirement.
Complaints are sparse, self-selected and reactive. Harm reaches patients before the signal appears, so this can't gate a release.
Correct. It turns 'safe' into a measurable gate: a defined test set covering hard implicit cases, a grader suited to subtle PHI, and an explicit pass bar.
This fails task fidelity for a medication-questions assistant. It also defines no metric, so it isn't a success criterion.

questions.stem: An insurer uses Claude to flag incoming claims that need urgent handling, such as a suspected injury or a vulnerable customer. About 3% of claims are urgent. A pilot report says the classifier is '97% accurate', and the operations director is ready to sign off. Which metric should the architect insist on before sign-off?
options: Recall and precision on the urgent class, measured on a labelled set with enough urgent examples to estimate both reliably.
Overall accuracy re-measured on a much larger random sample of claims, because 97% on a small pilot may not hold at production volume.
The average confidence Claude reports for its labels, to confirm that the model is sure about its urgent and non-urgent decisions.
Mean latency per claim, because urgent claims have to reach a handler quickly once they are flagged.
explanations: Correct. With a 3% positive rate, a classifier that never flags anything is 97% accurate. Recall on the urgent class shows how many urgent claims are caught, and precision shows the cost in false alarms.
A bigger sample still measures the wrong thing. Overall accuracy stays dominated by the 97% majority class.
Self-reported confidence isn't a validated measure of correctness and doesn't show whether urgent claims are being missed.
Latency matters operationally, but it says nothing about whether urgent claims are detected at all.

questions.stem: An e-learning company is adding a streaming tutor chat to its web app. Separately, a nightly job generates written progress reports that teachers read the next morning. Product asks the architect for 'one latency target' covering both features. Which metric choice is BEST?
options: For the chat, mean total response time across all conversations; for the nightly reports, p99 time to first token on each individual request in the batch, reported per teacher.
A single mean end-to-end latency target applied to both features, so that the team has one number and one dashboard to watch.
For both features, the model's output tokens per second, since faster generation improves every kind of workload.
For the chat, p95 time to first token; for the nightly reports, completion of the whole job within the delivery window, with per-request latency treated as secondary.
explanations: This is backwards. A streaming chat should track time to first token, and nobody is waiting on each request of an overnight job.
The two features have different latency needs. A mean also hides the slow tail that users notice in chat.
Generation speed is one input to latency, not a user-facing target. It ignores time to first token for chat and the job deadline for reports.
Correct. With streaming, the user's experience is driven by time to first token, and a percentile captures the tail. For an overnight job, what matters is finishing before teachers need the reports.

questions.stem: A travel company's booking agent will change customers' reservations with no human in the loop. In evaluation, every task runs for 3 independent trials. On one important task the agent succeeds in about 80% of trials. The product lead reports 'pass@3 is 99% on this task, so it's ready.' Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: pass@3 is the right release metric here because a customer who hits a failure can simply ask the agent again, so a 99% figure shows the agent is ready for unattended use.
The per-trial success rate doesn't matter once pass@3 is high, so report pass@3 and use it as the release gate.
Run more trials until pass@k reaches 100%, which will prove that the agent handles this task reliably.
Use pass^3, the chance that all three trials succeed: about 51% at 80% per trial. Each customer gets one attempt, so consistency is what has to be measured.
explanations: pass@k counts a task as solved if any one of k attempts works. That suits tools where one success is enough, not an unattended agent acting on each customer's booking.
The per-trial rate is exactly what each customer experiences. Gating on pass@3 would ship an agent that fails about one booking in five.
pass@k rises with k by construction, so a high value proves nothing about reliability on any single attempt.
Correct. 0.8³ ≈ 0.51. pass^k captures the consistency a customer-facing agent needs, while pass@3 (1 − 0.2³ ≈ 99%) hides a 1-in-5 failure rate per attempt.

questions.stem: A logistics SaaS vendor's agent reads inbound supplier emails and can call tools that update shipment records and issue credit notes. The security lead asks which security metrics belong in the release criteria. Which TWO are BEST? Select TWO.
options: Overall refusal rate on normal, legitimate supplier emails, on the basis that a model that refuses more often is less likely to be manipulated by an attacker into misusing its tools.
Attack success rate on a maintained set of prompt-injection emails, with instructions hidden in bodies and attachments, run in a sandbox on every release.
Number of tokens in the system prompt's security section, as a proxy for how thoroughly the rules are specified.
Rate of tool calls outside the agent's permitted scope, such as credit notes above its authorised limit, across the sandboxed suite, with a target of zero.
Satisfaction score from suppliers who receive the agent's automated replies.
explanations: A higher refusal rate on legitimate email is a usability cost, not evidence of security. It doesn't measure whether attacks succeed.
Correct. It measures the outcome that matters (does injected content steer the agent?) on a maintained adversarial set, run repeatably on every release.
Prompt length is an input proxy. It says nothing about whether the agent resists attacks.
Correct. Out-of-scope actions are the actual harm, so measuring them in a sandbox against a zero target tests the agent's permission boundaries directly.
Satisfaction is a business metric that is blind to whether an attacker has manipulated the agent.

questions.stem: A public-sector agency wants a Claude-based service that extracts data from benefit application forms. The programme director sets the target at '100% accuracy, no exceptions.' Manual keying today has a measured field error rate of about 2%. What should the architect do FIRST?
options: Accept the target and plan to reach it by moving to the most capable model at its highest effort setting and adding more detailed extraction instructions to the prompt.
Agree to the 100% target in the project charter and add a disclaimer that production results may vary.
Decline the project, because no LLM-based system can ever be guaranteed to meet a 100% accuracy requirement, and recommend that the agency keeps keying forms manually until the technology matures.
Measure a prototype's field-level accuracy on a labelled sample, agree targets anchored to that baseline and to manual keying, and send records that fail validation to human review.
explanations: This commits to a target that nobody has measured or shown to be achievable. A bigger model and more instructions don't guarantee 100%.
Signing up to a target you expect to miss sets the stakeholder relationship up to fail and leaves no measurable gate.
The business problem is valid. Manual keying isn't perfect either, so the right move is to set evidence-based targets with review, not to refuse.
Correct. Achievable criteria are anchored to measured baselines and the human comparison. Designing human review for the residual errors handles the 'no exceptions' concern at the process level.

questions.stem: A law firm's research assistant answers lawyers' questions from the firm's precedent library and cites passages. The team scores it with ROUGE-L against reference answers written by associates. After a prompt change the score rose 6 points, yet partners say the answers have become less trustworthy. Which TWO metrics should the architect add to the success criteria? Select TWO.
options: A higher ROUGE-L threshold, so that future prompt changes have to beat the reference answers by a wider margin.
Citation support rate: the share of claims whose cited passage actually supports them, graded against the source text.
Average answer length, since longer answers give lawyers more material to review.
BLEU against the same associate-written reference answers, to confirm the ROUGE-L gain with a second, independent overlap metric before the change is rolled out to all lawyers.
Answer correctness on a partner-written rubric, graded by an LLM judge that has been calibrated against partner verdicts on a sample.
explanations: The overlap metric is the problem. It rewards matching associate wording, not being right or well grounded.
Correct. For a legal tool, groundedness is the relevant criterion. It directly measures whether citations back the claims.
Length isn't quality and can hide unsupported content. It also raises cost and reading time.
A second overlap metric repeats the same blind spot and won't explain why partners distrust the answers.
Correct. Expert-defined correctness, graded at scale by a judge validated against partners, captures what the stakeholders actually care about.

questions.stem: A pharmacy chain's assistant drafts replies to customer questions. On the eval, prompt A scores 93% correct and prompt B scores 91%. Reviewing the failures shows that A's errors include 12 cases of wrong dosage-timing advice, while B's errors are almost all over-cautious 'please ask your pharmacist' replies. The team can't agree which to ship. What should the success criteria have contained to settle this?
options: A higher overall accuracy bar, such as 95% on the same eval set, so that neither version would have qualified and the team would keep iterating on the prompt until one of them cleared it.
Defined error-severity classes, such as 'unsafe advice' and 'unhelpful but safe', with a near-zero threshold for the severe class alongside the accuracy target.
A tie-break rule that the version with higher overall accuracy wins, so decisions stay objective and fast whenever the team disagrees.
A tone criterion graded on a Likert scale, so that cautious replies are penalised less than curt ones.
explanations: Raising the bar postpones the decision without capturing the real difference between the two versions, which is how harmful their errors are.
Correct. Multidimensional criteria that weight error severity separately (with both classes clearly defined) make B's safe failures acceptable and A's unsafe ones disqualifying.
This would ship A, the version making unsafe errors, because overall accuracy treats every error as equal.
Tone isn't the issue. Wrong dosage timing is a safety failure, whatever the tone.

questions.stem: At a fintech, every candidate prompt for a transaction-dispute assistant is graded by two compliance analysts who hand-score the same 40 examples. Each iteration takes two days. Engineering wants to iterate several times a day without losing the analysts' judgement. Which change BEST fits Anthropic's evaluation guidance?
options: Keep the 40 hand-graded examples but have one analyst score them instead of two, which halves the turnaround for each prompt iteration.
Stop running pre-release evals and ship each prompt change directly to production, using the weekly volume of customer disputes escalated to a human as the quality signal instead.
Have the model that wrote each answer rate it from 1 to 10 in the same request, and keep the analysts for final sign-off only.
Grow the set to several hundred cases from real disputes, grade them with code checks plus a rubric-based LLM judge, and have the analysts score a sample to confirm the judge agrees with them.
explanations: This saves a day but keeps a tiny, slow, human-only eval. It also drops the second rater who checks consistency.
