Production signals are reactive and sparse. Customers would find regressions before the team did.
Self-grading in the same request is a weak, biased grader. Anthropic suggests grading with a different model from the one that produced the output.
Correct. Anthropic favours more automatically graded cases over a few hand-graded ones. Analysts are best used to calibrate the LLM judge rather than to grade every run.

questions.stem: An airline's support assistant must (1) state the correct refund amount from the fare rules, (2) keep an empathetic, professional tone with upset customers, and (3) never reveal another passenger's booking details. The architect is choosing a grader for each criterion. Which THREE choices are BEST? Select THREE.
options: Refund amount: ROUGE-L overlap between the reply and a reference reply written by an experienced agent.
Refund amount: a code-based check comparing the amount in the reply with the value computed from the fare rules for that case.
Tone: human graders score every output on every run, because tone is subjective.
Tone: an LLM grader with a detailed 1–5 rubric that reasons before scoring, preferably a different model from the generator, spot-checked against human ratings.
Leakage: in the same conversation, ask the assistant to review whether its last answer revealed anything it shouldn't have, and treat a 'no' as a pass for that test case.
Leakage: an LLM binary classifier that flags any reply containing another passenger's details, run over test cases with both direct and indirect extraction attempts.
explanations: An overlap metric can score a wrong amount highly if the surrounding wording matches. The amount has an exact right answer, so check it exactly.
Correct. When a criterion has a deterministic right answer, code-based grading is the fastest and most reliable option.
Human grading is slow and expensive. Use it to calibrate an automated grader, not to score every run.
Correct. LLM grading suits nuanced judgements. A detailed rubric, an empirical scale, reasoning before the score and human calibration make it reliable.
Self-review in the same context is unreliable and biased toward confirming its own output.
Correct. A binary LLM classifier can catch subtle or implied disclosures that pattern rules miss, and the test set covers the hard cases.

questions.stem: A telecom's support agent should hand the conversation to a human when a customer asks to cancel or mentions a legal complaint. Every case in the eval set is one where escalation is required, and the agent scores 100%. In production it also escalates many routine billing questions. What is the BEST fix to the eval?
options: Add cases where escalation should not happen, such as routine billing and plan questions, so the eval measures both under- and over-escalation.
Remove the escalation tool and route all cancellations through a fixed menu instead.
Add the instruction 'only escalate when it is really necessary' to the system prompt, then re-run the current eval set to confirm the agent still scores 100% on it.
Raise the pass threshold so that the agent must escalate earlier in the conversation in the existing cases.
explanations: Correct. Balanced sets test when a behaviour should and shouldn't happen. A suite with only positive cases can't detect over-triggering.
This removes a capability the business needs instead of fixing how it is measured.
A prompt tweak may help, but without negative cases the eval can't tell whether it worked or broke the required escalations.
This tightens the same one-sided test and would reward even more eager escalation.

questions.stem: An HR SaaS company's agent eval suite has scored 99–100% for four months. Leadership now wants the agent to handle multi-country payroll queries, which it currently handles poorly. An engineer proposes deleting the existing suite because 'it no longer tells us anything.' What should the architect recommend?
options: Make the existing tasks harder by adding stricter formatting and wording checks to the graders, so the overall score falls back into a range where it shows improvement.
Keep the saturated suite as a regression suite run on every change, and build a separate payroll capability suite that starts at a low pass rate so progress is visible.
Keep the existing tasks unchanged, add the payroll tasks to the same suite, and report one combined pass rate for the agent.
Delete the suite and replace it with payroll tasks, because a suite scoring 100% provides no information.
explanations: Arbitrary grader strictness makes the eval brittle and penalises valid outputs. It manufactures difficulty instead of measuring the new capability.
Correct. A saturated eval still guards against backsliding. New capabilities need their own suite with headroom, a hill to climb.
A combined rate dilutes the payroll signal and blurs regression and capability tracking.
Deleting the suite discards protection against regressions on behaviour the business already relies on.

questions.stem: A hotel group's booking agent is evaluated by an LLM grader that reads the agent's final message and passes the trial if it says the booking was confirmed. The eval pass rate is 96%, but the front desk keeps finding stays that customers were told were booked but that don't exist in the property system. Which change BEST fixes the evaluation?
options: Require the agent to call its tools in a fixed sequence, and fail any trial that departs from it.
Tighten the LLM grader's rubric so that it requires the final confirmation message to include a booking reference number in the expected format and the correct stay dates.
Grade the outcome: after each trial, query the test environment's reservation system and pass only if the expected booking exists with the right details.
Run each task more times and report pass@k so that occasional failures don't distort the overall score.
explanations: Checking a fixed path is brittle and punishes valid alternative approaches. It still doesn't confirm that a booking exists.
The agent can still claim a reference number that doesn't exist. The grader is still checking words, not the result.
Correct. Grade what the agent produced (the end state of the environment), not what it says it did.
pass@k makes things look better while hiding the failures. More trials don't fix a grader that measures the wrong thing.

questions.stem: A SaaS company compares two support-reply prompts on the same 150-question eval. Prompt B scores 86% and prompt A scores 84%. The product manager wants to announce that B is better and ship it this week. What should the architect do?
options: Ship B, because it scored higher on exactly the same questions and the eval set was drawn from production traffic.
Re-run both prompts once more on the same questions and ship whichever one wins the second run.

Report the paired difference on the 150 questions with its standard error and confidence interval. If the interval includes zero, enlarge the set (sized with a power analysis) or resample before deciding.
Score B on a fresh, larger set of different questions while keeping A's original 84%, so the comparison isn't biased by B having been tuned on the first 150 questions and having seen them repeatedly.
explanations: At about 85% on 150 items, each score has a standard error of roughly 3 points, so a 2-point gap may well be noise.
One more noisy run is still noise. 'Best of two' doesn't give you a confidence statement.
Correct. Treat eval scores as estimates. A paired analysis on shared questions removes question-difficulty variance, and power analysis tells you how many items you need to detect a 2-point effect.
Comparing scores from different question sets throws away the pairing and adds set-difficulty variance, so the comparison gets less reliable, not more.

questions.stem: A legal-tech firm's eval has 400 questions: 10 questions about each of 40 contracts. A new retrieval setting raises accuracy from 71% to 75%, and a paired standard error that treats all 400 questions as independent says the gain is significant. A reviewer isn't convinced. What is the MOST likely flaw in the analysis?
options: 400 questions is too many: a large sample makes the standard error artificially small and overstates significance, so the eval should be cut back to around 100 questions.
Accuracy is the wrong metric for a retrieval change; the team should report ROUGE-L against reference answers instead.
Questions about the same contract are correlated, so the standard error should be clustered by contract. It can be much larger, and the gain may not be significant.
The new setting should have been tested on a different set of contracts to avoid bias carried over from the old configuration.
explanations: More independent data gives an honest, smaller error. The problem here is that the data isn't independent, not that there is too much of it.
Changing the metric doesn't fix the statistical flaw, and an overlap metric is weaker evidence of correctness.

Correct. Cluster standard errors on the unit of randomisation. Anthropic reports clustered errors on popular evals can be more than three times the naive ones, which turns false 'wins' into non-results.
Testing on different contracts would remove the paired comparison and add variance. The flaw is in how the errors are computed.

questions.stem: A retailer evaluates its product-description generator on 200 items with an LLM grader. Re-running the same prompt with no changes moves the score anywhere between 78% and 83%, so the team can't tell whether small prompt edits help. Which change BEST reduces this noise?
options: Ask the grader for a longer free-text critique of each description before its verdict, so that its judgements are more detailed and therefore more stable from run to run.
Drop the items whose scores change between runs and keep only items that always pass or always fail.
Run several trials per item for each prompt version, average the per-item scores, and compare the versions on the same items.
Compare each new prompt against the best score the current prompt has ever reached, rather than its average.
explanations: Asking the grader to reason before its verdict can improve grading accuracy, but it doesn't remove the main noise source: sampling variance in the generated descriptions, scored once per item across only 200 items.
Removing hard, variable items biases the eval toward easy cases and hides exactly where prompt changes matter.
Correct. Resampling and averaging per item shrinks within-item variance, and comparing on the same items (paired) removes between-item variance.
Comparing against a lucky maximum is biased against every new version and makes the noise worse.

questions.stem: An online education platform is A/B testing a new tutoring prompt in production. Each incoming request is randomly assigned to prompt A or B, so a student can see both within one session. An analyst checks the dashboard daily and plans to stop the test as soon as B's lesson-completion rate is ahead. Which TWO changes BEST fix the design? Select TWO.
options: Give variant B the more capable model tier and a higher effort setting so that any difference between the variants becomes large enough to detect within a few days.
Randomise by student (or by conversation) so that each student consistently gets one variant and outcomes can be attributed to it.
Serve variant A during the day and variant B at night, so the two variants never interfere with each other.
Replace lesson-completion rate with average response length, which moves faster and needs fewer samples.
Fix the primary metric, guardrail metrics and required sample size before starting, and decide when that sample is reached instead of stopping when B first leads.
explanations: This confounds the prompt with the model, so the test no longer measures the prompt change.
Correct. Lesson completion is a per-student outcome. Mixing variants within a session contaminates it.
Time of day becomes a confounder, because day and night students differ.
Response length isn't the business outcome. A metric that moves fast but is irrelevant can't justify a decision.
Correct. Stopping the first time B leads inflates false positives. Pre-registered metrics and sample size make the result trustworthy.

questions.stem: A media company's summarisation team changed the prompt wording, switched to a different model tier and raised the effort level, all in the same release. Eval scores dropped 5 points and nobody can say why. Which practice would have prevented this confusion?
options: Wait for a full quarter of production data before making any further changes to the summarisation pipeline.
Use the most capable model tier for every experiment so that model choice can never be the cause of a regression.
Change one variable at a time against a versioned baseline and re-run the eval after each change.
Ask the model to explain which of the three changes made its summaries worse.
explanations: Waiting slows iteration and still wouldn't separate three simultaneous changes.
This fixes one variable by over-spending, and it doesn't separate the prompt and effort effects.
Correct. Isolating each change against a versioned baseline shows which one caused the drop, and lets you roll back just that change.
The model can't reliably attribute its own regressions. Attribution needs controlled experiments.

questions.stem: A government benefits agency iterated its eligibility-explanation prompt 30 times against the same 120-case eval set and reached 98%. After launch, caseworkers judge quality to be closer to 85%. What should the architect change in the iteration process?
options: Stop using offline evals and rely on structured caseworker feedback instead, because this eval has now been shown not to predict production quality for this service.
Keep iterating on the 120 cases until the score reaches 100%, then relaunch with the improved prompt.
Raise the effort setting so that the model generalises better to cases it hasn't seen in the eval.
Keep a held-out test set that isn't used during tuning, refresh both sets with new cases from production failures, and gate releases on the held-out score.
explanations: Feedback is sparse and reactive. The fix is a better eval process, not dropping evals.
This overfits further to the same 120 cases. The gap with production would likely grow.
Effort doesn't fix overfitting in the prompt or an unrepresentative eval set.
Correct. After 30 rounds of tuning on one set, its score no longer predicts unseen cases. A held-out set gives an honest estimate, and production failures keep the data representative.

questions.stem: A bank adds 25 tasks to its agent eval to cover a new account-reconciliation feature. Across 10 trials each, six of the tasks score 0% while the rest pass most of the time. An engineer starts rewriting the system prompt to fix those six. What should happen FIRST?
options: Read the failing transcripts and check the six tasks and their graders for ambiguity or bugs; 0% across many trials often signals a broken task.
Remove the six tasks from the suite so that they stop pulling down the overall pass rate.
Rerun the six tasks on a more capable model tier and compare the results with the current model.
Increase to 50 trials per task so that the 0% estimate becomes statistically reliable before anyone spends time investigating or changing the prompt.
explanations: Correct. With frontier models, a 0% pass rate across many trials usually means the task is unclear or the grader rejects valid answers. Reading transcripts shows whether a failure is fair before anyone changes the prompt.
Removing tasks before understanding them can hide a real gap in a feature the bank needs.
If the task or grader is broken, a stronger model will also score 0%, and the money is wasted.
More trials will confirm the 0% but won't explain it.

questions.stem: A ride-hailing company needs a driver-support assistant that responds in under 2 seconds. The team started with the smallest model tier and a heavily shortened prompt. Quality is poor, and they can't tell whether the task is achievable at all. What does Anthropic's guidance suggest?
options: Keep the smallest tier and keep adding few-shot examples and stricter instructions until quality improves, since the 2-second latency is the hard requirement here.
First build a prompt that works well without model or latency limits to see what top performance looks like, then apply latency reductions and measure the trade-off.
Set a low max_tokens value so that responses come back faster, then assess quality afterwards.
Drop the latency requirement, because users always care more about answer quality than about speed.
explanations: Without a quality ceiling the team can't tell whether the tier, the prompt or the task is the limit. Long few-shot blocks also add latency.
Correct. Anthropic advises engineering for quality first, then reducing latency (smaller tier, shorter prompts and outputs, streaming). Optimising too early can hide what is achievable.
max_tokens is a blunt cap that cuts responses off mid-output. It isn't a quality-preserving latency fix.
Latency is a real business constraint. The task is to find the best trade-off, not to drop the requirement.

questions.stem: A retail group runs Claude workloads for marketing, customer service and analytics, each in its own workspace in one Claude Console organisation. Finance wants a monthly cost breakdown by department. Which approach is BEST?
options: Ask each department to download its own invoice from the Console and add the totals together in a spreadsheet.
Have each application add up output_tokens from its own responses each month and multiply the total by the published list price for the model it calls.
Query org cost data through the Admin API cost report (or the Usage and Cost Analytics API) with an admin credential, grouped by workspace.
Call the cost report endpoint with each department's workspace API key, so that each key returns only that department's spend.
explanations: Billing is at the organisation level. Per-department totals come from grouping cost data by workspace, not from separate invoices.
This ignores input, cache and server-tool costs and drifts from billing. Anthropic's cost reporting exists so you can reconcile with what is actually billed.
Correct. Org cost data can be grouped by workspace for chargeback, and the endpoints need an admin-level credential.
The usage and cost endpoints need an Admin API credential. Workspace API keys don't work for them.

questions.stem: A SaaS company wants to be alerted within about 15 minutes when Claude spend on any API key spikes unexpectedly, for example because an agent is stuck in a loop. Org usage is reported through Anthropic's Admin API. Which design BEST meets the requirement?
options: Poll the usage report in 1-minute or 1-hour buckets grouped by API key, estimate cost from tokens, alert on deviations, and reconcile with the daily cost report.
Wait for the monthly invoice, because the API reports cost only after the billing period has closed.
Request the cost report endpoint with 1-minute buckets grouped by API key, and alert when any bucket exceeds that key's threshold.
Log every request's full prompt and response to a data warehouse and run a nightly query that estimates the cost for each API key from the logged text and token counts.
explanations: Correct. The usage endpoint supports 1m, 1h and 1d buckets with grouping by API key, and data typically appears within about 5 minutes, which is enough for near-real-time alerting. The daily cost report is for reconciliation.
Usage and cost data are available through the API well before invoicing. Waiting a month defeats the purpose.
The cost report only supports daily (1d) buckets, so it can't drive a 15-minute alert.
A nightly job misses the 15-minute target, and logging full content adds privacy risk that cost monitoring doesn't need.

questions.stem: A software consultancy is rolling out Claude Code to 300 developers and wants organisation-wide token and cost metrics in its OpenTelemetry collector. The security team requires that prompt text is never exported. Which TWO actions are BEST? Select TWO.
options: Commit the telemetry variables to each repository's .claude/settings.json so they apply to every developer who clones it.
Set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1, the exporter variables and the OTLP endpoint in the env block of the managed settings file.
Set OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 and strip prompt text out in the collector before it reaches storage.
Leave OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS unset, because prompt content is redacted by default.
Ask every developer to export the telemetry variables in their own shell profile, and confirm compliance each quarter through a short internal survey.
explanations: Claude Code ignores OpenTelemetry exporter variables in a repository's .claude/settings.json, so this doesn't enable export.
Correct. Managed settings apply the env block to every user, which makes telemetry org-wide and centrally controlled.
This exports prompts first and relies on a downstream scrubber, which breaks the requirement that prompt text is never exported.
Correct. Prompt text is redacted unless OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1, so the default already meets the security requirement.
Developers can change shell profiles at will, and a survey isn't enforcement or evidence.

questions.stem: A healthcare-scheduling company's agent makes 5–20 model and tool calls per patient request. Its logs record each API call separately, with nothing linking them, and engineers spend hours reconstructing why a request ended in the wrong appointment. Which change BEST addresses this?
options: Give every user request a trace ID that is attached to each model and tool call, recording tool names, inputs and results (PHI redacted), stop_reason, and tokens and latency per step.
Log only the final response for each request, because that is what the patient actually sees.
Extend log retention from 30 days to one year and index every call by timestamp, so that more historical calls are available and searchable when incidents are investigated.
Add a dashboard of hourly average latency and error rate across all calls the agent makes.
explanations: Correct. A per-request trace turns scattered calls into a replayable transcript, so engineers can find the failing step. Redaction keeps PHI out of the logs.
The final response hides the step where the agent went wrong, such as a bad tool result or a wrong argument.
Longer retention keeps more unlinked fragments. The investigation is still slow.
Aggregate latency and error rates won't explain why a specific request produced the wrong appointment, which usually still returns 200.

questions.stem: An insurance broker's quote-explanation assistant has had no prompt or model changes for three months. Over the last month, complaints about wrong explanations have doubled, while error rates and latency are flat. The business recently began selling pet insurance through the same channel. Which TWO monitoring changes would MOST directly surface this kind of problem early? Select TWO.
options: Alert when HTTP 5xx rates exceed 1%, since quality problems usually show up as server errors.
Track the distribution of request categories (product line and intent) over time, and alert when the mix shifts beyond a set threshold.
Track daily total token spend, on the basis that a quality problem will show up as higher costs.
Score sampled production conversations with the rubric-based grader and report the results per category, so a drop in one segment is visible even when the overall average looks stable.
Keep the full text of every conversation indefinitely so that analysts can search it later for problems.
explanations: Wrong explanations come back as successful responses, so server-error alerts miss them, as the flat error rate shows.
Correct. A new product line changes the input distribution, which is a classic drift trigger that HTTP metrics never show.
Spend may barely move when quality drops. It is a cost signal, not a quality signal.
Correct. Sampled quality scoring per segment catches degradation that an overall average hides, and the failures feed back into the eval set.
Indefinite full-content retention adds privacy and compliance risk and is reactive. It doesn't raise an alert.

questions.stem: A health insurer's engineers want to send the full prompt and response of every Claude call to a third-party observability platform 'to make debugging easier.' Requests contain members' health information. What should the architect recommend?
options: Log metadata by default (request ID, model, prompt version, tokens, latency, stop_reason, status) and keep content only redacted or sampled, access-controlled, with set retention.
Disable application logging entirely for this service, so that members' health information can never be exposed through the logs or the third-party platform.
Log full prompt and response content, but only for requests that return an HTTP error status, since those are the calls that engineers actually need to debug.
Approve full logging, because the observability vendor encrypts all data at rest and in transit by default.
explanations: Correct. Metadata covers most debugging and cost needs. Redacted or sampled content, under access control and retention limits, minimises exposure of health data.
This removes the signals needed to operate and debug the service, and the architect needs those.
Most quality problems return 200, so this captures the wrong calls and still sends PHI to a third party.
Encryption doesn't address data minimisation, access or retention. Full PHI would sit with a third party by default.

questions.stem: A legal-research SaaS caches a 30,000-token system prompt. After a release, daily input cost rises sharply although traffic is unchanged. Per-request logs show cache_read_input_tokens near zero and cache_creation_input_tokens near 30,000 on most requests. What is the MOST likely cause, and which signal should the dashboard track from now on?
options: Responses became longer after the release, which raises the price of cache creation. Track average output tokens per request.
The model's tokenizer changed in the release, so the same 30,000-token system prompt now produces far more tokens per request. Track total input tokens per request against the previous release.
The release put per-request content, such as a timestamp, into the cached prefix, so each request writes a new entry. Track cache reads as a share of total input tokens per prompt version.
The release shortened the cache lifetime so that entries now expire after every response. Track the TTL configured on each cache breakpoint.
explanations: Output length doesn't affect whether the input prefix is read from cache.
A tokenizer change would raise total tokens, but it wouldn't turn cache reads into cache writes on every request.

Correct. Any change in the prefix (tools, then system, then messages) invalidates the cache from that point on. Reads near zero and writes near the full prompt on every request mean the prefix differs each time.
The default 5-minute lifetime is refreshed on each use. Steady traffic keeps it warm, and an entry doesn't expire after each response.

questions.stem: A US hospital network has HIPAA readiness enabled on its Claude API organisation under a signed BAA. A developer building a discharge-summary extractor uses structured outputs and, to improve matching, generates the JSON schema per request with an `enum` of the patient's full name and the names of their listed caregivers. Prompts and responses are otherwise handled as PHI. What should the architect require?
options: Keep the per-request schema but hash the names inside the `enum`, so the schema no longer contains readable identifiers.
Move the extractor to a separate organisation without HIPAA readiness so that schema caching rules no longer apply to it.
Use a fixed, generic schema with no patient-specific values, and pass the names in the message content instead.
Leave the design as is, since the BAA covers every part of a request sent to a HIPAA-ready organisation, including schemas.
explanations: Hashed names of a specific patient are still patient-specific data in the schema, and the hashing also defeats the matching the developer wanted.
That removes the HIPAA safeguards from a workload that processes PHI; it moves the problem rather than fixing it.
Correct. The docs say compiled schemas are cached separately from message content without the same PHI protections, so PHI must stay out of property names, `enum`, `const` and `pattern` values.
The docs explicitly exclude JSON schema definitions from the protections given to prompts and responses.

questions.stem: An EU insurer plans a Claude-based assistant that reads medical reports attached to claims and recommends whether each claim should go to fast-track payment or manual investigation. The project is in design; no customer data has been processed yet. The data protection officer has not been involved. What should the architect do FIRST on the compliance side?
options: Start a data protection impact assessment with the DPO before any claim data is processed.
Add a system-prompt instruction that the assistant must process health data in line with GDPR.
Build the pilot on production claims so that the DPO can review a working system with real outputs.
Wait for the first data subject complaint, then assess whether the processing was high-risk.
explanations: Correct. Large-scale processing of health data to assess people is high-risk, and GDPR requires the DPIA before the processing starts, which also shapes minimisation, review and retention decisions.
A prompt cannot make processing lawful or assess its risks; it changes nothing about the organisation's obligations.
Processing real health data before assessing the risk is exactly what the DPIA requirement is meant to prevent.
A DPIA is a prior assessment; waiting for complaints inverts the obligation and exposes the insurer.

questions.stem: An HR SaaS platform stores employee chat transcripts with its Claude assistant, chunks and embeds them into a vector index for long-term 'memory', and copies some conversations into an evaluation dataset. When an employee exercised the right to erasure, the platform deleted the transcript rows, but a later audit found the person's details still being retrieved into prompts. What is the BEST fix?
options: Add a retrieval filter that hides chunks whose source transcript no longer exists, leaving the chunks stored until the index is next rebuilt.
Tag every derived copy (chunks, embeddings, eval samples, logs) with a subject key, and run erasure and retention TTLs across all of them.
Add a system-prompt rule telling the assistant to ignore any information about employees who have asked to be forgotten.
Encrypt the vector index and evaluation dataset at rest so the remaining personal data is protected even though it was not removed.
explanations: Hiding is not erasure; the personal data is still held in the index and eval copies.
Correct. The root cause is missing lineage from source to derived stores; a subject key on every copy lets erasure and retention reach all of them.
The data still sits in the stores and still enters the context; a prompt cannot erase anything and may not be followed.
Encryption protects data that you are allowed to keep; it does not satisfy a request to delete it.

questions.stem: A fintech has a Zero Data Retention arrangement for its Claude API organisation, and its legal team requires that no customer content is retained by the model provider. A developer adds an API feature that the published eligibility table marks as not ZDR-eligible, because it stores uploaded files server-side until they are deleted. Integration tests pass and nothing in the API responses signals a problem. What should the architect put in place?
options: An approved-feature allowlist enforced in the app's API gateway, checked against the eligibility table during design review.
Enable HIPAA readiness on the same organisation, because it blocks ineligible features with an error and will catch the problem.
Nothing extra: under ZDR the API rejects any request that uses an ineligible feature, so passing tests confirm compliance.
A nightly job that deletes uploaded files, which brings the feature back inside the ZDR arrangement for future requests.
explanations: Correct. Because ZDR does not block ineligible features, the architect has to control which features the application may use and review them against the eligibility table.
HIPAA readiness is a different arrangement for PHI with a BAA and is permanent once enabled; it is not a feature-linting tool for a fintech.
The docs state the opposite: under ZDR the API does not block ineligible features; using one is a choice to step outside the arrangement for that data.
Your own cleanup schedule is not zero retention; the feature's own retention policy still applied while the files existed.

questions.stem: A lender uses Claude to draft affordability assessments that underwriters approve or amend. The regulator requires that, for any decision, the lender can show what information the AI used and who signed off. Today the app logs only the final text. A proposal is to 'log everything': full prompts and responses kept indefinitely in the application database, readable by all engineers. Which approach BEST meets the requirement?
options: Log per decision the model ID, prompt version, document IDs, tool calls, output and reviewer action, in restricted append-only storage with set retention.
Re-run the original request at temperature 0 when an audit arrives, and use the regenerated output as the record of what happened.
Ask the model to append a short summary of its reasoning to each draft and store that summary as the audit record.
Adopt the proposal, since full prompts and responses kept indefinitely give the most complete record and avoid any later gaps in evidence.
explanations: Correct. It records what was used and who approved it, with references rather than copies where possible, restricted access, and a defined retention.
Outputs are not guaranteed identical on re-run, and models are retired; reproduction is not a record of what actually happened.
A model-written summary is not evidence of the inputs and versions used, and it says nothing about the human sign-off.
Unbounded retention of full personal data with broad access conflicts with minimisation and access control, and makes the logs a new risk.

questions.stem: A telehealth company processes PHI through the Claude API under a BAA with HIPAA readiness enabled. Product wants to connect a third-party SaaS clinical-search service as an MCP server so the agent can send symptom descriptions and patient history to it during a consult. The vendor's marketing site says it is 'healthcare-grade'. What should the architect do?
options: Treat the vendor as a separate processor: due diligence, its own BAA, and only the minimum fields it needs, or host the capability internally.
Connect it, since the BAA with the model provider extends to tools the model calls during a request covered by HIPAA readiness.
Connect it, but add a system-prompt instruction that the agent must never include patient names in calls to the clinical-search tool.
Connect it through a separate workspace of the same organisation so that the vendor's traffic is logically isolated from the other PHI workloads.
explanations: Correct. The docs exclude third-party integrations from Anthropic's data arrangements, so the vendor needs its own review and agreement, and minimisation limits what it receives.
Data processed by external tools or services is explicitly outside HIPAA readiness; the agreement does not extend to them.
A prompt rule is not a control for PHI flowing to an unvetted processor, and history and symptoms are PHI even without names.
Workspace separation inside your own organisation does nothing about PHI leaving to a vendor that has not been assessed.

questions.stem: A European retail bank is launching a Claude-based assistant that drafts replies to customer complaints. The prototype passes the whole customer record (including date of birth, national ID and full transaction history) into every prompt, stores prompts and drafts in an unrestricted analytics table with no expiry, and plans to reuse them for marketing segmentation. Which THREE changes BEST address the bank's GDPR obligations? (Select THREE.)
options: Pass only the fields needed to answer the complaint, enforced by the code that builds the prompt.
Set and enforce a retention period for stored prompts and drafts tied to the complaint-handling purpose.
Add a line to the system prompt instructing the assistant to comply with GDPR when writing replies.
Restrict access to the stored data by role, and log who accesses it.
Keep the marketing reuse, since the customer gave the data to the bank and the complaint log already holds it.
Switch to the most capable model tier so that fewer drafts contain mistakes about the customer.
explanations: Correct. Data minimisation, enforced where the prompt is built.
Correct. Storage limitation needs a defined, enforced retention tied to the purpose.
A prompt line cannot implement minimisation, retention or access control.
Correct. Access control and an access log protect the stored personal data and support accountability.
Reusing complaint data for marketing is a new purpose that needs its own lawful basis; it is not automatically allowed.
Model quality does not address minimisation, retention, purpose limitation or access.

questions.stem: A property-management company uses Claude to summarise rental applications and recommend 'proceed' or 'decline' to leasing agents. A tenant advocacy group alleges that applicants from certain neighbourhoods are declined more often. The application form does not ask for ethnicity. What should the architect do FIRST?
options: Remove the postcode field from the input and announce that the recommender no longer uses location.
Report the overall approval rate, which matches the regional average, to show that the system is fair.
Ask the model to explain each past decline and check whether those explanations mention a neighbourhood.
Build a counterfactual test set where cases differ only in name, postcode or language, and measure the recommendation gap.
explanations: Removing one field without measuring may miss other proxies (names, writing style) and gives no evidence the gap closed.
An overall rate that matches the average can hide large differences between neighbourhoods.
Post-hoc explanations are not reliable evidence of which factors drove the decision.
Correct. Varying only the demographic signals in otherwise identical cases, as in Anthropic's discrimination research, shows whether and where a gap exists before you change anything.

questions.stem: An online furniture retailer launches a support chat with a friendly persona named 'Emma', powered by Claude. Survey comments show many customers believe they are chatting with a human employee, and some share sensitive information on that basis. What should the product team do?
options: Clearly disclose in the chat interface, at least at the start of each session, that users are talking to AI.
Mention in the terms of service that some support conversations may be handled by automated systems.
Rename the persona to 'Emma (Support)' so that it sounds more like a team account than a person.
Tell the persona to reveal that it is an AI only if a customer asks directly whether they are talking to a bot.
explanations: Correct. Anthropic's Usage Policy requires consumer-facing chatbots to disclose they are AI, at minimum at the start of each chat session or in the product interface.
A clause buried in the terms is not a clear disclosure in the conversation itself.
A different label still does not tell users they are talking to AI.
Disclosure on request leaves most users misled; the policy requires proactive disclosure.

questions.stem: A health insurer's claims system uses Claude to recommend whether to deny claims. To hit throughput targets, adjusters see only the recommendation and an 'Approve' button, and approve 99.6% of recommendations in under ten seconds. Members are not told AI was involved. Which TWO changes BEST address the ethical and policy concerns? (Select TWO.)
options: Give adjusters the evidence and criteria behind each recommendation and the authority and time to change or reject it.
Replace the adjuster step with a second model that reviews each recommendation, to reduce cost.
Tell members whose claim decision used an AI recommendation that AI was used to produce it.
Auto-deny only when the model reports confidence above 0.95, and send all remaining recommendations to adjusters for review.
Add a disclaimer to the internal adjuster tool that recommendations may contain errors.
explanations: Correct. The Usage Policy requires a qualified person to meaningfully review high-risk recommendations with authority to modify them; a one-button screen invites rubber-stamping.
A model reviewing a model is not the qualified human review the policy requires for insurance decisions.
Correct. For high-risk uses, people who are the subject of a decision based on an AI recommendation must be clearly told that AI was used.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and auto-denial removes human review from the highest-impact outcome.
An internal disclaimer changes neither the quality of review nor what members are told.

questions.stem: A city government's benefits assistant, built on Claude, scores 94% on its evaluation set, and the programme director wants to announce that it 'works for all residents'. Complaints from Spanish-speaking and Vietnamese-speaking residents report wrong eligibility guidance. The evaluation set was written by the English-speaking project team. What should the architect recommend?
options: Announce the 94% result, since it was measured on a held-out set, and track complaints after launch.
Add Spanish and Vietnamese cases to the eval set, report results per language, and fix gaps before launch.
Add 'answer accurately in the user's language' to the system prompt and re-run the existing evaluation set.
Switch the assistant to answer only in English so that every resident gets the quality the eval measured.
explanations: The 94% only describes English queries; claiming it for all residents is not supported by the evidence.
Correct. Disaggregated evaluation exposes the segments the aggregate hides, and the claim should match what was measured.
Re-running an English-only set cannot show whether the change helped other languages.
Restricting the language excludes the residents who are already poorly served; it removes them rather than fixing the gap.

questions.stem: A recruiting platform uses Claude to score résumés against a role's published criteria for a recruiter to review. Candidates may ask why they were not shortlisted. The current plan is that, when a candidate asks, an engineer sends the résumé back to the model with 'Explain why this candidate scored 4/10'. Which design BEST supports transparent, accurate explanations?
options: Keep the on-request approach but use a more capable model tier so that the generated explanations are more detailed and convincing.
Have the model output, with each score, a per-criterion rating citing résumé evidence; store it and give it to the recruiter.
Return only the numeric score to candidates, since any explanation risks revealing how the screening model works.
Show candidates the model's full raw reasoning text from the original scoring call, unedited, as the explanation.
explanations: A later, separate call produces a fresh rationalisation that may not match what drove the original score; a more persuasive one is worse, not better.
Correct. An explanation produced with the decision, structured by the published criteria and tied to evidence, can be checked by the recruiter and shared with the candidate.
Withholding explanations undermines transparency and leaves candidates no basis to contest an error.
Raw intermediate text is not a reviewed, criteria-based explanation and may confuse or mislead the candidate.

questions.stem: Counterfactual testing of a small-business credit pre-screening assistant shows that applications differing only in the owner's first name receive 'refer to underwriter' scores up to 0.08 lower for one group of names. Underwriters make the final decision. Which TWO actions BEST address the finding? (Select TWO.)
options: Remove the owner's name and other unneeded personal details from the input, and tell the model to score only on the stated criteria.
Add a calibration offset of +0.08 to applications from the affected group of names so that the average scores across groups match exactly.
Run the counterfactual suite as a release gate on every prompt or model change and monitor score gaps in production.
Rely on the underwriters to correct any unfair scores, since they make the final decision anyway.
Switch to the most capable model tier, which can be assumed to be free of name-based bias.
explanations: Correct. Removing an input the decision doesn't need and stating explicit criteria addresses the cause; Anthropic's research found careful prompting reduced discrimination.
A group-based offset treats people differently by inferred demographic, hides the cause and can create new unfairness.
Correct. A regression gate and production monitoring stop the gap from returning silently after later changes.
Underwriters see a biased score and may anchor on it; human review complements a fix but does not remove the bias.
No model tier can be assumed bias-free; the fix must be measured, not assumed.

questions.stem: A legal-tech SaaS company's contract-review tool uses Claude to flag risky clauses. It was evaluated on 200 US software licence agreements with 97% recall on the team's labelled clauses. Marketing wants to tell law firms the tool 'catches 99% of risky clauses in any contract' and to present flags without marking them as AI-generated. What should the architect advise?
options: Use the 99% claim, since recall on licence agreements is close enough and law firms will review outputs anyway.
Re-run the same 200-contract evaluation several times until a 99% result appears, then publish that best figure together with its scope.
Avoid publishing any performance figures, so that customers cannot hold the company to a specific number.
State the measured result with its scope (contract type, sample size), label flags as AI-generated, and link each flag to its clause.
explanations: The claim overstates both the number and the scope; other contract types and jurisdictions were never measured.
Selecting the best of repeated runs misrepresents expected performance and still overstates the scope.
Saying nothing deprives customers of the information they need to rely on the tool appropriately.
Correct. Honest claims match what was measured, and labelled, traceable flags let lawyers judge each one.

questions.stem: A hospital network asks an architect to build a Claude-based assistant that drafts discharge summaries from clinician notes. In the first two workshops only the CIO's office and two physicians took part. The architect wants to avoid a redesign late in the project. Which TWO groups should be added to discovery now? (Select TWO.)
options: The privacy and compliance office, which must approve how patient data is processed, logged and retained.
The model vendor's sales team, who can confirm which model tier will meet the clinical accuracy target.
Nurses and care coordinators who consume discharge summaries downstream and know which omissions cause harm.
A wider panel of physicians from other hospitals, so the assistant reflects every specialty's writing style from day one.
The marketing team, so the launch announcement can be drafted in parallel with the design work.
explanations: Correct. Privacy and compliance approve PHI handling (minimisation, retention, audit, platform and region). Bringing them in late is a classic cause of redesign.
Model fit for this workload comes from a spike on the hospital's own data, not from a vendor's sales claims. The vendor is not a requirements stakeholder.
Correct. The people downstream who rely on the summary define what 'complete' and 'safe' mean, and they supply the edge cases the success criteria must cover.
More physicians repeats a stakeholder group that is already represented and adds style preferences, not missing constraints or approvers.
Launch communications don't shape requirements or constraints, and drafting them before success criteria exist is premature.

questions.stem: A logistics company wants to 'use Claude to decide which shipments get expedited'. In discovery the architect finds that today's decision is a written policy: expedite when the delivery promise is under 48 hours and the carrier's capacity flag is green, with no judgment involved. What should the architect recommend?
options: Fine-tune expectations by running Claude and the policy side by side for a quarter before deciding on the architecture.
An agent with read and write tools for the shipment and carrier systems, so it can reason about each shipment individually and adapt automatically as the expedite policy evolves over time.
A Claude prompt that contains the written policy, with few-shot examples to make sure it applies the 48-hour rule consistently.
Implement the policy as a deterministic rule in code; reserve Claude for any genuinely unstructured part of the process, if one exists.
explanations: A quarter-long side-by-side test spends time proving what the policy already defines. Nothing about the decision needs a model.
An agent adds cost, latency and unpredictability to a decision that has no open-ended steps. Agents are for tasks whose steps can't be predicted in advance.
Asking a model to apply a deterministic rule is less reliable and harder to audit than code that applies it exactly.
Correct. Discovery showed a fixed, fully specified rule. The simplest solution that meets the requirement is code. Use an LLM only where there is real ambiguity.

questions.stem: A retail bank's operations director wants a Claude assistant to help agents answer card-dispute emails and expects it to 'pay for itself within a year'. No one has measured the current process. What should the architect do FIRST to make that goal testable?
options: Estimate token costs for the expected email volume and present them as the business case for funding the project.
Run a two-week pilot with the assistant on live dispute emails and survey the agents at the end about whether they feel faster and would recommend it.
Choose the cheapest model tier so the payback period is as short as possible.
Measure the current baseline (emails per day, handle time, rework or error rate, cost per case) and agree the target improvement.
explanations: Token cost is only one side of the ROI equation. Without the baseline benefit there is nothing to compare it with.
A pilot without a baseline produces subjective impressions, so the payback can't be shown either way.
Choosing a tier before success criteria exist puts the design ahead of discovery, and cheaper tokens don't help if quality causes rework.
Correct. A measured baseline turns 'pays for itself' into a measurable success criterion and lets you compare the pilot with today's process.

questions.stem: An insurer's claims team supplies 25 hand-picked example claims so the architect can scope a Claude-based triage feature. All 25 are clean, single-incident claims with typed forms. Production volume is 4,000 claims a week, many with scanned handwriting, multiple incidents or missing fields. What should the architect do?
options: Proceed with the 25 examples because they represent the intended input format; scanned, multi-incident and incomplete claims can be scoped as a separate later phase once the clean path works.
Ask the claims team to rewrite the messy claims into clean form so the feature can be evaluated on consistent inputs.
Generate several hundred synthetic claims with Claude based on the 25 examples to reach a statistically useful sample size.
Request a random sample of a few hundred recent claims, de-identified as policy requires, including the messy cases and claims that adjusters disagreed on.
explanations: Curated happy-path samples hide the hard part of the problem and inflate feasibility. The messy claims are the production workload, not a later phase.
Cleaning the inputs by hand changes the task being measured. Production won't arrive pre-cleaned.
Synthetic data generated from 25 clean claims inherits their bias. It can supplement real samples, but it can't replace them.
Correct. Success criteria and feasibility have to be measured on data that reflects the real distribution, including edge cases and cases where experts disagree, handled under the data policy.

questions.stem: A SaaS company wants a Claude agent that can issue account credits, change subscription plans and close accounts on behalf of support staff. The architect is preparing the discovery questions that most directly determine the agent's autonomy and controls. Which THREE should be on the list? (Select THREE.)
options: Which of these actions are irreversible or hard to reverse, and what does a wrong action cost the business and the customer?
Which model tier and agent framework the support leadership team would prefer to standardise on.
Above what monetary amount, or for which account types, must a human approve the action before it executes?
What tone of voice the agent should use when it explains plan changes to customers.
Which systems of record hold credits, plans and account status, and what audit trail must each action leave?
How many words the system prompt can contain before it becomes hard to maintain.
explanations: Correct. Reversibility and the cost of errors decide which actions can run autonomously and which need gates.
Model and framework are design decisions the architect makes against measured criteria. Stakeholder preference doesn't set autonomy.
Correct. Approval thresholds define where human-in-the-loop sits, which is a core control requirement.
Tone matters for user experience, but it doesn't determine autonomy or controls for actions that change accounts.
Correct. Systems of record define the tool surface and permissions, and audit needs define what has to be logged for each action.
Prompt length is an implementation detail, not a requirement that governs autonomy.

questions.stem: At a regional tax authority, the operations lead wants Claude to approve routine refund claims automatically, while the compliance lead insists a human reviews every decision. Both positions are firm, and the project is stalled. What should the architect do in discovery to move the decision forward?
options: Side with compliance and design for 100% human review, since regulated decisions should always default to the most conservative option.
Break claims into risk tiers with both leads (amount, flags, claimant history), measure volume and error cost per tier, and propose review rules per tier.
Build the fully automated version as a working demo on last quarter's claims so the compliance lead can see how well it performs before the two leads decide whether human review is needed.
Escalate to the agency head and ask for a ruling on whether automation is allowed before any further discovery.
explanations: Defaulting to full review ignores the operations requirement and may make the system pointless. The disagreement is about risk, which can be quantified.
Correct. Splitting the decision by risk turns opposing positions into a quantified trade-off: automate low-risk tiers, review high-risk ones, with thresholds both sides can accept.
A demo doesn't resolve a disagreement about where risk is acceptable, and building before agreement wastes effort.
Escalating before the trade-off has been quantified hands leadership an all-or-nothing choice without the data needed to make it.

questions.stem: A university's admissions office wants Claude to flag incomplete applications. In discovery, the director says missing a genuinely incomplete application is 'a minor nuisance', but wrongly flagging a complete one delays an offer and has led to formal complaints. How should this finding shape the requirements?
options: Add an instruction to the prompt asking Claude to be cautious about flagging applications.
Record it as a soft preference and keep a single overall accuracy target, since accuracy captures both kinds of error.

Move to the most capable model tier available, because a model with higher overall accuracy will reduce false flags and missed applications by roughly equal amounts, which addresses the director's concern.
State separate targets that weight false positives more heavily (for example a precision floor), and route borderline flags to a human before applicants are contacted.
explanations: A vague prompt instruction isn't a measurable requirement. It might be part of the implementation later, but it isn't how the requirement is captured.
One accuracy number hides the asymmetry. A system can score well overall and still produce the costly false flags.
A bigger model isn't guaranteed to shift the error balance the way the business needs. Requirements should state the target first and measure tiers against it.
Correct. Asymmetric error costs should become explicit metrics and thresholds, with human review where a mistake reaches the applicant.

questions.stem: A legal-services firm wants to commit to clients that a Claude-based clause extractor will reach 98% field-level accuracy, citing a public benchmark where a frontier model scored highly on contract tasks. The firm's contracts include scanned PDFs and bespoke clause wording. What should the architect advise before any target goes into a client agreement?
options: Run a time-boxed feasibility spike on a few hundred labelled firm contracts, measure per-field accuracy, and set the commitment from those results.
Accept the 98% target, since public benchmark results on contract tasks are a reasonable proxy for the firm's documents.
Lower the commitment to 90% as a safety margin below the benchmark and proceed with the design.
Ask the client what accuracy level it actually requires, write that number into the agreement, and then iterate on the prompts and few-shot examples until the extractor reaches it.
explanations: Correct. Achievable targets come from measurements on your own data. A spike shows where the model struggles (scans, bespoke wording) before anything is promised.
Public benchmarks don't reflect this firm's documents, so they aren't evidence that 98% is achievable here.
An arbitrary discount from a benchmark is still guesswork. It could be too optimistic or too pessimistic.
The client's need matters, but committing to a number before testing feasibility risks a promise the system can't keep.

questions.stem: An architect has 10 minutes with a retailer's executive committee to get approval for scaling a Claude-based returns assistant from one region to all regions. Which framing is MOST appropriate for this audience?
options: A walkthrough of the prompt chain, tool schemas and model tier, so executives understand how the system works internally.
Cost per resolved return and resolution time versus the pre-pilot baseline, the measured error rate and its controls, and the projected impact at full volume.
Cost per million input and output tokens for each model tier under consideration, with a month-by-month projection of total token spend once every region is live at the new request volume.
Public benchmark scores showing the chosen model ranks highly, to build confidence that the technology is mature.
explanations: Internal mechanics matter to engineers. Executives deciding on scale need outcomes, cost and risk.
Correct. Business outcomes measured against a baseline, honest residual risk with controls, and the impact at scale put the trade-off in the executives' units.
Token prices are inputs, not outcomes. On their own they don't show value or compare against the current process.
Benchmarks say nothing about this workload's measured results, which is the evidence the committee needs.

questions.stem: A CFO asks why the architect recommends a Sonnet-tier model for invoice exception handling when a Haiku-tier model costs much less per token. On the team's 400-case eval, the Haiku tier resolved 81% of exceptions without human rework and the Sonnet tier 95%; each rework costs about $6 of analyst time. How should the architect explain the recommendation?
options: Explain that more capable models are generally worth the premium for finance workloads because errors are costly.
Agree to switch to the Haiku tier to satisfy the CFO's concern about cost, then monitor rework.
Show the total cost per resolved exception, token cost plus expected rework at each tier's measured failure rate, at projected volume.
Offer to run both tiers side by side in production for a full quarter, so the finance team can see the difference in rework for itself before committing to the more expensive option.
explanations: A general claim without numbers won't persuade a CFO and doesn't show that the premium is justified here.
Switching without analysing the eval evidence the team already has trades a visible saving for a hidden rework cost.
Correct. Comparing cost per completed task, including the human cost of failures, is the right unit. Rework at a 19% failure rate can outweigh the token savings.
A quarter of parallel production running is slow and costly when the existing eval data can already answer the question.

questions.stem: During a review of a Claude-based policy Q&A assistant at a pension fund, the chief compliance officer asks: 'Can you guarantee it will never make up an answer?' The assistant answers from retrieved policy documents with citations, and 3 of 500 eval answers contained an unsupported statement. What is the BEST response?
options: Yes. Grounding answers in retrieved documents with citations eliminates fabrication, so the risk can be recorded as closed.
Explain that the system prompt instructs Claude to answer only from the documents, which prevents it from making up answers.
No. The measured rate is 0.6% on 500 cases; explain the controls (citations, a no-answer path, human review of flagged answers) and how the rate is monitored.
Recommend delaying the launch until the eval shows zero unsupported statements across all 500 cases, since a compliance function needs certainty before it can sign off on a member-facing assistant.
explanations: Grounding and citations reduce hallucinations but don't eliminate them. Claiming a guarantee misleads the compliance officer.
A prompt instruction is a behavioural nudge, not a guarantee, and presenting it as a control overstates its effect.
Correct. Honest residual risk, measured with a stated sample size, plus the controls that limit its impact is what a compliance stakeholder needs to make a decision.
Zero on a finite eval isn't proof of zero in production, and the target is unrealistic. The decision should rest on residual risk plus controls.

questions.stem: A telecom's engineering team pushes for a multi-agent design with an orchestrator and five specialist subagents for order-change requests. The architect chose a fixed prompt chain with a routing step: on the eval it matched the multi-agent prototype's accuracy at lower latency and cost per task, and every request follows one of four known paths. How should the architect communicate the decision to the engineering team?
options: Explain that Anthropic's guidance says multi-agent systems should never be used for production customer workflows.

Approve the multi-agent design to keep the team motivated: both options met the accuracy target, and engineering morale has a measurable effect on delivery speed and on retaining the people who will run the system.
Share the eval comparison and the predictability argument, record the multi-agent option as a rejected alternative in an ADR, and state what evidence would reopen the decision.
Tell the team the decision is final and redirect them to implementation, since revisiting architecture slows delivery.
explanations: Anthropic's guidance favours the simplest solution that works and describes when multi-agent systems help. It doesn't ban them, so this misstates the source.
Choosing the more complex design for morale adds latency, cost and failure modes the eval showed you don't need.
Correct. Evidence plus a recorded decision with a revisit trigger respects the engineers and keeps the reasoning auditable. Known, fixed paths favour a workflow.
Shutting down the discussion without sharing evidence loses buy-in and leaves the reasoning undocumented.

questions.stem: A product owner at an e-learning company asks the architect to 'just pick the best option' for generating course quizzes. There are three viable configurations with different quality, latency and cost profiles. What should the architect bring to the decision meeting?
options: Only the recommended configuration, so the product owner isn't overwhelmed by technical detail.

All three configurations with their full technical specifications (model tier, prompt design, effort, caching), and let the product owner choose freely without a recommendation that might bias the decision.
The configuration with the highest eval score, since quality is the safest choice for an education product.
The three options compared on eval quality, latency and cost per quiz, with a clear recommendation and the reason for it.
explanations: Hiding the alternatives removes the stakeholder's ability to weigh trade-offs they may value differently from the architect.
Options without a recommendation push technical judgment onto the product owner, which is the architect's job.
The highest score may cost more or respond more slowly than the product can afford. Quality alone isn't the decision.
Correct. Quantified options in business-relevant units plus a reasoned recommendation is the standard way to present an architectural trade-off.

questions.stem: Two weeks before go-live, a regional health insurer's Claude-based prior-authorisation summariser scores 88% on the agreed rubric against a contractual target of 93%. The sponsor is under pressure to launch on schedule. What should the architect do?
options: Launch on schedule and keep improving the prompts in production, since an 88% score is close to target and real traffic will provide better data.
Re-grade the eval set with a more lenient rubric so the score reflects what reviewers would actually accept in practice.
Hold the result until the final week before go-live and report it then, in case another round of prompt tuning closes the gap and the problem never needs to be escalated to the sponsor at all.
Raise the gap with the sponsor now, with the failure analysis and options: narrower scope, human review on low-confidence cases, or a revised date.
explanations: Launching below a contractual target without the sponsor's informed decision shifts risk onto members and the business.
Moving the goalposts after the fact undermines the eval and hides the real quality from stakeholders.
Delaying the news removes options and erodes trust if the gap persists.
Correct. Bad news delivered early, with data and concrete options, lets the sponsor make an informed trade-off between scope, controls and timeline.

questions.stem: A bank's security team objects to a Claude agent that connects to an internal MCP server exposing 22 tools, including payment initiation. The agent's use case is answering balance and transaction-history questions. How should the architect address the objection?
options: Explain that Claude models are trained to be helpful, honest and harmless, so having extra tools available carries minimal practical risk as long as the use case itself is a read-only one.
Reassure the team that the system prompt tells Claude never to call payment tools, so the exposure is theoretical.
Propose a scoped tool set with only the read-only tools the use case needs, show the permission matrix and blast radius, and document it.
Offer to log every payment-tool call so the security team can review them after the fact.
explanations: Model safety training doesn't replace least privilege. It doesn't stop a prompt injection or a mistaken call from reaching a payment tool.
Prompt instructions don't enforce permissions. Security teams rightly reject that as a control.
Correct. The objection points to a real root cause, capability bloat. Removing the tools the use case doesn't need, and presenting it in security's terms, fixes it.
After-the-fact logging is a compensating control. It doesn't prevent an unauthorised payment from being initiated.

questions.stem: A media company runs a nightly job that generates 80,000 article summaries with the Messages API. The architect proposes moving it to the Message Batches API and must explain the trade-off to the head of content operations, who is not technical. Which TWO points belong in that explanation? (Select TWO.)
options: Batch processing costs about half as much as the current approach for the same requests.
Summaries will be noticeably higher quality because batch requests use a more capable model.
Results arrive asynchronously, usually within an hour but up to 24 hours, so this suits an overnight job, not anything a user is waiting on.
Batches guarantee that summaries come back in the same order the articles were submitted.
Batches remove the need for any monitoring because failed items are retried automatically until they succeed.
explanations: Correct. The Batches API is priced at a 50% discount, which is the main benefit to communicate.
Batch requests use whatever model you specify. Batching changes cost and timing, not quality.
Correct. The trade-off is immediacy: most batches finish within an hour, but processing can take up to 24 hours, which fits a nightly workload.
Batch results can come back in any order. Requests are matched by `custom_id`.
Individual requests can error or expire, so results still need checking and failures need handling.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company's head of R&D asks the architect to load every study report (about 3,000 documents) into each request 'since Claude has a huge context window', instead of using the retrieval pipeline the team has built. How should the architect respond?
options: Explain the trade-off in measured terms: per-request cost and latency at that context size, retrieval's eval results, and that more context doesn't guarantee better answers.
Explain that the corpus is far larger than any context window, so the request is technically impossible and needs no further discussion.
Agree, since a long context window removes the need for retrieval and simplifies the architecture for this corpus.
Agree to try it on the most capable model available, because a larger model with stronger long-context reasoning will make good use of all 3,000 documents and outperform the retrieval pipeline.
explanations: Correct. Putting the stakeholder's idea in quantified cost, latency and quality terms, backed by eval evidence, is how to communicate the trade-off.
Brushing the idea off without engaging misses the chance to explain the underlying trade-off the stakeholder cares about, which applies even to corpora that would fit.
Even where content fits, stuffing it all in raises cost and latency on every call and can dilute attention. It isn't a free simplification.
A bigger model doesn't fix the cost, latency and relevance trade-offs of putting the whole corpus in context.

questions.stem: Users of an internal HR assistant complain that it 'feels slow', and the product manager asks whether switching to the smallest model tier will fix it. Responses are currently returned only once complete, and the total response time is acceptable to HR. What should the architect explain?
options: Moving to the Message Batches API will reduce wait times because requests are processed in parallel.
Switching to the smallest tier is the only reliable way to make the assistant feel faster, so the team should accept some loss of answer quality as an unavoidable cost of fixing the complaint.
Raising `max_tokens` will make responses arrive sooner because the model won't need to plan for a length limit.
Streaming the response will make it feel faster because text appears as soon as the first tokens are generated, without changing model or quality.
explanations: Batches are asynchronous and can take hours. They're unsuitable for an interactive assistant.
A smaller tier may help raw speed but trades away quality, and it isn't the only option. Streaming targets the perceived-latency complaint directly.
`max_tokens` is a ceiling on output length. Raising it doesn't make responses arrive sooner.
Correct. The complaint is about perceived latency. Streaming reduces time to first visible output while total time and quality stay the same.

questions.stem: A fintech architect reports to the risk committee that a new Claude-based KYC document checker scored 96% on a 50-document eval. The committee plans to approve it for all 20 document types the business handles. The eval covered 6 document types. What should the architect communicate?
options: That 96% is a strong result and the committee can approve all 20 document types, with monitoring after launch.
That the score should be rounded down to 90% as a conservative estimate for all 20 document types.
That the eval's small size and coverage of only 6 types limit what it shows; recommend approval for the tested types and expanding the eval before the rest.
That the model's general capabilities make per-document-type testing unnecessary for standard KYC documents such as passports, utility bills and bank statements.
explanations: Approving untested document types based on a small eval overstates the evidence. Monitoring after launch isn't a substitute for pre-launch evaluation in a regulated process.
An arbitrary discount says nothing about the 14 untested types, which could perform much worse.
Correct. Being explicit about sample size and coverage, and scoping the approval to what was tested, is honest communication of uncertainty.
General capability doesn't replace task-specific evaluation. Different document types have different failure modes.

questions.stem: A government benefits agency's steering committee must choose between routing all eligibility-letter drafting to an Opus-tier model or a Haiku-tier model with escalation of complex cases to the Opus tier. The architect is writing a two-page decision brief. Which THREE items should it contain? (Select THREE.)
options: Each option's pass rate on the agency's own labelled eval set, including the complex-case subset.
The public leaderboard rank of each model, as an independent third-party view of general capability that the committee can trust.
Cost per completed letter at projected volume, including expected human corrections.
The per-token price of each tier, as the primary basis for comparing options.
p95 latency per option and its effect on caseworker workflow.
A statement that both options will produce error-free letters once prompts are tuned.
explanations: Correct. Quality measured on the agency's own data, including the hard subset, is the core evidence.
Leaderboards don't reflect this workload, so they shouldn't drive a steering-committee decision.
Correct. Cost per completed outcome, including rework, is the right unit for comparing the options.
Per-token price alone ignores token volume, escalation rates and rework, so it misleads the comparison.
Correct. Latency in the users' workflow is a real operational trade-off the committee should see.
Promising error-free output is false, and it sets an expectation the system can't meet.

questions.stem: An airline's customer-service team wants a contractual p95 response-time SLA for a Claude-based rebooking assistant. The only data so far comes from about 30 demo calls on an idle staging system, all under 3 seconds. Peak production load is expected at 600 requests per minute. How should the architect set the SLA?
options: Load-test at projected peak with realistic prompts, then set the SLA from the measured distribution with headroom and a defined window.
Take the model provider's typical published output speed, multiply by the expected response length to calculate an expected response time, and commit to that figure plus a small safety margin.
Commit to p95 under 3 seconds, since every demo call met that bar and production hardware will be the same as staging.
Avoid committing to any latency figure, since LLM response times are inherently unpredictable and can't be meaningfully bounded in a contract.
explanations: Correct. SLAs should come from the latency distribution measured under realistic load, with headroom and a clear measurement method.
Generic speed figures ignore your prompt sizes, output lengths, tool calls and load, so they can't support a contractual commitment.
Thirty calls on an idle system don't represent behaviour at peak, so the SLA would rest on an unrepresentative sample.
Latency can be measured and bounded statistically. Refusing to commit to anything fails the stakeholder's legitimate need.

questions.stem: An e-commerce platform's business unit asks for 99.99% availability on a Claude-powered product-description generator used by merchants in its admin portal. The service makes a synchronous call to a single model endpoint and has no fallback path. What should the architect do?
options: Refuse to define any availability target because the upstream dependency is outside the team's control and any number would be misleading to the business unit.
Accept the 99.99% target and rely on SDK retries with exponential backoff to cover transient upstream errors.

Accept the 99.99% target and provision a second API key in the same organisation, so that requests can automatically fail over to the other key whenever the first one returns errors during an incident.
Design degraded modes (queue and notify, merchant-written fallback) and set an SLA that reflects the dependency, with exclusions written down.
explanations: Dependencies outside your control are normal. The answer is to account for them in the target and the design, not to refuse a target.
Retries absorb brief blips but can't deliver availability higher than the single dependency provides during a real incident.
A second key on the same service and organisation doesn't add independent capacity or redundancy against a service-side incident.
Correct. Your SLA can't exceed your dependency's unless you design fallbacks. Pair realistic targets with defined degraded behaviour and exclusions.

questions.stem: A wealth-management firm wants to include a quality commitment in the internal service agreement for a Claude-based meeting-notes summariser used by advisers. Which commitment is BEST?
options: At least 95% of a weekly random sample of 200 summaries pass the agreed rubric under a defined grading method.
Summaries will be accurate and will never omit material client instructions.
The summariser will always use the most capable model tier, guaranteeing the best available quality at any given time.
Every summary will be reviewed and signed off by an adviser before it is filed to the client record, so the quality guarantee rests with the adviser instead of with the system itself.
