explanations: Correct. A quality SLO should be statistical, measurable and tied to a defined rubric, grader and sample, with a feedback loop for misses.
'Never' can't be measured or met by a probabilistic system. It sets an expectation that will be broken.
Committing to a model tier specifies an input, not an outcome. It promises nothing measurable about summary quality.
Mandatory review may be a valid control, but it doesn't define a quality target for the system itself.

questions.stem: A software company's Claude-based in-app help assistant has a thumbs-up/down widget. Over three months it has collected 4,200 thumbs-down ratings with comments, which appear on a dashboard. The answer quality hasn't measurably improved. What is the MOST effective change?
options: Add a line to the system prompt telling Claude that users have been unhappy and it should try harder.
Make the feedback widget more prominent so more users rate their answers and the dashboard has more data.
Triage and label the negative feedback, add representative failures to the regression eval set, fix the causes, and release changes through the eval gate.
Switch to a more capable model tier, since 4,200 negative ratings in three months show clearly that the current model isn't good enough for in-app help and further prompt work won't close the gap.
explanations: A vague exhortation doesn't address specific failure causes and can't be verified.
More data that nobody acts on doesn't improve anything. The loop isn't closed.
Correct. Feedback only improves quality when it is turned into eval cases and fixes that go through a controlled release.
Without triage you don't know whether the failures come from retrieval, missing docs, prompt design or the model, so changing tier is a guess.

questions.stem: Week two of a pilot of a Claude-based contract-redlining assistant at a manufacturing company. The agreed pilot criteria (rubric pass rate at least 90% over 300 sampled outputs, reviewed weekly) are being met at 93%. During a demo, the general counsel sees one badly wrong redline and asks for the pilot to be halted. What should the architect do?
options: Halt the pilot immediately as requested, since the general counsel's confidence in the tool matters more than aggregate metrics and the pilot can resume once the team has investigated the failure.
Triage the case with the general counsel, add it to the eval set, and decide against the agreed thresholds and severity rules.
Add a rule to the system prompt that specifically forbids the type of change seen in the bad redline.
Ignore the incident, since it is a single case and the agreed metrics are within threshold.
explanations: Halting on one anecdote abandons the criteria everyone agreed. If the case is severe, the agreed severity rules should trigger the halt instead.
Correct. Pre-agreed criteria turn an anecdote into a data point: take it seriously, triage it, feed it into the evals, and decide on agreed rules.
Patching the prompt for one example without root-cause analysis or evaluation risks regressions elsewhere.
Dismissing a senior stakeholder's concern damages trust, and the case could be a severe error class the aggregate rate hides.

questions.stem: A public-sector agency is about to start an 8-week pilot of a Claude assistant that drafts responses to freedom-of-information requests. What should the architect agree with stakeholders BEFORE the pilot starts?
options: The list of model tiers to try during the pilot, so stakeholders can compare them informally as they go.
Measurable success and exit criteria, sample size, review cadence and who decides whether to scale, extend or stop.
A commitment that the pilot will scale to full production if users like it.
A launch date for full rollout, so the team has a fixed deadline to work towards throughout the pilot and stakeholders can plan resourcing.
explanations: Informal tier comparisons don't produce a decision. The criteria for judging the pilot have to come first.
Correct. Agreeing criteria, measurement and decision rights in advance keeps expectations aligned and makes the pilot's outcome decidable.
'Users like it' isn't a measurable criterion, and pre-committing to scale defeats the purpose of a pilot.
Fixing the rollout date before the pilot produces evidence sets an expectation that may not be supported.

questions.stem: A travel company's Claude-based trip-planning chat shows a 92% thumbs-up rate among users who rated answers, but only 3% of conversations are rated, and complaints from the corporate-travel segment are rising. Which TWO actions give stakeholders a more reliable view of quality? (Select TWO.)
options: Grade a random sample of production conversations against a rubric each week, not only the rated ones.
Report the 92% thumbs-up rate as the headline quality KPI, since it reflects real user sentiment.
Segment quality metrics by customer segment, intent and prompt version to expose where failures concentrate.
Offer users an incentive to rate more conversations so the thumbs-up rate becomes statistically representative of all users.
Remove the thumbs-down button so negative ratings don't skew the KPI.
explanations: Correct. Random-sample grading removes the self-selection bias of voluntary ratings.
A 3% self-selected sample is biased. The headline number can hide a failing segment.
Correct. Segmenting shows that a failure is concentrated (here, corporate travel) where an aggregate number hides it.
Incentives change who rates and why, adding new bias rather than producing a representative sample.
Suppressing negative signals hides real problems and destroys the feedback loop.

questions.stem: A bank's finance team asks for its Claude-based month-end reconciliation commentary (about 50,000 items) to be 'real-time'. In discovery, the architect learns the commentary is reviewed the next business morning and nobody reads it sooner. What should the architect propose?
options: Build real-time capacity anyway, with a large rate-limit increase, because the stakeholder explicitly asked for real-time processing and changing the requirement risks the relationship.
Agree a next-morning SLA and run the job with the Message Batches API, which costs half as much and returns results within 24 hours.
Process the items with streaming responses so that commentary appears as quickly as possible for every item.
Use the smallest model tier to make real-time processing affordable at month-end volume.
explanations: Building for a stated requirement that discovery shows isn't real wastes money. The expectation should be realigned with evidence.
Correct. Aligning the SLA with the real need makes asynchronous batch processing possible, at a 50% discount and with results within the 24-hour window.
Streaming improves perceived latency for a waiting user. Nobody is waiting here.
Changing tier to afford a requirement that doesn't exist may cost quality for no benefit.

questions.stem: A utility company launches a Claude-based customer assistant on its website. In early sessions many customers ask it to look up their latest bill or remember details from yesterday's chat, which it can't do, and satisfaction scores drop. What is the BEST response?
options: Set expectations in the product: state what the assistant can and can't do, offer escalation for account-specific requests, and track whether those capabilities should be built.
Take the assistant offline until it can handle every kind of request customers send through the website, including account lookups, to avoid any further damage to satisfaction scores.
Switch to a more capable model so it can infer the customer's billing details from the conversation.
Add an instruction to the system prompt telling Claude to pretend it has access to billing data so customers feel helped.
explanations: Correct. The gap is between expectations and capability. In-product disclosure and escalation fix the experience, and the demand data feeds the roadmap.
Waiting for full coverage throws away value the assistant already delivers and isn't a realistic bar.
No model can infer data it has no access to. Billing lookup needs an integration, not a different tier.
Pretending to have data the assistant doesn't have creates fabricated answers and serious trust and compliance problems.

questions.stem: Midway through delivery of a Claude-based English-language support assistant for a hardware retailer, the sales director asks to 'just add French, German and Spanish' before launch next month. What should the architect do?
options: Agree, since Claude handles those languages well and the change is only a matter of adjusting the prompts and retesting the English flows.
Decline the request outright, since any scope change after design approval puts the launch date at risk.
Agree, and translate the existing English eval set automatically after launch to confirm the new languages work.
Treat it as a change request: estimate the impact on evals, cost, latency and timeline, and let the product owner prioritise.
explanations: Multilingual capability doesn't remove the need for language-specific evaluation, content and support processes. The impact is bigger than a prompt tweak.
Declining without analysis ignores what might be a legitimate business need. The owner should weigh the trade-off.
Evaluating after launch means unverified quality reaches customers, and machine-translated evals can miss language-specific failures.
Correct. Running scope changes through change control with a quantified impact keeps expectations aligned and the decision with the owner.

questions.stem: A healthcare SaaS vendor is drafting the service-level section for a Claude-based clinical-note summarisation API that hospital customers will integrate with. Which THREE elements should the section include? (Select THREE.)
options: A latency target stated as a percentile over a defined measurement window, with how it's measured.
A guarantee that the underlying model version will never change for the full duration of the contract term, whatever the provider does.
A quality target measured on sampled outputs against a named rubric, with the grading method.
A commitment that every summary will be free of errors.
Exclusions and defined degraded-mode behaviour when the upstream model service is unavailable.
A fixed number of output tokens per summary regardless of note length.
explanations: Correct. Percentile latency with a window and method is measurable and enforceable.
Models are deprecated and retired on a published lifecycle. The vendor should instead commit to how model changes are evaluated and communicated.
Correct. A statistical quality target with a defined rubric and grader turns 'quality' into something both sides can verify.
Error-free output can't be guaranteed by a probabilistic system. The commitment would be broken.
Correct. Stating exclusions and degraded behaviour sets realistic expectations about the upstream dependency.
Output length should follow the content. A fixed token count isn't a meaningful service level.

questions.stem: A logistics company's architecture repository has an ADR titled 'Model choice' whose entire body is: 'We use a Sonnet-tier model for delivery-exception summaries.' A new tech lead can't tell whether the choice still makes sense. What is the ADR MISSING?
options: The context, the alternatives considered, the evidence behind the choice and its consequences, including when to revisit it.
The full system prompt and every tool schema the summariser uses, so the record is a complete technical specification of the summariser.
A list of everyone who attended the meeting where the model was chosen, with their roles and sign-off dates.
A link to the model provider's marketing announcement for the chosen model, as the source for its capabilities.
explanations: Correct. An ADR records why: context, the options weighed, the evidence, and the trade-offs accepted. That lets a successor judge whether the decision still holds.
Prompts and schemas belong in versioned code. Putting them in the ADR bloats it without explaining why the choice was made.
Attendance doesn't explain the reasoning. A status and date are useful, but the substance is context, alternatives and consequences.
Marketing material isn't evidence for this workload. The ADR should link the team's own eval results.

questions.stem: An insurer's ADR-007 (accepted last year) chose the Claude API directly. The company has now decided to move the workload to Amazon Bedrock to consolidate on its AWS agreement and IAM. How should the architecture record be updated?
options: Edit ADR-007 in place to say Bedrock, so the repository shows only the current state and readers aren't confused by outdated decisions.
Write a new ADR for the move that supersedes ADR-007, and mark ADR-007's status as 'Superseded'.
Delete ADR-007 and write a new ADR, since keeping superseded decisions around clutters the repository.
Add a comment to the platform configuration file noting the change, since infrastructure code is the real source of truth.
explanations: Rewriting an accepted ADR erases the original reasoning and the audit trail of how the decision evolved.
Correct. ADRs are append-only. A new record supersedes the old one, and both stay so the history is traceable.
Deleting history removes the evidence auditors and future maintainers need to understand past choices.
A config comment records what changed, not the reasoning, alternatives or consequences.

questions.stem: An architect is writing the ADR for running a Claude-based underwriting assistant through Amazon Bedrock instead of the Claude API. Which TWO consequences should the ADR record so future teams aren't surprised? (Select TWO.)
options: Model retirement dates for this workload follow Bedrock's own published schedule, which can differ from the dates on Anthropic's deprecations page.
Prompts written for the Claude API must be completely rewritten, because Bedrock uses a different family of Claude models.
Feature availability can differ between platforms, so each feature the design depends on must be confirmed on Bedrock before use.
Bedrock removes the need for an eval suite because the platform provider validates model quality.
Moving to Bedrock automatically satisfies all of the company's data-residency requirements in every region where the underwriting assistant will be offered to brokers.
explanations: Correct. Anthropic's documentation says partner-operated platforms such as Amazon Bedrock set their own retirement schedules. Lifecycle planning must use theirs.
The same Claude models are offered on Bedrock. Integration details change, but prompts don't need a wholesale rewrite.
Correct. Features and their rollout can differ by platform. Recording this in the ADR prompts teams to check before depending on a feature.
Eval responsibility stays with the team. No platform validates your task-specific quality.
Residency depends on the regions and configuration you choose and must be verified. Choosing a platform doesn't satisfy it automatically.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a shared Claude gateway that eight product teams will integrate with. Early adopters copied snippets from chat threads, and now each team logs different fields and handles 429 errors differently. What is the MOST effective implementation guidance?
options: A comprehensive wiki page describing every API parameter and recommended practice, which teams are asked to read before starting.
A mandatory two-day training course for every engineer who will integrate with the gateway, with a certificate to complete.
A maintained reference client that encodes the conventions (config-driven model ID, standard log fields, 429/529 backoff), with examples.
A code-review checklist that the platform team applies to each product team's integration after it has been written.
explanations: Long prose is easy to skip and drifts from reality. It doesn't stop inconsistency at the source.
Training helps understanding, but without shared code each team still reimplements the conventions differently.
Correct. Encoding conventions in runnable shared code fixes the root cause: teams copy what works, and consistency becomes the default.
Reviewing after the fact catches problems late and is a compensating control rather than a fix.

questions.stem: An architect is writing the implementation guide for teams building on a bank's Claude platform, which uses current Claude models. Which THREE practices should the guide prescribe? (Select THREE.)
options: Read the model ID from per-environment configuration and change it through review, evals and a staged rollout.
Set `temperature` to 0 on every request so outputs are deterministic and easier to test.
Log `request_id`, model, prompt version, `usage`, `stop_reason` and latency for every call.
Use structured outputs when a response must match a JSON schema, instead of parsing free text.
Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace to force JSON output.
Disable the SDK's automatic retries so that every 429 and 529 surfaces immediately to the caller.
explanations: Correct. Pinned, configurable model IDs with controlled changes are the basis of lifecycle management.
Current models reject sampling parameters such as `temperature` with a 400 error. Guidance must not prescribe them.
Correct. These fields let teams trace outputs to a configuration, debug with support, and monitor truncation and cost.
Correct. Structured outputs keep responses schema-valid, which is more reliable than parsing free text.
Recent Claude models return a 400 error for a prefilled final assistant turn. Use structured outputs instead.
The SDK retries transient errors with exponential backoff and honours `retry-after`. Disabling that pushes avoidable failures onto users.

questions.stem: A health-tech company's data protection officer must review a Claude-based symptom-triage assistant before launch and asks for 'the architecture documentation'. The team has a component diagram and API docs. What should the architect add to support this review?
options: A data-flow view: sources, redaction steps, the platform and region processing each request, what is logged and retained for how long, tool access and trust boundaries.
A sequence diagram of the retry and backoff logic used when the model API returns errors, including the maximum number of attempts and the timeout at each stage.
The eval results showing the assistant's triage accuracy across every symptom category, broken down by age group and urgency level, so the DPO can see the system is clinically safe.
The system prompt, highlighting the instruction that tells Claude not to retain or share patient data.
explanations: Correct. A privacy review needs to see where personal data goes, how it's minimised, where it's processed, and what's stored and for how long.
Retry logic is an engineering concern. It doesn't describe personal-data processing.
Accuracy matters for clinical safety, but it doesn't answer the DPO's data-protection questions.
A prompt instruction doesn't control retention or data flows. Presenting it as a privacy control misleads the reviewer.

questions.stem: A retail platform team is publishing internal MCP servers that other teams' Claude agents will use. Agents keep calling the wrong order-lookup tool and retry failed calls with the same bad input. What documentation change addresses the root cause?
options: Rewrite tool names and descriptions for the model, with unambiguous parameters, and return actionable error messages.
Add more narrowly scoped order-lookup tools that cover each edge case separately, so the agent always has a precisely matching option and never has to choose between general-purpose tools.
Write a separate developer wiki explaining which tool to use in which situation, for human engineers to read.
Add a line to each agent's system prompt listing all tools in order of preference.
explanations: Correct. Tool descriptions are loaded into the agent's context and steer its behaviour. Actionable errors guide the agent to correct its input instead of repeating it.
More overlapping tools make selection harder. Anthropic's guidance favours fewer, clearer tools.
The agent never reads a human wiki. The confusion is in what the model sees.
A preference list in each consuming agent's prompt is a workaround that every team must duplicate. The tool contract is the root cause.

questions.stem: An auditor reviewing a Claude-based loan-document checker asks why the human-review threshold is set at a confidence score of 0.82. The configuration file has the value, but nobody remembers how it was chosen. What should the architect put in place so this question can be answered in future?
options: Add a code comment next to the threshold in the configuration file explaining that 0.82 was agreed with the risk team in a meeting, so the next person who reads it knows who to ask.
Lower the threshold to 0.5 so more cases go to human review, which is easier to defend to an auditor.
Record the threshold in an ADR that links the eval run, precision and recall at candidate values, and the risk owner's sign-off.
Remove the threshold and send every case to human review until the original reasoning can be reconstructed.
explanations: A comment states who agreed, but not the evidence or the trade-off. Auditors need the reasoning and the data.
Changing the value arbitrarily doesn't solve the documentation gap, and it may overload reviewers.
Correct. Linking the decision to eval evidence and an accountable owner makes the threshold auditable and repeatable when it's revisited.
Reviewing every case is a costly compensating control that avoids rather than fixes the missing record.

questions.stem: An operations team is taking on-call ownership of a Claude-based claims-intake service. The architect is writing the runbook. Which entry is MOST useful?
options: 'If quality seems off, contact the architecture team.'
A general overview of how large language models generate text, so on-call engineers understand the technology.
'If `stop_reason: max_tokens` exceeds 2% for 15 minutes: check the latest deploy, roll back via flag X, then inspect input lengths.'
A copy of the full system prompt and tool definitions so engineers can inspect them during incidents and suggest wording changes to the on-call lead.
explanations: A vague escalation instruction gives no symptom, threshold or action, and it keeps dependency on the original team.
Background knowledge doesn't tell an operator what to do when an alert fires.
Correct. A runbook entry maps a measurable symptom to concrete diagnostic steps and a rollback, which is what on-call needs.
Editing prompts during an incident is risky. The runbook should point to rollback, not ad-hoc prompt changes.

questions.stem: An architect must document a Claude-based document-intake system for three audiences: the executive sponsor, the engineering team and the compliance team. Which approach is BEST?
options: One detailed document containing everything, shared with all three audiences so everyone works from the same source.
Only engineering documentation, with other audiences briefed verbally as needed.
Separate, independently maintained documents for each of the three audiences, each written by a different person so that it matches its readers' vocabulary, level of detail and preferred format.
One architecture model shown in tailored views: context for executives, components and sequences for engineers, data flow and controls for compliance.
explanations: A single exhaustive document buries what each audience needs and is rarely read in full.
Verbal briefings leave no auditable record, which compliance in particular needs.
Independently maintained documents drift and contradict each other over time.
Correct. One consistent model with audience-specific views gives each stakeholder what they need without the views drifting apart.

questions.stem: A software vendor's team ships Claude-based features quickly, but each feature's prompts, eval cases and decisions are scattered across notebooks and chat threads. A new team is about to take over two of the features. What should the architect require as the standard documentation for each feature?
options: Prompts, eval set, rubric and thresholds versioned together in the repo, with a changelog tying prompt versions to eval results and ADRs for key decisions.
A requirement that the original authors stay on call for the new team for six months after handoff, answering questions about prompts, eval cases and design decisions as they come up.
An export of the chat threads in which the features were designed, stored in a shared drive folder.
A slide deck per feature summarising its purpose and the model used, updated at each quarterly review.
explanations: Correct. Versioning prompts with their evals and decisions makes the feature reproducible and safe to change. The eval threshold becomes the definition of done.
Depending on individuals is fragile. Documentation should make the new team self-sufficient.
Raw chat exports are hard to search and mix abandoned ideas with real decisions.
A quarterly deck drifts from reality and doesn't let the new team reproduce or safely change the feature.

questions.stem: A public-sector agency's architect documents the design of a Claude-based correspondence assistant. The design doc says: 'Residency: the system prompt instructs Claude to keep all citizen data within the country.' A reviewer flags this line. What should the documentation say instead?
options: The same instruction, strengthened with capitals and repeated at the end of the system prompt so the model is less likely to ignore it.
A note that data residency is entirely the model provider's responsibility under its terms of service and is therefore out of scope for the agency's own design document and review.
That residency is covered because the system does not store any data permanently.
That residency is enforced by the platform and region chosen for processing and by where logs and outputs are stored, citing the configuration.
explanations: A prompt can't control where processing happens. Emphasis doesn't change that.
Choosing the platform, region and storage is the agency's architectural decision, so it belongs in the design.
Retention and residency are different requirements. Data can be processed out of region even if it isn't stored.
Correct. Residency is a deployment and configuration control. The documentation should state it and point to the configuration that enforces it.

questions.stem: An architecture team built a Claude-based invoice-matching service for a manufacturing group and is handing it over to the group's IT operations team, which will own it from next quarter. Which THREE items should the handoff package include? (Select THREE.)
options: The regression eval suite with its pass thresholds, and instructions for running it before any prompt or model change.
A recommendation to switch to whichever new model is released next, so the service stays current without further evaluation.
Dashboards and alerts (quality sampling, `stop_reason` mix, error rates, cost) with a runbook that maps each alert to an action and a rollback step.
The personal API keys of the engineers who built the service, so operations can keep using them without re-provisioning.
Named owners, version history of prompts and model IDs, known limitations, and a period of joint on-call before full transfer.
A promise that the architecture team will make all future prompt changes on the operations team's behalf.
explanations: Correct. The eval suite and thresholds let the new owners change the system safely.
Upgrading without evaluation is exactly the kind of uncontrolled change a handoff should prevent.
Correct. Operators need visibility and a symptom-to-action runbook to run the service.
Personal credentials should never be handed over. The service needs its own provisioned keys with owners and rotation.
Correct. Ownership, version history, documented limitations and a shadowing period make the transfer real.
Keeping changes with the original team defeats the handoff and leaves operations dependent on it.

questions.stem: A retail bank runs its Claude-based dispute assistant on Amazon Bedrock. A planning spreadsheet uses the retirement dates from Anthropic's model deprecations page to schedule migrations. What should the architect point out?
options: Nothing: retirement dates are identical on every platform where Claude models are offered.
Bedrock sets its own retirement schedule, so the plan must use Bedrock's published dates for the models in use.
Models on Bedrock are never retired, so no migration plan is needed for this workload while it stays on Bedrock.
Bedrock automatically upgrades workloads to the recommended replacement model on the retirement date, so the plan only needs a post-upgrade eval run.
explanations: Anthropic's documentation says its dates apply to Anthropic-operated platforms. Partner-operated platforms can differ.
Correct. Partner-operated platforms such as Amazon Bedrock set their own retirement schedules, so lifecycle planning has to follow the platform actually in use.
Models on partner platforms are retired too, just on that platform's schedule.
Assuming an automatic upgrade risks failures and untested behaviour. The team should plan and evaluate the migration itself.

questions.stem: A SaaS company receives notice that a Claude model it has used for two years is deprecated. Several teams created API keys over that time, and nobody is sure which keys still call that model. Using Anthropic's tooling, what is the quickest way to find out?
options: Export usage from the Usage page in the Claude Console, which breaks usage down by API key and model.
Wait until the retirement date and see which services start returning errors, then fix those.
Ask Anthropic support to send a list of every request your organisation made to the model, with the code locations that sent them.
Rotate all API keys at once so that every team must re-register and declare which models it uses.
explanations: Correct. Anthropic documents a usage export from the Console Usage page, broken down by API key and model, for finding remaining use of deprecated models.
Waiting for failures turns a planned migration into an outage. Requests to retired models fail.
Support doesn't know your code locations, and the self-service usage export already answers the question.
Rotating every key at once causes widespread disruption and still doesn't tell you which model each service uses.

questions.stem: A media monitoring company is migrating a news-classification service to the recommended replacement for its deprecated model. On the regression eval the new model matches quality, but average output tokens per request rose 35% and two old prompt lines ('CRITICAL: you MUST always...') now cause over-cautious labels on a small subset. Retirement is seven weeks away. What should the architect do?
options: Ship the new model to 100% of traffic now, since quality matches, and look at cost after retirement has passed.
Stay on the deprecated model until the retirement date, then switch, so the team can collect more data on the old model first.
Remove the outdated emphatic lines and re-evaluate, review the cost change with stakeholders, then canary with rollback triggers.
Cap `max_tokens` at the old model's average output length so that the new model's cost per request matches the old one exactly, then move all traffic across in one step to finish the migration early.
explanations: Ignoring a 35% output increase surprises the budget owner, and a full cutover with no canary removes the safety net.
Waiting until retirement leaves no time to fix problems, and requests to the old model fail after that date.
Correct. Re-tune the prompts for the new model, make the cost change visible to stakeholders, and release gradually with rollback triggers, all with time to spare.
A hard cap at the old average will truncate longer valid outputs (`stop_reason: max_tokens`), and an all-at-once rollout skips the canary.

questions.stem: A university is retiring a Claude-based course-advising chatbot after replacing it with a new student portal. The chatbot used an API key and an MCP server with read access to student records. Which TWO steps belong in the decommissioning plan? (Select TWO.)
options: Revoke the chatbot's API key and the MCP server's credentials to student records once traffic has stopped.
Keep the MCP server running indefinitely in case a future project wants to reuse the integration.
Apply the university's retention policy to stored conversation logs and outputs, deleting or archiving them as it requires.
Leave the API key active but remove the chatbot from the website, since an unused key carries no risk.
Copy all stored conversations into the new portal's training data so its answers improve.
explanations: Correct. Credentials that outlive the service are an unnecessary access path to sensitive data.
An unowned server with access to student records is a security liability. Rebuild the integration if a future project needs it.
Correct. Stored conversations hold personal data, and retirement is when the retention policy has to be applied.
Unused but active keys can still be leaked and misused. Revoke them.
Reusing personal conversations for a new purpose raises privacy and consent issues and isn't part of a clean decommission.

questions.stem: Six months after launch, a Claude-based HR policy assistant at a logistics firm shows a steady HTTP success rate and stable latency. However, weekly rubric grading of sampled answers dropped from 94% to 86% after HR published a large set of revised policies. No prompt or model change was deployed. What is the BEST next step?
options: Diagnose the failing samples (likely retrieval or index freshness), add them to the eval set, fix the cause, and release through the eval gate.

Switch to a more capable model tier to compensate for the drop: prompts and models weren't changed, so the current model is evidently struggling with the larger and more complex body of revised policies.
Do nothing, since the service is healthy by its error and latency metrics and the rubric is only a sample.
Add an instruction to the system prompt telling Claude to prefer the newest policies when answering questions.
explanations: Correct. The iteration loop is: diagnose from the failing samples, turn them into eval cases, fix the root cause (here probably stale or poorly chunked content), and release through the regression gate.
Changing tier without a diagnosis treats a probable data or retrieval problem as a model problem.
Quality regressions still return HTTP 200. Sampled rubric grading exists to catch exactly this.
If the new policies aren't retrieved correctly, a prompt instruction can't make Claude prefer content it never sees.
